articles.title: NSW government to resume pill testing at music festivals but rejects calls for wider community rollout
articles.excerpt:
Use of sniffer dogs and searches will continue despite health and harm reduction groups arguing they could lead to riskier drug taking

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Dru...
articles.body_text:
Use of sniffer dogs and searches will continue despite health and harm reduction groups arguing they could lead to riskier drug taking

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Drug testing will resume at New South Wales music festivals from October, but will not be rolled out into the wider community despite calls from peak health and harm reduction groups, while the controversial use of sniffer dogs and searches will continue.

On Wednesday the state government announced NSW Health will consult with the music festival industry and harm reduction organisations to roll out pill testing at up to 15 music festivals each year.

There will be no change to the use of sniffer dogs at music festivals, a government spokesperson confirmed, which has been found to prompt risky drug taking. Police, security guards, bag searches and sniffer dogs at music festivals can lead to riskier drug use as people may “pre-load”, or take all of their substances at once, to avoid detection.

Detection of drugs through sniffer dogs has also been used by police to justify strip-searches, which courts and legal experts have found to be unlawful.

The testing rollout follows a 12-month trial which ended in February and which saw 1,480 drug samples tested across 12 NSW music festivals.

The trial was free and anonymous, and meant festival goers could hand over a small sample of substances they intended to use to health staff to test for purity, potency and contaminants.

An independent evaluation led by the University of Sydney, also made public on Wednesday, found people changed their approach to drug taking after getting their drugs tested, particularly when substances differed from what they expected.

Unexpected substances were found in 8% of samples, while high-dose MDMA was found in 4% of MDMA samples where a dose could be calculated. High doses of MDMA increase the risk of organ failure and death, especially in hot environments or when combined with other substances.

A range of unexpected psychoactive substances were detected through the testing, including ketamine analogues (human-made substances which copy ketamine’s chemical makeup, but can produce different and dangerous effects) and heroin.

The University of Sydney evaluation also surveyed people about their views towards pill testing and found “a consistent concern … was the conflict between policing activities (such as drug detection dogs) and access to the service site, which may have dissuaded potential service users from accessing harm reduction services”.

A report from a landmark summit into how to reduce drug-related harms, published in 2025, recommended NSW consider ceasing the use of drug detection dogs and strip-searches at music festivals.

The chief executive of Unharm, Dr Will Tregoning, said the searches need to be scrapped.

“Drug detection dogs are intensive operations that have a track record of clearly contributing to increased overdoses,” he said.

“People see the dogs and take all of their drugs at once out of fear of being detected, and we know police have been strip-searching people at an industrial scale. These searches are also deeply traumatic for people, and affects predominantly young people.”

Ahead of the announcement, peak health and harm reduction groups including the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, the Alcohol and Drug Foundation, and Unharm wrote to NSW’s premier, Chris Minns, and health minister, Ryan Park, on Tuesday calling for pill testing services to be offered in the community.

The ACT and Victoria have both moved beyond festivals to fund community drug checking, where staff provide people with the results along with non-judgmental health and harm reduction advice.

“Drug checking at festivals reaches people who can get to a festival. It cannot reach the people dying at home,” the letter says.

“We ask you to commit to a next phase of drug checking in NSW that includes community-based services, designed for the communities they serve and independently evaluated from the start.”

The letter said that 72% of fatal drug overdoses in Australia happened at home in 2024.

Minns told budget estimates in August that there were no plans to roll out testing to the community.

articles.title: Macquarie University swaps in-person psychology classes with AI chatbot for two subjects
articles.excerpt:
University’s move is part of trend that critics within academia say will lead to further staff cuts and the loss of ‘everything that makes the job worth doing’

An Australian university has swapped in...
articles.body_text:
University’s move is part of trend that critics within academia say will lead to further staff cuts and the loss of ‘everything that makes the job worth doing’

An Australian university has swapped in-person classes with an AI chatbot, online quizzes and optional online tutorials in two subjects as institutions give the technology more teaching responsibilities.

Macquarie University’s “Virtual Peer” is part of each week’s learning in two mandatory Psychology units, programmed to ask students questions and guide them through scenario-based exercises.

The university said the AI activities are optional and only “supplement” the “core learning” of online readings, quizzes and videos.

However, neither the core nor AI activities are mandatory. Students are only assessed on separate research tasks and exams.

Both subjects had in-person classes in the first semester of this year. The university said in-person classes would return in 2027 in alternate semesters so students could pick the format that suits their circumstances.

One student, who asked to remain anonymous, said they felt “short-changed” after issues with their degree structure forced them to enrol in the online option.

Each individual psychology subject costs $2,174 for Australian students with commonwealth supported places in 2026. A three-year undergraduate degree now costs over $50,000.

“Instead of a group discussion or a tutor teaching you, it’s a class activity done with a robot,” the student said. “I feel like I’m teaching this robot how to take jobs away from my teachers.”

Macquarie said the tool was designed in partnership with educators to support, not replace, them.

Professors who use Virtual Peer upload the information it uses and check it, the university says, making it more tailored than general-purpose AI tools. Experts say that could make the tool potentially less prone to “hallucination”, or inventing content without evidence. Macquarie can also monitor student conversations on the service, according to the university.

The subjects still have paid tutors, who run optional Zoom sessions each week. One introductory-level subject has six sessions a week for its 400 students, while the other final-year subject has 10 sessions a week for its 700 students – or roughly one class for every 70 students.

Students who want to speak to a human for feedback are encouraged to attend. Macquarie said attendance at these was variable and rose around assessment due dates.

Virtual Peer was also used for learning activities in other subjects but was not available in all classes, Macquarie said.

Its use has accelerated, answering close to 80,000 student questions in all of 2025 but nearly as many in just the first half of 2026, most of which were administrative questions. The university said staff and students overwhelmingly found the tool valuable or recommended its use when surveyed.

Macquarie has been one of a handful of Australian universities to systematically incorporate AI into teaching, alongside the University of Melbourne and the University of Sydney, as the technology attracts growing student use – and backlash.

Meena Jha, an associate professor at Central Queensland University, said she had not previously heard of any universities simultaneously cutting in-person teaching and introducing AI chatbots in her research into AI in higher education.

“Students require that human touch … [and] engagement will be a very big issue if we replace everything with virtual tutors,” said Jha, who is also the head of CQU’s pedagogy and technology cluster.

CQU is piloting its homegrown AI tool, named “Birdy”, as a “service/support tool” in 24 units. Jha has gone further, building an AI avatar in her likeness, named Neena Chatbot, to answer her students’ questions about subject matter.

“You have to give a bit of time for people to try it, use it, see value in it, and in doing so you need to guide them how they can use it,” Jha said.

The University of Sydney has positioned itself as a leader in the field, with hundreds of academics using its education-focused generative AI platform, “Cogniti,” for chatbots and scenario exercises. It has shared Cogniti with other institutions in Australia, New Zealand and the Netherlands.

The university in late August released a discussion paper that envisions futures where AI takes on even greater responsibilities, delivering personalised teaching for each student in each unit, while staff-student contact hours decline.

A university spokesperson said Sydney was only supporting staff to use technology to improve student experience.

“Human judgement, accountability and relationships are essential to everything we do, and can never be replaced by technology,” the spokesperson said. “This isn’t a cost-saving measure in any way.”

Peter Chen, president of the university’s national tertiary education union (NTEU) branch, said the paper had added to growing staff concern about their future at the university as funding shortfalls left fewer academics to run bigger classes, Chen said.

“For some staff, they’re afraid they’re going to lose their jobs,” Chen said.

“For other staff, the concern is that everything that makes the job worth doing will be lost … and they will be there simply to take the blame when things go wrong.

The university’s staff plan to go on strike on Wednesday, fighting for AI protections and other support against growing workloads and job insecurity. Chen said the union would not accept a deal that did not address AI.

The university said it would continue to engage in bargaining but Wednesday’s strike was “premature”. AI’s rapid evolution meant it should be governed at the university’s discretion through policy, rather than set in a three-year enterprise agreement, its spokesperson said.

But Dr Alison Barnes, national president of the NTEU and a Macquarie academic, said staff across the sector would fight for workplace agreements that address AI.

“University staff are being hammered by a workload crisis, but simply papering over those cracks with piecemeal AI rollouts could actually create even more damaging issues,” Barnes said.

articles.title: House prices head for historic 10% drop as fourth interest rate hike looms
articles.excerpt:
Cotality data reveals property prices are now falling in more than 90% of Australian suburbs, while analysts expect market downturn to continue

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news pod...
articles.body_text:
Cotality data reveals property prices are now falling in more than 90% of Australian suburbs, while analysts expect market downturn to continue

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The prospect of the steepest property market downturn in history will not stop the Reserve Bank from delivering a fourth interest rate hike as it battles to bring inflation back under control, economists say.

New data from Cotality revealed house prices are now falling in more than 90% of Australian suburbs, amid a perfect storm of higher borrowing costs, a weak economy, and a once-in-a-generation change in the tax treatment of property investors.

Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, said average home values would continue falling for the next six to nine months, by which time property prices nationally would be about 10% down from their recent peak.

“That would be the worst in the postwar period,” Oliver said, although the figure is not hugely out of line with previous property market corrections in the order of 8% – most recently in 2022-23.

In response to the evidence of a more rapid and wider decline, CBA analysts predicted an eventual 12-13% drop in Sydney and Melbourne property prices alongside 8% falls in Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide.

Even then, the losses will not put a dent in Australia’s chronically unaffordable housing, Oliver said.

“In some ways this just takes us back to where we were a year ago for many cities across the country. And we were complaining about housing affordability then, so not much will change.”

Michele Bullock, the Reserve Bank’s governor, told reporters at her post-meeting press conference on 11 August that the housing market downturn was “not the main game” when it came to rate decisions, and noted that property prices were still 50% higher than they were in 2020.

Oliver said it was clear it would be a discussion point at upcoming RBA board meetings at the end of this month and in November.

“I think they will think twice but they’ll continue to hike for the simple reason that the bigger problem right here, right now is inflation – and house prices have only just flicked off the top,” Oliver said.

Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, agreed that the weakness in the property market would not be enough to prevent another interest rate hike, which, like Oliver, he believed would come at the meeting in early November.

Kearns, a former senior RBA official, said while the property market correction was coming harder and faster than anticipated, “it’s not large enough for them to say we don’t need to hike”.

Even as inflation remains too high for comfort, some experts warned that national accounts figures on Thursday morning could show the economy barely grew through the three months to June.

Belinda Allen, CBA’s head of Australian economics, said she expected GDP to have expanded by just 0.1% in the most recent quarter, in what would be the weakest growth in two-and-a-half years.

“If these numbers print as expected tomorrow [Thursday] it does show that the Australian economy has slowed, but inflation has not,” Allen said.

“Rolling supply shocks, more Australians spending money domestically than offshore and weaker productivity growth are acting to keep inflation high and the RBA has more work to do.”

articles.title: Inside knowledge or ‘making stuff up’? Charles Perrottet’s advice to Jean Nassif put under microscope by Icac
articles.excerpt:
Brother of former treasurer and premier faces questions about texts that appear to indicate he was aware of fast-tracking policy before it was announced

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily...
articles.body_text:
Brother of former treasurer and premier faces questions about texts that appear to indicate he was aware of fast-tracking policy before it was announced

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Did the former premier’s brother, Charles Perrottet, have prior knowledge of a Covid-era New South Wales government policy to introduce a fast track to approve major developments?

Did he take steps to ensure that developments owned by the fugitive developer, Jean Nassif, were successful through the fast track?

On his third day in the witness box at the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption, Charles Perrottet was asked about meetings and texts that indicated he was aware of the government’s plans well before they were announced.

The Icac is investigating allegations that Charles Perrottet, Jeremy Greenwood and Christian Ellis – all active members of the right faction of the Liberal party – took a $2m payment from Nassif, in breach of the NSW Electoral Funding Act. NSW has had a longstanding ban on political donations from developers.

Nassif had offered to appear on Friday via video link but produced a medical certificate to excuse himself.

Icac is also investigating allegations that Nassif had sought political outcomes including the removal of the NSW Building commissioner, David Chandler, who had issued a number of remediation orders against Nassif’s Toplace buildings and removal of Liberal councillors at Hills Shire council.

There is particular interest in Charles Perrottet, because he was the brother of Dominic Perrottet, the former NSW treasurer and later premier.

Dominic Perrottet is not a person of interest in the Icac inquiry.

Over the last three days, Charles Perrottet has told Icac that he gave general advice to Nassif via a consultancy firm, Beckington.

This included that Nassif should use a new fast-track process established by the NSW government and that Nassif should join the Property Council.

Charles claims he was not paid for his advice and it was not work, but instead the payments were made to his wife, Anita, as a kind of thank you from Beckington for his help.

But Dwyer has begun zeroing in on what else Charles Perrottet might have done to assist Nassif. That includes a meeting between Charles Perrottet and Greenwood and Nassif, on 11 December 2019, at which a payment described as “1%” was discussed.

Charles Perrottet agreed that 1% was a reference to a share of the value of Nassif’s properties that were fast-tracked but was unsure about quite when.

Three developments were mentioned – Mascot, “189”, and “Garthowen”.

Counsel assisting Dr Peggy Dwyer SC read out texts from 11 December 2019 sent from Greenwood’s phone to Ellis.

Greenwood: “The meeting was insane, ha ha ha ha.”

Greenwood: “Yeah, but I’m definitely not putting the contents in the message, ha ha, ha ha.”

As the Covid pandemic brought the NSW economy to a halt in 2020, many industries, including the construction industry, begged the then NSW treasurer, Dominic Perrottet, who was leading the government’s Covid economic strategy, for support.

On 3 April 2020, Dominic Perrottet, and the planning minister, Rob Stokes, jointly announced a new fast-track approval process for construction projects.

The fast track introduced a “one-stop shop” for industry to progress projects that may be “stuck in the system” and fast-track assessments of state significant developments, rezonings and development applications (DAs). A key criterion was whether the projects would create jobs within the next six months. They needed to be well advanced in terms of planning.

The program was rolled out in six tranches. The first tranche was mainly government projects, such as Snowy Hydro, schools and industrial projects such as recycling plants.

In tranche three, on 21 June 2020, the government announced it was fast-tracking an amendment to the Hills Shire local environment plan relating to North Castle Hill.

Nassif owned about 6,000 sq metres of property spread over nine blocks on Garthowen Crescent and Old Northern Rd, Castle Hill.

According to reports at the time, the foreshadowed change increased the area’s zoning to high density creating an estimated 60% increase in land value, delivering a windfall to Nassif. After Toplace collapsed in April 2023 the site was sold to another developer.

In August 2020, another one of Toplace’s projects, 189 Macquarie Street, Parramatta, was approved as part of tranche five.

It was one of only a handful of high-rise residential projects that were fast-tracked through the scheme. The approval allowed Toplace to increase the height of the residential tower to 167 metres making it the tallest building in Parramatta and increasing its floor space.

The Mascot project was not mentioned in the first six tranches.

A subsequent NSW Audit Office report found the program had generally been well run but said it had not adequately managed conflicts of interest.

On Monday, Charles was shown texts between himself and Nassif from January 2021.

“Hi, Jean. Thanks for lunch and the chat today. I’ve made a few calls. Short summary. Mascot. Got a call with the department on Monday to advance progression to the panel. 189. Spoke to my PDU [planning delivery unit in the department] contact. We are meeting on Monday for me to show her and raise our concerns. Garthowen. I will have an approach plan for this week.”

Charles Perrottet told Icac that he often lied to Nassif about political manoeuvring he was doing on his behalf and that he exaggerated his role.

“I gave him updates on the ascendancy of the right. It was one of the things I used to get him to pay his bills to Beckington,” Charles said.

Charles was shown text messages that he had sent to Nassif’s lawyer, Sharangan Maheswaran, after a dinner he had had with Nassif at Nobu in Melbourne in May 2021.

The text appeared to link achievement of political outcomes that Nassif sought, namely the removal of Chandler, and ending the career of Baulkham Hills MP, David Elliott’, with payments for progress on two projects, 189 Macquarie Street, Parramatta and Garthowen.

Dwyer asked: “So what you’re saying there is that you suggested to Sharangan Maheswaran that you can deal with Chandler and Elliot if you get money from 189 and Garthowen, those two developments, correct?”

Charles Perrottet agreed that he had been given a video by Maheswaran or Nassif of the building commissioner speaking at a building site where he said he had a list of dodgy certifiers that he would provide to the banks.

Charles told Icac he thought this might amount to third-line forcing – coercing a business to deal with a particular supplier – and suggested to either Nassif or Sharangan that they take it to the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, which regulates anticompetitive conduct.

In 2022 a video circulated in NSW parliament and was used to undermine the building commissioner to the fair trading minister, Eleni Petinos.

It was eventually reported by The Australian in July 2022 with a suggestion that Chandler had misled a parliamentary committee.

Chandler is not accused of wrongdoing by Icac, and is not under investigation. He told Icac last week that he was subjected to a campaign to undermine him in his role.

Charles was also asked about Nassif’s concerns about receiving what appeared to be an extortion attempt he had received via an anonymous email. It suggested the payment of $5m to a lawyers account would get the building commissioner off Nassif’s back.

Charles said he had suggested it should be taken to police, but he had done nothing himself.

articles.title: Logan Webb and Paul Skenes face off as struggling Giants visit Pirates in pitching duel
articles.excerpt: Paul Skenes stops by the MLB on FOX set pregame to discuss the impact of playing for the United States ahead of the World Baseball Classic final vs. Venezuela and the energy in the locker room, includ...
articles.body_text:
Paul Skenes stops by the MLB on FOX set pregame to discuss the impact of playing for the United States ahead of the World Baseball Classic final vs. Venezuela and the energy in the locker room, including sporting Team USA Hockey jerseys pregame.

Sports are fun for many reasons, but one main reason is that we expect one thing and then get something different. The idea that on any given night an underdog can beat a favorite, or that a bench player can have a career night, is what makes them so engaging. It can be incredibly frustrating as a sports bettor, but as a fan, it is awesome. As a sports bettor, there are a lot of people frustrated by these two teams and pitchers from this season as the Giants take on the Pirates.

The San Francisco Giants are one of the worst teams in baseball, which is quite surprising. The Giants are 57-81 for the season, and with their next loss, they will guarantee they are going to have a losing season. It was pretty unlikely they would go undefeated this month, but they are likely to lose between 90 and 95 games. This is another team in the league with plenty of talent, but they just couldn't put it together. Can it be blamed on their manager? The front office? Or is it just a lack of success from the pitching and offense combined?

Giants pitcher Logan Webb deleted his X account after a wild meltdown fighting online critics. (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Getty Images) ((Photo by Dustin Bradford/Getty Images))

I'd put most of the blame on the pitching staff as they carry a 4.34 ERA and a 1.35 WHIP into today's game. As usual with this pitching staff, the lone bright spot has been Logan Webb. This season, Webb is 8-8 with a 3.72 ERA and a 1.10 WHIP. He is in a bad situation tonight, though. On the road, he has a 4.16 ERA, and in night games, he has a 4.98 ERA. Both are worse than his home and day starts. He did have a rather strong August with only one bad start. In four outings, he allowed four earned runs over 26 innings. In the lone bad start, he allowed five earned runs in 2.2 innings. The Pirates hitters haven't been great against him, with just 12 hits in 58 at-bats.

The Pittsburgh Pirates were expected to compete for a Wild Card spot this season, but it hasn't gone as expected. The team is just four games under .500, so they still have a chance to end the season at .500 or better, but the chances of them making the postseason are slim. The hitting has improved, and that is a big reason for the improvement overall for the team this year. However, the pitching staff hasn't performed as well as needed this season despite having high hopes.

Pittsburgh Pirates starting pitcher Paul Skenes delivers a pitch against the Toronto Blue Jays in the first inning at Rogers Centre in Toronto on May 23, 2026. (Dan Hamilton/Imagn Images)

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

It is easy to have high hopes for the team when you have the reigning Cy Young leading the roster. However, it has been a bit of a disaster season for Paul Skenes. Look, a lot of pitchers would love to have Skenes numbers - 9-11 record, 3.79 ERA, 1.12 WHIP, and 175 strikeouts. The WHIP and strikeouts are the better numbers, but his ERA and record are a bit rough. In his young career, this 3.79 ERA is two full runs higher than it was in his first two seasons. Skenes has been better at night and at home this season, so maybe he is in his optimal spot here. He had a decent August, going 20.1 innings over four starts and allowing just seven earned runs.

Pittsburgh Pirates pitcher Paul Skenes delivers during the second inning of a baseball game against the Chicago Cubs in Pittsburgh, Tuesday, Sept. 16, 2025. (AP Photo/Gene J. Puskar, File)

My favorite prop, though, is to take under 6.5 strikeouts from Skenes. The Giants don't strike out a ton, and Skenes doesn't go overly deep into games, as the team is probably trying to conserve him for next year.

articles.title: Judge tells jury in Lindsay Clancy trial to keep deliberating after deadlock
articles.excerpt:
Clancy does not deny strangling her three children but says postpartum psychosis led to her actions

The judge has told the jury in the Lindsay Clancy trial to keep deliberating after it said it was u...
articles.body_text:
Clancy does not deny strangling her three children but says postpartum psychosis led to her actions

The judge has told the jury in the Lindsay Clancy trial to keep deliberating after it said it was unable to come to a unanimous decision in the controversial case of the mother who killed her three children.

Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse in Massachusetts, does not deny strangling her children but says postpartum psychosis led to her actions. Prosecutors argue she knew what she was doing. Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility.

The jury could convict her of murder or manslaughter, or acquit her if jurors believe her deteriorating mental health was to blame. A conviction could lead to a life prison sentence. If she is acquitted, a judge could still order her confined to a mental health facility if an evaluation determines she is a danger to the public.

Tuesday marked the fourth day of jury deliberations, which began after closing arguments on Thursday.

Clancy’s lawyer argued at the trial that she loved her children, but killed them because she had lost her grip on reality – and on herself – due to postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness that can follow childbirth. In the months before the killings, Clancy sought treatment for her worsening mental health, including a stay in a psychiatric hospital.

Prosecutors said Clancy strangled the children because she was depressed and tired of living, and made a conscious choice to kill them before attempting suicide.

To be found guilty, Massachusetts law requires defendants to retain “the substantial capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness or criminality of their conduct and to conform their conduct to the requirements of the law”.

Clancy’s former husband, Patrick, was among those to testify during the trial, in addition to relatives, psychologists and physicians who treated her. Jurors learned that Clancy had been prescribed 13 different sleep and anxiety medications, with her attorneys maintaining that may have exacerbated her depression symptoms.

After Clancy’s criminal trial, the focus is going to shift to civil litigation brought by both Lindsay and Patrick against her medical and mental healthcare providers. The former couple accused the providers of medical malpractice, contending they failed to properly diagnose, treat and monitor her severe postpartum psychiatric condition.

articles.body_text:
President Donald Trump could not help but poke fun at the New York Mets for losing "all the time" despite their sky-high payroll this season.

The baseball season has entered the final month of the regular season. It is hard to believe how quickly everything is moving, but there is no slowing down, so we need to keep up. The NFL is about to start, College Football is back already, and the WNBA playoffs begin soon. Next month we get back the NHL and NBA, but first we need to finish this regular season and see how the playoffs stack up. The Mets won't be in the postseason, but today's opponent, the Rays, will be.

The New York Mets had another disappointing season. They are currently 62-76 for the season and have losing home and road records. The problem has never been talent. They have plenty of big names on their roster, which is part of what makes it so hard to understand why the Mets are losing. Francisco Lindor, Juan Soto, Bo Bichette, Luis Robert Jr., etc. These are all guys that have All-Star appearances and a lot of success in the past, but for whatever reason it just hasn't been able to click for the team.

New York Mets shortstop Francisco Lindor throws to first for an out on San Francisco Giants' Heliot Ramos during the first inning of a baseball game in San Francisco, California, on Saturday, July 26, 2025. (AP Photo/Godofredo A. Vásquez)

The offense hasn't been great, but it isn't like the pitching staff has been much better. Tonight they send out Sean Manaea to the mound. He has bounced between the starting rotation and the bullpen. Manaea has appeared in 28 games, and exactly half of them have been starts. Overall, he has a 4.55 ERA, and opponents are batting .258 against him. He really isn't that much different as a starter as opposed to as a reliever. August wasn't a great month, but it did start well. In the first two games, he turned in 13 innings and allowed just three earned runs. In the final three, he allowed 14 earned runs in 18 innings of work. Overall, Rays hitters are 5-for-25 against Manaea, with Yandy Diaz and Nick Fortes both having two homers off of him.

The Tampa Bay Rays are one of the best teams in baseball, and you probably couldn't list almost anyone outside of their rotation on their team. They are a bunch of professional hitters. Junior Caminero is a very good player, and he has racked up homers and RBIs and is even batting .282 this season, but he still isn't a household name. Overall, the Rays are batting .260 as a team, and they are only middle of the pack in runs scored, so they need to find a way to get more people across the plate, because they aren't struggling to get guys on base.

Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays grounds out to the pitcher during the first inning of the MLB All-Star Game at Citizens Bank Park in Philadelphia, Pa., on July 14, 2026. (Al Bello/Getty Images)

The good news is their pitching has been phenomenal this season, and that helps with lower-scoring games. Today they send out a guy they traded for from the Mets, Freddy Peralta. For the season, Peralta is 6-11 with a 5.11 ERA and a 1.41 ERA - part of the reason the Mets struggled, and he was traded away. His starts with the Rays have been a bit of a mixed bag. He had two starts where he allowed five or more earned runs. The other three outings were three starts of three earned runs or fewer. He's been great against Mets hitters, holding them to a .131 average against him.

articles.title: Is Trump wooing Russia again – and why?
articles.excerpt: United States President Donald Trump’s administration appears to be taking steps to increase contact with key figures in Moscow, even as Russia’s war in Ukraine continues and US-backed peace efforts r...
articles.body_text:
United States President Donald Trump’s administration appears to be taking steps to increase contact with key figures in Moscow, even as Russia’s war in Ukraine continues and US-backed peace efforts remain stalled.

The latest signs that the US wants to step up relations include a rare visit to Moscow by CIA Director John Ratcliffe and the surprise appearance of Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov at a Group of 20 meeting hosted by the US on Monday.

However, this contact does not necessarily amount to a restoration of US-Russian relations, analysts said.

Washington continues to back sanctions against Moscow while it wages war on Ukraine and major differences over territory remain unresolved.

So what were these latest contacts about, and are US-Russian relations on the up?

The most significant meeting recently was Ratcliffe’s visit last week to Moscow, where he held talks with Russian intelligence officials.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said President Vladimir Putin was informed about the discussions but did not personally meet Ratcliffe.

Trump described the visit as “semiroutine” and said it was connected to efforts to end the war in Ukraine. US media reported that Ratcliffe also raised concerns about a possible Russian attack on NATO members and Russia’s relationship with Iran.

Trump, who claimed he would end the Ukraine war within “24 hours” of starting his second presidential term in January 2025 but has since failed to broker an agreement, has generally sought to play down tensions between Washington and Moscow. After Ratcliffe’s visit, he said the CIA director had had “good talks” with Putin. “He’s not going to be attacking a NATO territory,” Trump said.

Despite that, Russia has warned recently that the United Kingdom could face “consequences” for supplying drones to Ukraine that have been used in long-range attacks inside Russian territory. “London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which ⁠it will have to answer,” the Russian embassy in London said in a statement in mid-August. “The deeper its involvement in the conflict and the greater its support for Kiev’s terrorist machinery, the higher the price it will pay.”

Separately, Siluanov made a surprise appearance at a G20 finance ministers meeting in the US state of North Carolina for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent met Siluanov on the sidelines of the G20 meeting.

According to the Reuters news agency, Bessent made clear there would be no financial agreements or economic relief for Russia until the war ends.

Hopes of a diplomatic breakthrough remain bleak as neither side is willing to concede territory to the other. US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks this year broke down chiefly over Moscow’s territorial demands. Moscow has demanded that Kyiv give up territory in eastern Ukraine while Kyiv has refused to surrender any land it still controls.

Last week, Ukraine’s top presidential adviser, Kyrylo Budanov, said talks involving Ukraine, Russia and the US could be happening “very soon”.

On Monday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had held “detailed and constructive” discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner about a possible visit to Ukraine and efforts to advance the peace process.

In the meantime, the deadlock continues. Russia and Ukraine continue to exchange attacks, targeting each other’s energy infrastructure and fighting intense battles in eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region.

On Tuesday, Russian air attacks killed 12 people and injured many more in Kyiv and surrounding areas, local authorities said. It was the sixth consecutive day of intense strikes on the capital.

Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Zelenskyy’s sanctions commissioner, told Reuters on Monday that he is due in the US capital on Tuesday on a trip that will include meetings with lawmakers.

The restoration of high-level contacts between the US and Russia began earlier in Trump’s second term.

In February, Washington and Moscow agreed to re-establish high-level military-to-military talks, which were suspended just before the Russian war on Ukraine began.

After the latest contacts, Keir Giles, an associate fellow of the Russia and Eurasia Programme at the think tank Chatham House, said evidence that “relations are being normalised between Washington and Moscow should deepen the sense of alarm”.

“The US treating Russia as a partner not an adversary is a fundamental problem for all those countries that are under direct threat from Moscow – not just Ukraine but America’s European allies too,” Giles told Al Jazeera.

Insiders have also warned that a rapprochement with Trump could further embolden Russia against NATO. In August after Moscow warned the UK of “consequences” for providing long-range missile components to Ukraine, former Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Fedorov told the BBC that these “consequences” could include the possibility of attacks. He said many military experts advising the Kremlin are convinced that NATO would not respond forcefully if Russia were to hit the UK. “Trump will not allow NATO to answer,” he said.

This week, Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski said he was unhappy to see Moscow represented at the G20 meeting on Monday. “We do not trust Russia. They lie constantly, and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them,” ⁠⁠he told Reuters.

On Tuesday, European Union economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis also said this is not the right moment to “normalise” Moscow’s participation in G20 gatherings. “I think the European position is known,” Dombrovskis told reporters on the sidelines of the North Carolina meeting.

articles.title: Norway’s new king swears oath of allegiance with daughter at his side
articles.excerpt:
Haakon VIII promises to uphold 1814 constitution but his queen misses ceremony because of post-surgery ‘complications’

King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance before Norway’s parliament on Tuesd...
articles.body_text:
Haakon VIII promises to uphold 1814 constitution but his queen misses ceremony because of post-surgery ‘complications’

King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance before Norway’s parliament on Tuesday in the first major stage in the passing of the crown since the death of his father after 35 years on the throne.

Wearing a ceremonial uniform, Haakon, who became king when Harald V died on Friday, promised to uphold Norway’s 1814 constitution with his 22-year-old daughter, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, by his side.

“I promise and swear that I will govern the kingdom of Norway in accordance with its constitution and laws, so help me God, the almighty and omniscient,” the 53-year-old king pledged to cabinet ministers and MPs in the main chamber of the 169-seat parliament.

Haakon’s wife, Mette-Marit, 53, was unable to attend the 17-minute ceremony because of complications after a lung transplant in June. Her doctors said such complications were not uncommon.

Are ​Holm, a pulmonologist at Oslo university hospital, said the queen had had “complications on some occasions with the operation, including today. As a ​result, she must be put under observation ​throughout the day today.”

Harald, whose funeral will be held in Oslo on 9 September, with heads of state from around the world invited to attend, was widely appreciated in Norway for his warmth, unassuming lifestyle and dedication to preserving national unity.

Tens ⁠of thousands of Norwegians have flocked to the royal palace to lay flowers, drawings, candles and flags.

A poll for the public broadcaster NRK found the monarchy’s popularity had risen over the past few months. The first survey since Harald’s death at the age of 89 found that about 72% of Norwegians supported the monarchy, compared with 54% in May. In February, while the royal family was mired in a succession of scandals, support for the institution fell to 60%.

Mette-Marit has faced strong criticism for her association with Jeffrey Epstein, while her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, is appealing against a four-year sentence for two rape convictions.

Responding to Haakon’s oath, Masud Gharahkhani, the parliament’s president, who arrived in Norway as a child refugee from Iran, said Harald had personified “the values that underpin our liberal democracy”, including compassion.

There will be no formal coronation of the new king and queen because Norway abolished the ceremony more than a century ago but Haakon may, like his father and grandfather, choose to have his accession consecrated at Trondheim’s Nidaros Cathedral.

Harald, who will be buried in the royal mausoleum at the Akershus Fortress in Oslo, died while being treated in hospital for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells.

articles.title: Israel captures top Hamas commander in Gaza strike, defense minister says
articles.excerpt: Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst shares an exclusive interview with U.S. special envoy Jared Kushner on his meetings with Hamas leadership and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu...
articles.body_text:
Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst shares an exclusive interview with U.S. special envoy Jared Kushner on his meetings with Hamas leadership and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 'The Story.'

The Israel Defense Forces captured Hamas' head of general security during a raid in Gaza, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said.

An Israeli security official identified the Hamas leader as Mu'in al-Arabid, head of the General Security Apparatus, saying he was arrested during an Israeli incursion deep inside Hamas territory in Gaza. The IDF carried out airstrikes to cover the raid's withdrawal, adding that there were no Israeli casualties.

"A short time ago, a senior Hamas terrorist was arrested, and this is our policy: We do not wait for threats. Instead, we pursue Hamas terrorists, thwart them, and destroy their terrorist infrastructure. We have built a strong and unprecedented security zone in Gaza to protect residents and IDF soldiers," Katz said in a statement.

HAMAS STRUGGLES TO FILL LEADERSHIP RANKS AS ISRAEL HUNTS OCT 7 TERRORISTS

Soldiers of the Israel Defense Forces stand on top of tanks at the borders with Gaza, on Oct. 10, 2025, the first day of the ceasefire with Hamas. (Ilia Yefimovich/picture alliance via Getty Images)

"Nearly 70% of the Gaza Strip has been destroyed, with no residents, no tunnels, and no homes, and the IDF controls the territory. We are not leaving Gaza until the Strip is demilitarized, Hamas is disarmed, and all terrorist tunnels are destroyed. Even after that, the IDF will remain in Gaza along defensive lines and ensure the security of the western Negev communities. Any attempt to bypass the security zone through aerial launches will be met with a harsh response," he added.

The raid comes weeks after President Donald Trump's administration demanded that Hamas disarm and give up control of Gaza in August. Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, traveled to Israel last month and said the IDF may receive U.S. backing to "finish the job."

NETANYAHU REJECTS BOARD OF PEACE'S GAZA PLAN: NO 'WITHDRAWAL UNTIL HAMAS IS GENUINELY DISARMED'

Joint press statements by the Greek Minister of National Defense, Nikos Dendias, and the Israeli Minister of Defense, Israel Katz, at the Ministry of National Defense, Athens, January 20, 2026. (Nick Paleologos / SOOC / AFP via Getty Images)

"If they don't follow through now on their commitment, everyone will see that they're not genuine about peace, and then Israel will have a lot more support from the U.S. and others to go and finish the job in the appropriate way," Kushner also told Fox News' Trey Yingst of the terrorist group.

The warning from Trump’s son-in-law followed a rare face-to-face meeting with Hamas in Egypt — only Kushner's second known meeting with the group.

KUSHNER TOUTS UNPRECEDENTED IRAN CONTACTS AS TEHRAN DENIES TRUMP BACKCHANNEL

"They said all the right things, but obviously, it's very, very hard to trust, you know, a terrorist organization that committed these terrible atrocities," Kushner continued. "But we had a very cordial meeting, and they said all the right things, and so we're going to give them a chance to perform."

Jared Kushner speaks during the inaugural meeting of the Board of Peace at the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 19, 2026. Kushner is facing pushback in Albania over a luxury development project. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"It's going to have to be based on actions and steps, and I hope it will be true."

The U.S.-led "Board of Peace" proposal centers on a phased ceasefire, demilitarization of Gaza, Israeli troop withdrawal, Palestinian technocratic governance and international reconstruction efforts.

Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

articles.title: Dyson launches £420 toothbrush that films ‘live cleaning footage’ inside your mouth
articles.excerpt:
James Dyson says ‘complete dental system’ will also include toothpaste and mouth rinse that each cost £8.50

It is the live stream you never wanted to see but may find impossible to resist: rolling fo...
articles.body_text:
James Dyson says ‘complete dental system’ will also include toothpaste and mouth rinse that each cost £8.50

It is the live stream you never wanted to see but may find impossible to resist: rolling footage beamed live from inside your mouth while you are cleaning your teeth.

Dyson, the home appliance maker that made its name inventing bagless vacuums and bladeless fans, has turned its attention to oral hygiene with a £420 all-singing, all-dancing toothbrush that can clean, floss and even spray tiny jets of mouthwash.

In simpler times, a handle and bristles were enough, but the Dyson toothbrush, which took six years and the brainpower of 661 engineers to develop, has a “100k pixel macro lens camera” and an “anti-gravity (mouthwash) tank” on board.

The camera functions as a “high-quality endoscope”, according to the company, enabling users to “see what their dentist sees”. The brusher can watch “live cleaning footage” on the MyDyson app and get feedback on their cleaning regime.

On Tuesday, James Dyson, the company’s founder and chief engineer, launched the hi-tech toothbrush at an event in Paris.

Engineers and scientists at the company – which despite the billionaire inventor’s support for Brexit moved its corporate base to Singapore in 2019 – had “spent well over a decade understanding oral care regimes and how nasties build up in the mouth”, Dyson explained. The rigorous process included developing a “proxy plaque” so it could test plaque removal accurately.

Flossing was an “awkward and time-consuming chore” and “few of us do it even though we know we should”, he said. “Our research has shown that people consistently miss the areas where plaque forms: the gaps between teeth.”

And while you will be familiar with the process of moving a toothbrush up and down with your hand, Dyson explained that by “combining a camera, machine learning, precision fluid dynamics, advanced brushing technologies, connectivity and wifi” the toothbrush offered an “entirely new way to keep your mouth healthy”.

When the camera detects gaps between teeth, the jet on the stem releases a burst of mouth rinse to remove plaque as you brush, while the brush head cleans along the gum line and lifts surface stains. The brush claims to remove “up to 72% more plaque than market leading electric toothbrushes”.

No dental routine would be complete without toothpaste, and Dyson’s claims to be a “complete dental system” with a non-foaming toothpaste and mouth rinse (so as not to obscure the camera lens) that each cost £8.50.

Dyson is entering a crowded market as there are already dozens of ultra-advanced toothbrushes, including smart models with apps, that promise everything from plaque and stain removal to tongue cleaning. The Phillips Sonicare DiamondClean, for example, which is available in Boots and John Lewis, comes with a £600 price tag.

If you don’t have a big toothbrush budget, the good news is that the British Dental Association (BDA) says you don’t need one. You just need to follow your dentist’s advice and brush twice a day.

Eddie Crouch, the BDA’s chair, said: “Patients shouldn’t be lulled into thinking the latest gizmos will solve all their oral health problems. Big brands with high price tags are no substitute for a proper routine.”

articles.title: Teen girl charged with murder over recording of San Diego mosque attack
articles.excerpt:
A 17-year-old girl has been charged with murder by aiding and abetting after prosecutors say she recorded a livestream of an attack on a San Diego mosque that left three people dead.

Prosecutors say ...
articles.body_text:
A 17-year-old girl has been charged with murder by aiding and abetting after prosecutors say she recorded a livestream of an attack on a San Diego mosque that left three people dead.

Prosecutors say the girl also published a manifesto from two teenage gunmen who carried out the attack on the Islamic Center of San Diego on 18 May.

The teenager, from North Carolina, was arrested last week and indicted by a grand jury on Monday, according to Forsyth County District Attorney Jim O'Neill.

Speaking at a news conference, O'Neill said: "The thought of her going back to school, with the weekend approaching, holy days approaching, we didn't know what she was capable of."

The teenager now faces three murder charges and one count of conspiracy. O'Neill explained that under North Carolina law, a person accused of aiding and abetting a crime can be held criminally responsible in the same way as the person who carried it out.

Authorities say the attack was carried out by two males - aged 17 and 18 - who opened fire at the mosque, before taking their own lives.

O'Neill said the pair had two aims that day: "Number one, to kill as many people as possible on that day. Secondly, they wanted this carnage and destruction recorded ... livestreamed."

A security guard at the mosque, Amin Abdullah, exchanged gunfire with the attackers and initiated a lockdown, helping protect around 140 children who were inside the building.

Abdullah and two worshippers - Mansour Kaziha and Nader Awad, who drew the attentions of the shooters in a parking lot - were fatally shot.

San Diego Police Chief Scott Wahl previously described Abdullah's actions as "heroic", saying they had "undoubtedly" saved lives.

According to investigators, the shooters recorded the attack using cameras mounted on GoPro-style helmets. O'Neill said the pair had also planned further attacks "at a local Jewish temple and finally at a predominantly African American high school".

Authorities said the teenagers had an arsenal of around 30 guns and a crossbow, which investigators say were taken from one of the shooter's parents.

The attackers also left behind writings containing racist and antisemitic views, as well as references to white supremacist ideologies.

The document, which was reviewed by the BBC's US news partner CBS News, pointed to a gunman who murdered 51 people at two mosques in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 2019, as one of their models.

articles.title: Burnham chairs cabinet meeting before first statement to MPs as prime minister – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
PM will tell Commons he wants to unlock ‘positivity’ after a summer of policy announcements and improved poll ratings

Good morning. Andy Burnham became prime minister six weeks ago, but today will be...
articles.body_text:
PM will tell Commons he wants to unlock ‘positivity’ after a summer of policy announcements and improved poll ratings

Good morning. Andy Burnham became prime minister six weeks ago, but today will be the first time he addresses MPs in the Commons. It will also be the first time he has spoken as a minister from the dispatch box in more than 16 years. As MPs return to Westminster, they will be telling each other about how they spent the summer holiday and, for Burnham, it has undoubtedly gone well. He has unveiled a blitz of announcements which, broadly, have had a good reception and he has delivered the kiss of life to Labour’s poll ratings.

Today Burnham will chair cabinet in the morning and then make a ministerial statement in the Commons after 3.30pm. Normally a prime ministerial statement has a specific focus; it will be about a major policy decision, or a foreign affairs crisis. From the briefing that we have had so far, it sounds as if Burnham’s will be more of a wide-ranging rehash of all the things that he has been talking about this summer. In her preview, Jessica Elgot says he will talk about his intention to bring more essential services back into public control.

According to the BBC’s preview, Burnham will say he wants to “unlock a feeling of positivity and possibility” in every part of the country.

For the past six weeks, Burnham’s tone has been relentlessly positive. He repeatedly says he wants to focus on “problem-solving, not point-scoring”, and he clearly means it. Labour MPs chose Burnham as leader because they thought Keir Starmer would not be able to stop Nigel Farage becoming PM, but over the summer Burnham has said very little in public critical about Farage, or Reform UK, or the Tories. He views partisan mud-slinging as part of the old politics that he would like to reject.

But can he do that when he has to perform politics in the House of Commons? It sounds as if Burnham will not have much new to announce in his statement and so journalists will probably focus instead on what Labour and opposition MPs say to him, and how he responds. Burnham may not approve of “point-scoring”, but in the Commons, tradition, culture and even the architecture (front benches supposedly two swords’ length apart) prioritise conflict and it will interesting to see if he can get through the afternoon without resorting to the usual aggressive ding-dong. This will be an even bigger challenge for him at PMQs tomorrow.

And even if Burnham can remain upbeat for two hours in the Commons chamber, he will soon find that there are some places in the country particularly resistant to “positivity” – like the newsrooms at the Mail and GB News.

Still, it is probably worth a try. Here is the agenda for the day.

Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

2.30pm: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, takes his seat as an MP after winning the Clacton byelection during the summer recess.

2.30pm: Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

After 3.30pm: Burnham gives a statement to MPs.

Late afternoon: Alex Norris, the justice secretary, gives a statement to MPs about changes to the prisoner early release scheme.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

Andy Burnham has vowed to “stamp out antisemitism for good” in a tribute to the victims of the Manchester synagogue terror attack.

double quotation markWe send our love and support to the Jewish community in Manchester and beyond who last night gathered to remember Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby, who were killed defending their synagogue last year. My thoughts are with their families and all those who have been affected by the attack.

I know for many Jewish people, the sorrow and fear from that day has not lifted and I know we must do more to protect communities across the country.

I want Jewish people to know that their safety is a priority of mine and I’m determined to stamp out antisemitism for good.

Andy Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises to fund higher public spending in the budget – although he has also played down the prospect of big changes.

In an article for the Times, Darren Jones, who was chief secretary to the PM under Keir Starmer but who left government when Burnham took power, has warned that higher public spending on its own won’t make Britain richer. He says:

double quotation markBritain is poorer than we often think. We won’t get richer based on higher public spending alone, and we can’t tax billionaires who don’t live here.

We shouldn’t rely on public spending as a route to some romantic version of making Britain great again as we look in the rearview mirror for a great history that is no longer available to us. We must face the future, and I know my colleagues are up to the challenge.

Jones says that the chancellor should avoid big tax rises in the budget and that the key decisions will come in the spending review. He calls for a focus on growth.

double quotation markCrucially, we must create the right conditions for a dynamic, thriving market. This includes getting ahead of what artificial intelligence will mean for our services-dominated economy.

Politically, we shouldn’t see conflict between growth and fairness, or business and workers, or the market and the state. These are false choices.

Economic growth is the foundation of a better life for the people we represent.

In his article Jones, who is seen as a Starmer loyalist, says Burnham has “done an impressive job this summer in cementing his positive ratings with the public and improving my party’s position in the polls”. But the article implies Jones is worried Burnham might cave in to pressure to embark on a leftwing spending spree.

The long-term cost of borrowing for the government has reached a 28-year high, Julia Kollewe reports on the business live blog.

Andy Burnham has been chairing cabinet. Here are pictures of some of the ministers arriving in Downing Street before the meeting started.

Last week it emerged that John Healey, the chancellor, will not set out how the UK will raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030 in the budget in October. Instead, he will set out plans to raise defence spending in the spending review next year.

The revelation led to Healey being accused of hypocrisy because he resigned as defence secretary in Keir Starmer’s government after Starmer refused to commit to raising defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030 in the defence investment plan published this summer. Healey’s resignation contributed to Starmer deciding to step down, and Healey returning to government in a more senior role as Andy Burnham’s chancellor.

In an interview with the Times, Healey has said he is “100%” committed to raising defence spending. He told the paper:

double quotation markFor the first time at the spending review, we will set out a clear path about how we will meet that Nato commitment in 2035, of 3.5% of GDP. And as part of setting out that clear path, we will set that target date for 3%.

The paper has headlined its story: “John Healey: I’ll prove I’m no hypocrite on defence.” But Healey did not use those words himself (it is the Times summarising his stance), and in the interview Healey did not confirm the 3% target would be met by 2030.

Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has insisted prisons will “still function properly” amid concerns over government plans to turn laundries into cells in a bid to tackle overcrowding.

As Ben Quinn reports, the Ministry of Justice announced overnight that it will spend £110m creating new cells in prisons using existing spaces like unused offices, laundry rooms and other areas.

Norris was giving interviews this morning and he said “hundreds of places” would be created by converting existing spaces inside prisons into accommodation.

He declined to confirm Tory claims that there are 700 fewer prison places than a year ago, noting that the estate “fluctuates” because of issues such as fire damage.

Asked where clothes would be washed if laundry rooms were converted into cells, Norris told BBC Breakfast:

double quotation markOf course we’re going to make sure that the prisons can still function properly.

This is a creative look, as I say, around our estate and being able to use some space that we can re-prioritise.

He said wider plans – including building entire new prisons – would see 14,000 new places on top of the 3,200 prison places delivered in the last two years, “but that takes time”, while the conversion plans would add “in the hundreds of spaces”.

Pressed on the Conservatives’ claim that there are 700 fewer prison places than in 2025, Norris said the estate “fluctuates” because of planned and unplanned events affecting the Victorian-era buildings.

double quotation markThose wouldn’t necessarily be the numbers I’d use, but it is possible that places come out of the estate. For example, you know, there can be damage, fire damage. We’ve got a very old estate.

In line with Andy Burnham’s emphasis on “positivity” (see 9.04am), the Home Office has put out a press release overnight saying that summer small boat crossings have been at a seven-year low this year. The figures aren’t particularly new, and anyone following the story closely will know that small boat arrival numbers have fallen sharply. But these statistics have not been publicised prominently in the rightwing media, which is one reason why almost half of Britons wrongly think small boat arrival numbers are going up.

double quotation markUsually some of the busiest months in the year, with criminal gangs exploiting good weather, latest data shows that June, July and August (up to the 30th August) recorded the lowest combined total of small boat crossings since 2019, and the lowest number of small boat migrant arrivals since 2020.

• August crossings (up to 30 August) fell to their lowest level since records began in 2018, down 46% on last year, with the lowest number of migrant arrivals since 2020, down 35% on last year.

• July saw the fewest crossings of any July since 2019, down 64% on 2025, with the lowest number of migrant arrivals since 2020, down 58% on last year.

• June recorded its lowest level of crossings since 2019, down 50% on 2025, with the lowest number of migrant arrivals since 2021, down 47% on last year.

It is important to recognise the distinction between small boat crossing numbers and arrival numbers. The number of people arriving on small boats has fallen significantly, but the number of small boat crossings (ie boats, not people) has fallen even more because people smugglers are using bigger boats (in part because smaller boats are being seized).

articles.title: At least 12 people killed in Russian overnight attacks on Ukraine – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
Zelenskyy says dozens more injured as strikes leave thousands without electricity in Odesa region

At least 12 people, including an Indian citizen, were killed in overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine ...
articles.body_text:
Zelenskyy says dozens more injured as strikes leave thousands without electricity in Odesa region

At least 12 people, including an Indian citizen, were killed in overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine with “dozens” more injured, the country’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

Zelenskyy said the Russian strikes also left “thousands” of families without electricity in the Odesa region, and a border crossing with Romania “deliberately damaged.”

Over the last few days, Ukraine suffered a series of prolonged Russian attacks, including daytime bombing, in the latest attempt to “wear down” the war-torn country. Kyiv has now been targeted for six consecutive days.

The issue of Russian threat will no doubt also come up during an informal meeting of EU defence ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, with some suggestions that Germany could be close to attributing last month’s Leipzig incidents to Russia.

A number of other countries also saw incidents believed to be linked with Russia, including a suspected arson of a drone factory in Poland on Sunday night. Both Estonia and Latvia briefly activated their air alert systems on Tuesday amid reports of drones near their airspace.

In other news, over in Norway, King Hakoon VIII will take his oath in the Norwegian parliament following the death of his father, King Harald. I will keep an eye on that, too.

It’s Tuesday, 1 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

If you want to keep an eye on the swearing-in ceremony of the new Norwegian King Haakon VIII, we now have a live stream up and running here:

Russia has described as “ridiculous” the Italian government’s decision to appoint Ukraine’s former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov as the country’s innovation adviser at the defence ministry.

“This is a perfect example of how western countries use Ukraine and Ukrainians,” said the Russian foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova.

“While ordinary citizens are being mobilised and sent to the trenches in Ukraine to face certain death, the managers of the Kyiv regime are turning military defeats into personal international contracts – and they are not ashamed of it.”

Italy’s defence minister, Guido Crosetto, disclosed the offer shortly after Fedorov was dismissed in July, praising him as a driving force behind military innovation who had helped Ukraine regain the initiative in its war against Russia.

“I understand that they would prefer decisions concerning Italy to be taken by someone who checks with Moscow first, but for the time being that is still not the case,” Crosetto told Ansa in response. “We make decisions thinking only about Rome, not Moscow, Kyiv or Washington.”

Fedorov, 35, was fired six months after his appointment, having initiated reforms around procurement and mobilisation that put him on a collision course with the military establishment and political rivals.

In a post on X, Fedorov thanked Crosetto for “his personal support” and for the offer to serve as his adviser.

“In this role, I will assist Italy in adopting modern warfare technologies, enhancing its defence sector, and adapting to emerging global security challenges,” he said.

Over in Brussels, the European Commission is just starting its first midday briefing of the autumn.

It opens with an announcement that Commission president Ursula von der Leyen will receive Nato’s Mark Rutte tomorrow. This comes amid growing scrutiny of Russia’s activities on the eastern flank.

I will keep an eye on more lines coming from that briefing for you.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s ⁠prime minister Sergii Koretskyi ⁠called ⁠on lawmakers ​on Tuesday to ⁠speed up voting ⁠on key ​legislation ‌to help ‌secure necessary ‌financing for Ukraine, as the country is facing ‌a $27bn deficit ​for defence.

Koretskyi added that ⁠his government would ​audit the ​needs ​of the ​defence ‌ministry, Reuters said.

Back to Germany and the Leipzig incident last month, we now have a confirmation that we will hear from the country’s interior and foreign ministers later today on the attempted Leipzig drone incident, believed to be linked to Russia (10:17).

Speaking on a foreign visit to Algiers, German foreign minister Johann Wadephul said “Germany will not be intimidated in any way, and that will continue to be the fundamental stance of our policy.”

“Russia must know that Germany is a stabilising force in Europe, one that is always prepared to negotiate, but which will not be intimidated in any way,” he said in comments reported by German news agency DPA.

I will make sure to keep an eye on this for you.

Over in Norway, we are waiting for the swearing-in ceremony of King Haakon, which should get under way in the next hour or so.

But the Norwegian media just reported that Queen Mette-Marit – who has recently come under scrutiny over scandals including a much-criticised association with the late US child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein – will not attend the ceremony owing to complications after her lung transplant in mid-June.

Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra will be there, though.

There is an interesting back story to today’s meeting of EU defence ministers in Wicklow, with the Irish Times reporting that a British warship and a helicopter designed to hunt submarines have been deployed off the coast of Ireland, just outside Irish territorial waters, in a bid to keep the meeting secure.

The move was needed as the Irish Defence Forces lack the capability to conduct long-range air defence operations, the Irish Times said.

UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband is also expected to join the meeting, the paper said, although it is understood that he will join the Gymnich meeting of foreign ministers, not the defence setting.

Ireland’s approach to defence has drawn close scrutiny in recent weeks given the country holds the EU’s rotating presidency.

Russia ⁠launched more ⁠than ⁠2,800 harder-to-shoot-down jet-powered ​drones at ⁠Ukraine in August, Ukraine’s ⁠air ​force ‌spokesperson ‌Yuriy Ihnat ‌said on Tuesday.

Their interception rate was ‌lower compared with ​other types of drones, ⁠at around ​60%, Ihnat ​told ​Ukrainian ​television in comments reported by Reuters.

Separately, we are picking up reports in the German press that Germany is set to formally blame Russia for last month’s failed drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane in Leipzig.

Bild newspaper says the German interior and foreign ministers are set to announce the results of their investigation into the incident later today. This is yet to be formally confirmed by any of the ministries involved.

Over the weekend, German chancellor Friedrich Merz sort of suggested that a formal response from the government was coming soon, but did not go into the details.

On behalf of the Irish presidency in the EU Council, Ireland’s defence minister Helen McEntee said the talks in Wicklow come “at a moment of profound challenge for all of us in terms of defence and security,” with closer cooperation needed “more than ever.”

Ukraine, maritime security, and resilience against hybrid and cyber threats will be top of the agenda today, she says.

Opening the meeting, EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said today’s talks in Ireland will primarily focus on the EU’s support for Ukraine, with further discussions on other current affairs, including maritime security and Lebanon.

She said that Nato remained “the cornerstone of our security,” but with the US urging its European partners to “assume greater responsibility for their own defence,” there is more scope for internal discussions.

She urged ministers to “challenge the conventional thinking to look beyond simply doing more of the same,” and look for ways in which Europe can innovate and offer new capabilities.

Curiously, Kallas also said she would be forming “a high-level group of former political and military leaders from several EU countries, but also the UK and Ukraine, to have a fresh look at how to respond to current and increasing, very real, military threats.”

articles.title: First Thing: Duane Keith Davis found guilty of 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur
articles.excerpt:
Jury took about three hours to reach verdict in case that relied heavily on confessions from the defendant. Plus, the woman who lived with and loved Freddie Mercury as her fiance

Good morning. A Las ...
articles.body_text:
Jury took about three hours to reach verdict in case that relied heavily on confessions from the defendant. Plus, the woman who lived with and loved Freddie Mercury as her fiance

Good morning. A Las Vegas jury has found the former South Side Compton Crips gang leader Duane Keith Davis guilty of the murder of Tupac Shakur, bringing the case to a close nearly 30 years after the rapper was gunned down. The jury took about three hours to reach a guilty verdict in a case that relied heavily on multiple confessions from Davis himself.

The 63-year-old, who was accused of instigating the deadly shooting but not pulling the trigger himself, had spent years telling investigators and interviewers alike of his direct involvement before he was arrested in 2023.

Who was Tupac Shakur? Shakur was born in 1971 in East Harlem, New York, and rose to fame in the early 90s with lyrics that doubled as a sharp commentary on social injustice, including systemic racism and police brutality. He was 25 when he died and is regarded among the greatest rappers to ever live, and continues to be celebrated around the world years after his life was cut short.

How have his family reacted to the trial? “We’ve been waiting 30 years to grieve properly,” Zayd Akinyela, Shakur’s cousin, told reporters outside the courtroom when the trial was under way. “A lot of people don’t get to grieve until they understand what happened to their loved one and how it happened.”

Why have authorities been so heavily criticised over the case? Las Vegas police faced criticism that they had bungled the investigation and failed to pursue crucial leads, including from a member of Shakur’s entourage who claimed he could identify the shooters. That witness died weeks later in a separate shooting.

The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to more than 1,000. More than 4,400 are missing on the two sides of the border. Rescue efforts have been complicated by difficult terrain, persistently high flood waters and bad weather.

With more than 40 bridges destroyed, rescuers are relying on helicopters, while India and China are sending prefabricated truss bridges to help restore access. The swollen Trishuli River has continued to change course unpredictably, making planning a challenge. Areas that were dry one day are flooded the next, and further floods are a constant concern.

The army secretary, Dan Driscoll, has handed his resignation to Donald Trump, the White House said Monday, becoming the latest high-profile figure to depart the defense department.

The resignation comes after months of turmoil at the defense department, from leak investigations and budget issues to the ousting of several senior officials including the army chief of staff, Randy George, in April. In June, the army commander of forces in Europe and Africa, Gen Christopher Donahue, unexpectedly stepped down.

What role had Driscoll been playing? An Iraq war veteran, tech investor and former adviser to JD Vance, Driscoll was tapped for the unusual role of key negotiator to try to end the war between Russia and Ukraine. He was also a major force behind trying to cut the red tape for military contractors to quickly develop more drones and counter-drone capabilities as warfare rapidly changes around the world.

A 17-year-old North Carolina girl who recorded a live stream of a shooting that killed three people at a San Diego mosque and disseminated the attackers’ white-supremacist writings has been charged with murder by aiding and abetting, a district attorney said.

The Forsyth county district attorney Jim O’Neill said the girl, whose name was not mentioned during the news conference, was arrested last week. On Monday a grand jury indicted her on three counts of murder and one count of conspiracy. Under North Carolina law, the aiding-and-abetting charges carry the same penalties as if the girl had committed the attack herself, O’Neill said.

A divided US supreme court has permitted Donald Trump to continue building his controversial $400m White House ballroom despite legal challenges, raising the likelihood it will be completed.

New York City police shot and killed a woman after she stabbed two people, one of them fatally, in Times Square, an act authorities described as “random and unprovoked”.

The US military has no plans to send troops to midterm polling sites, the highest‑ranking US military officer has said.

US health officials have excluded two measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania from their counts. RFK Jr, the health secretary, has suggested the deaths were “fabricated” while the CDC said it was reviewing them.

The Tennessee Volunteers will be honoring Dolly Parton with a helmet sticker this season, the college football team’s head coach, Josh Heupel, announced.

The US’s main trade regulator and 22 states have sued Amazon, alleging the online retailer “secretly and systematically overcharged” advertisers, leading to higher costs for customers on items such as groceries and other essential goods. Amazon described it as a “misguided lawsuit” with which it “strongly disagrees”.

She spent the biggest moment of her career at the Paris Olympics thrashing around like a toddler having a tantrum – then went viral globally. Now, a Netflix film reveals how the much-mocked breakdancer Raygun got over it.

Freddie was loud, flamboyant, confident, supremely camp and gay. Mary was quiet, inhibited, diffident and strictly heterosexual. Simon Hattenstone speaks to the late Queen singer’s former fiance about their life together.

We are used to the idea that our fellow humans may intentionally mislead or manipulate us, but the idea that machines can now do the same is deeply unsettling, as Snigdha Poonam’s long read explores.

Scientists have long warned that the climate crisis will create stronger extremes and destructive shifts between wet and dry conditions, and the flash flooding in the Arizona tourist destination, which killed at least two people, was likely triggered by compounding climate factors such as local drought, recent wildfires and warming in the Pacific Ocean.

Dale Sanders said he fell 71 times on the more than 2,000-mile Appalachian Trail but completed the journey as “people are motivated and given encouragement by my efforts”.
