articles.title: Price rises gather pace in UK shops amid higher energy costs
articles.excerpt:
In-store inflation rises to an annual 1.5% in August, according to a survey for the British Retail Consortium

The pace of price rises in UK shops rose to its highest level in two years in August, a t...
articles.body_text:
In-store inflation rises to an annual 1.5% in August, according to a survey for the British Retail Consortium

The pace of price rises in UK shops rose to its highest level in two years in August, a trade body index shows, with higher energy costs pushing up the price of food and AI chip demand making technology more expensive.

In-store inflation stepped up to 1.5% year on year in August, up from 0.9% in July, led by prices for tinned and packaged food which increased by 2.5% against 1.1% in the prior month, according to data from the research company NIQ for the British Retail Consortium.

Inflation for fresh produce remained high at 3%, amid pressure on growers from the hot dry summer plus hefty fuel and energy costs. However, that marked a slight easing off from the 3.1% recorded in July,

Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the consortium, said: “The impact of higher energy, input and commodity costs is beginning to filter through into prices, particularly for ambient foods which are typically imported and processed.

“In non-food, electrical prices rose amid the ongoing AI boom, which is forcing up the price of memory chips and storage. Meanwhile, retailers kept clothing prices low to offer value for families getting ready for the new school year.

“The months ahead look challenging for households, with rising bills putting further pressure on budgets.”

Mike Watkins, head of retailer insight at NIQ, said he expected price competition between retailers to intensify in the autumn months as businesses competed to attract families concerned about potentially higher energy bills.

However, Dickinson said companies were facing “persistently high operating costs” that limited their ability to absorb price rises. She added: “If the government is serious about supporting growth while keeping the cost of living in check, it must address the cost of doing business, including by tackling the growing burden of business rates, packaging and employment taxes.”

The evidence of higher shop prices comes after the boss of Asda said he was seeing inflation on some fresh food begin to rise after a hot dry summer that affected crop yields.

Cereals including wheat and barley were hit particularly badly, according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board. Its first harvest report of 2026 said the hot weather had resulted in the earliest harvest since records began in 2006.

The rise in shop price inflation adds to the challenge for Andy Burnham’s government in achieving its aim of granting “breathing space” to hard-pressed households

Wider consumer price inflation across the UK rose to 2.9% in July with the Iran war affecting energy prices, according to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics. The agency said inflation rose from a 15-month low of 2.6% in June, driven by more costly gas and electricity.

Despite government measures to ease electricity costs, households in Great Britain face the sharpest summer increase in energy bills in four years.

articles.title: Burnham warned running prison capacity near limit is ‘big risk’
articles.excerpt:
U-turn on early release scheme will create ‘stresses and strains’ on prison system, says former justice secretary

Andy Burnham is taking a “big risk” by seeking to continue running prison capacity to...
articles.body_text:
U-turn on early release scheme will create ‘stresses and strains’ on prison system, says former justice secretary

Andy Burnham is taking a “big risk” by seeking to continue running prison capacity to the limit, according to the former justice secretary appointed by Keir Starmer to oversee a review of sentencing.

As parliament resumes on Tuesday, the government will confirm its U-turn on its early release scheme, which would have seen thousands of prisoners released early as part of a plan to ease prison overcrowding.

About 5,000 prisoners had been due to be released early from October under the plans, down from 6,000 after ministers intervened to exempt rapists and “serious” child sexual abuse offenders.

However, David Gauke, the former Conservative minister who led Starmer’s independent review of sentences, warned of the “stresses and strains” from choosing to run prison capacity at a “red hot” level, even as he recognised options available to Burnham were limited.

“He is in a bind. I have some sympathy for any government that is wrestling with this, but that is why we came forward with the recommendations we came forward with,” Gauke told the Guardian.

“I am going to see what Alex Norris [the justice secretary] says in parliament, but my concern – and I hope this isn’t the case – is that they are essentially taking a big risk on prison capacity.”

Gauke said that Burnham’s political strategy was in contrast to his predecessor in that the new prime minister was “very sensitive to public opinion”.

He also said it would be “irresponsible” to release prisoners serving indefinite jail terms, which Burnham has pledged to abolish. The government is pinning some hope of increasing capacity on reducing the number of prisoners serving Imprisonment for Public Protection (IPP) sentences, and deporting more foreign prisoners more swiftly.

“In terms of public protection, releasing IPPs comes with much higher risks than the categories excluded from the early release scheme,” said Gauke, who examined them when he was justice secretary in Theresa May’s government but said it was clear from prison disciplinary records why such prisoners had not been released.

The intervention came as the government said on Monday night that the largest prison-building programme since the Victorian era would be accelerated through a £110m investment.

The funding will go towards speeding up the construction of hundreds of prison places with plans to add 14,000 extra spaces by 2031, and cells being created from existing space within prisons including unused offices, laundry rooms and other areas.

The Ministry of Justice also said on Monday there would be investment to buy new land to secure potential sites for future prisons.

“This government is serious about fixing the broken prison system we inherited, which is why we’ve already delivered more than 3,200 prison places in just two years,” said Norris.

However, the Conservatives sought to keep up political pressure over the early release scheme, saying that it left at least 23 categories of serious violent and sexual offences eligible for automatic early release, including trafficking, strangulation and assault by penetration.

“Labour’s plan to stop the release of dangerous criminals is to release a whole new group of dangerous criminals,” said the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, who called for a delay to the scheme and emergency primary legislation to exclude the worst offenders.

The victims minister, Alex Davies-Jones, insisted during interviews on Monday that “release does not mean freedom” for those let out under the early release scheme.

“When these offenders come out of prison, the presumption will be that they will all be placed on a GPS monitoring tag,” she said.

In terms of capacity, she told the BBC’s Today programme: “We will have capacity in the system with those numbers but we will run it very tight, which is why we have been tasked to look at what more we can do.”

A leading police chief, meanwhile, warned that tracking people let out of prison under the early release scheme would be an additional challenge on the strained resources of police officers.

Jason Hogg, the chief constable of Thames Valley police, told LBC on Monday: “The police haven’t received any additional funding for this additional work, so I’m going to be having to move resources away from one area of business to another to seek out, arrest and bring before the court individuals who don’t follow the restrictions that they will be set.”

articles.title: Dry weather sewage discharges soar as water companies face scrutiny
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: 7,280 suspected illegal spills in rivers and sea recorded in first five months of 2026

The number of suspected illegal discharges of raw sewage into rivers and seas by water companies duri...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: 7,280 suspected illegal spills in rivers and sea recorded in first five months of 2026

The number of suspected illegal discharges of raw sewage into rivers and seas by water companies during dry weather increased significantly during the first five months of 2026.

Dumping raw sewage into waterways during dry spells via overflows amounts to pollution. It is considered a breach of the permits given to water companies and is illegal. Discharging during dry weather increases the toxicity of the sewage pollution entering waterways. Rivers have less flow and volume, and there is no rainwater to dilute the sewage pollution entering the waterway.

Last year, in what regulators said was tougher action on sewage pollution, water companies in England were for the first time required to report to the Environment Agency the number of times they discharged raw sewage from combined sewer overflows during dry weather. A dry day spill is flagged when an overflow operates despite little to no rainfall that day and the previous day.

In 2025, water companies in England and Wales reported 8,576 dry spill pollution discharges. But according to freedom of information requests submitted by Environment Agency whistleblower Robert Forrester, the pollution is getting worse, not better, despite the regulator’s promise of tougher action.

Between January and May this year alone, water companies discharged raw sewage into rivers and seas during dry weather 7,280 times. The data is comparable as it is based on the same instruction and taken from the same data recording system.

The water industry said the figures were as yet unverified and it was too early to describe them as dry spills.

Forrester, an Environment Agency officer for more than 20 years, revealed failures by the agency to take on water companies’ illegal practices before leaving his job.

“Dry day spills will almost always be deliberate and illegal, otherwise there would be non-stop raw sewage spilling from pipes,” said Forrester.

“The huge increase in a much drier year appears to show that water companies have quotas of sewage to dump and will do whatever the weather, and whatever the risk to the public and the environment. Making money is the primary focus.” He said the regulator was no deterrent to the actions of the water companies.

“This level of criminality shows that water companies do not believe they, or the government, will ever do anything meaningful to stop them.”

Combined sewer overflows are an emergency system designed to be used in extreme weather to relieve pressure in the sewage system. But decades of underinvestment by the privatised water industry have led to the outflows being used regularly to discharge sewage.

In the first five months of 2026, South West Water, which operates across Devon, Cornwall and parts of Dorset and Somerset, discharged raw sewage on dry days 1,299 times. This compares with 2,451 times during the whole of 2025.

Water companies are facing outrage across the country for discharging raw sewage via storm outflows in August following the first moderate spell of rain after more than six weeks of drought. Public mapped data revealed water companies including Southern Water and South West Water discharging raw sewage from storm overflows within hours of the first significant rain.

In the south-west, after weeks of drought, the company’s own data suggested it discharged sewage into rivers and the sea for a combined total of almost 300 hours in the third week of August.

Ed Tyldesley, a Liberal Democrat county councillor in north Devon, said the company’s own figures showed 664 separate spills across 184 sites despite just 16.5mm of rain across the south-west.

“They are using a storm system when there are no storms. It is unbelievable. The worrying thing is that this all seems to be getting worse,” he said.

Tyldesley said he had been told by the water company that its live monitoring data could sometimes contain false readings. “That leaves two possibilities. Either the South West Water data is correct and sewage was discharged into our rivers and seas for 299 hours in a single week, or their legally mandated monitoring system is so unreliable that hundreds of apparent sewage spills are being reported to the public, which may not actually have happened.”

A spokesperson for Water UK, the trade association for the water industry, said: “These are unverified figures, and it is too early to describe them as dry day spills. Nonetheless, no spill is ever acceptable. Water companies are working to end them as fast as possible by tripling investment. Companies are investing £12bn to halve spills from storm overflows by 2030, including relining and sealing sewers to prevent groundwater infiltration – one of the main causes of dry day spills.”

South West Water has said the company publishes near real-time monitoring data, which has to be validated before being used for regulatory reporting.

“Storm overflow activations can happen for a range of reasons and aren’t determined by rainfall figures alone.

“We continue to invest in our monitoring and are spending record amounts to reduce storm overflow use across the region. We’re reviewing the locations raised by the councillor so we can provide a full response.”

A Defra spokesperson said: “It is totally unacceptable that some water companies are failing to deliver value for money for customers and polluting our rivers, lakes and seas.

“After years of failure, we have taken immediate action to make water companies more accountable, and, for the first time ever, they are now required to report dry day spills as pollution incidents, providing the government with the evidence to go after water companies where performance falls short.”

articles.title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
articles.excerpt:
Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of people

The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were...
articles.body_text:
Watch: BBC's Lyse Doucet reports on the biggest cross-border movement of people

The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind.

"It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.

The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins.

"But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.

Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.

They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.

Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.

Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.

Trucks carrying returnees parked along the highway near the border

The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR.

"In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan.

"We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.

It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.

Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all.

"I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry.

"We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says.

"But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."

Afghan returnees deported from Pakistan arriving at the Torkham crossing

Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.

The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law".

Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.

The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".

In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.

The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".

The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".

But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".

Zarina, 40, is among the million Afghan who have returned this year alone

Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children.

Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?

Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."

Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified.

"I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house.

"We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."

He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work.

"I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country.

Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.

Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.

But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.

Zarina says she is worried about the future of the girls who cannot attend school in Taliban-run Afghanistan

At the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face.

"There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."

In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide.

The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition.

"No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.

But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".

Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.

The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.

But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states.

As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"

We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense.

All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.

Five years after the Taliban swept to power, does the West have any influence?

Iran drives out 1.5 million Afghans, with some branded spies for Israel

Divorce, smartphones and control - BBC sees how Taliban run Afghanistan

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy’s future could rest with ‘prosecution doctors’ as case echoes infamous Maine killings: expert
articles.excerpt: Retired Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Jack Lu said a not guilty by reason of insanity verdict would be no easy out, because the officials deciding Lindsay Clancy's release are viewed as "the pros...
articles.body_text:
Retired Massachusetts Superior Court Judge Jack Lu said a not guilty by reason of insanity verdict would be no easy out, because the officials deciding Lindsay Clancy's release are viewed as "the prosecutor's hired guns."

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

A retired Massachusetts Superior Court judge says that a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity wouldn't be an easy out for Lindsay Clancy, saying that "prosecution doctors" would be the ones deciding when she would be released, and are likely more inclined to keep her locked up.

Clancy, 36, faces three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of her children — Cora, Dawson and Callan, all under age 6 — who were found strangled at the family's home in January 2023.

Retired Massachusetts Superior Judge Jack Lu told Fox News Digital that even if Clancy is found not guilty by reason of insanity, she would likely face a significant amount of time in a mental institution.

ACCUSED NC KILLER MOM PLANS INSANITY DEFENSE — AS RETIRED JUDGE SAYS MORE MAY FOLLOW LINDSAY CLANCY STRATEGY

Lindsay Clancy and her attorney Kevin Reddington arrive for day 3 of deliberations in her murder trial. (Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger via AP)

He said a group of mental health officials would be responsible for periodically reviewing her commitment at the facility, but noted these are people who overwhelmingly side with prosecutors and usually testify on their behalf.

LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS COME ACROSS AS 'TONE DEAF,' 'UNCARING' AND 'SNARKY,' DEFENSE ATTORNEY SAYS

The empty Plymouth Superior Court jury box during the Lindsay Clancy murder trial in Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger via AP)

"They're viewed as an arm of the prosecution," Lu said of the officials. "I'm going to be very frank, they kind of view this through the lens of if in doubt, lock them up...The people making release decisions have a prosecutorial mindset."

Lu said, if Clancy is committed to a mental hospital, "I imagine she'd be committed year after year after year for some period of time."

"If you are committed on a mental health basis because of a major criminal case in Massachusetts, it is hard to get out... It is very difficult," he said.

He said there is another way for Clancy to be released from a mental institution if found not guilty by reason of insanity, which would be through the courts.

"The other way she could get out is if the government kept moving to commit her and the doctors did not really decide that she should be released, and then it goes to court and then a judge would decide whether she is a danger to herself or others," Lu said. "It could be more of a contested hearing, and if she were to win that contested hearing, that is the second way that she gets out."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Lindsay Clancy arrived for day 3 of deliberations. (Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledger via AP)

Clancy's case has drawn parallels with Constance Fisher, a then-24-year-old Maine woman who drowned her three children in a bathtub in 1954, according to the New York Times.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

She was committed to a mental hospital, and after several years, she returned home. She was accused of drowning three more children in 1967 and was sent back to the mental hospital, before she escaped and was found dead in the Kennebec River.

PROSECUTOR IN INFAMOUS KILLER MOM CASE SAYS WOMEN ON LINDSAY CLANCY JURY MAY BRING ‘STRANGE TWIST’ TO VERDICT

Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

The jury in Clancy's case, consisting of nine women and three men, led by a female foreperson, concluded a third day of deliberations on Monday without coming to a verdict.

The jurors asked Judge William Sullivan around 4 p.m. to be dismissed for the day, and will return on Tuesday morning to continue deliberations.

Adam Sabes is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Adam.Sabes@fox.com and on Twitter @asabes10.

articles.title: Grand Canyon water pipeline damaged again as flooding complicates repairs
articles.excerpt: Fox News senior national correspondent William La Jeunesse reports on search and rescue operations at the Grand Canyon after a flash flood left one person dead and 15 hikers missing. National Park Ser...
articles.body_text:
Fox News senior national correspondent William La Jeunesse reports on search and rescue operations at the Grand Canyon after a flash flood left one person dead and 15 hikers missing. National Park Service teams evacuated dozens by helicopter as search crews scoured the Kaibab Trail and areas along the Colorado River to locate unaccounted individuals.

The one pipeline that supplies water for millions of visitors in Grand Canyon was badly damaged by flash flooding over the weekend, setting up a complicated repair scenario and disrupting a yearslong project to upgrade the aging line across rugged terrain where helicopters are often needed for even basic maintenance.

Park officials estimate after conducting flyovers that about 40% of the pipeline sustained damage. The 12.5-mile long Transcanyon Waterline has suffered dozens of breaks in recent years. A more than $200 million repair and replacement project was well underway when the floods began.

The long-term impacts on the park’s infrastructure, visitors and year-round residents were not immediately clear.

BELOVED TEXAS CHIROPRACTOR KILLED IN GRAND CANYON FLASH FLOOD, 2 FRIENDS STILL MISSING AFTER HIKE

Floodwater and debris are seen in Bright Angel Canyon after a significant flash-flood event near Phantom Ranch on Aug. 29, 2026. (J. Thompson/NPS Photo)

"We anticipate miles of the pipeline being destroyed," Grand Canyon Deputy Superintendent Brian Drapeaux said.

A full survey of the devastation will not be completed until Tuesday at the earliest.

At least two people died in the floods, and one person remained missing as of Monday night after roughly 80 people were rescued over the weekend, according to officials.

The park stopped overnight accommodations, with officials saying significant water reductions are needed. This includes limiting shower time, turning off the tap while brushing teeth and flushing toilets selectively to protect the limited stored water on the South Rim, where most visitors frequent.

"They have got to keep law enforcement going, they have to keep rescue operations going, backcountry operations, park admin going, the clinic and the campground," longtime river runner and Grand Canyon hiker Tom Martin said, adding that the park has hauled water in tanker trucks in the past.

The pipeline, which was completed in the 1970s, has broken more than 85 times since 2010.

The pipeline moves water from one side of the canyon, down to its base, across a bridge and back up the other side of the rough landscape. Any attempt to fix a break from rock falls or flash floods is precarious and costly and can take time, so fixing the latest damage will be complicated.

Buildings are seen in a flood damaged Bright Angel Canyon at the Grand Canyon, Monday, Aug. 31, 2026, in Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona. (AP Photo/John Locher)

The pipeline upgrade project, which began in 2023, took more than a decade to design and fund. The project involves installing helicopter pads, building water treatment facilities and replacing several miles of pipeline. It also seeks to move the water intake for the pipeline further down the canyon to Bright Angel Creek, which would put it closer to Phantom Ranch, a popular lodge at the base of the canyon.

A 2018 evaluation of the project said key infrastructure for the intake would be outside of areas likely to flood.

Officials said even basic decisions proved to be complicated.

For example, the original pipe was aluminum, which is lighter and easier to move into the steep canyon but is more susceptible to breaking. Engineers chose a flex-steel material to balance weight and durability.

Even routine pipeline breaks lead to water restrictions. A decade ago, a hotel on the canyon’s rim that offers luxury dining and highlights its history hosting presidents had to reduce dishwashing and use paper plates and plastic utensils.

In 1995, a nearly month long repair on the pipeline required officials to truck in water.

The park had water conservation initiatives in place even before the latest flooding and damage.

MISSING GRAND CANYON HIKER, 83, RESCUED AFTER GETTING SEPARATED FROM COMPANION

Tourists look down into the Grand Canyon off of the south rim, Monday, Aug. 31, 2026, at Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona. (AP Photo/Josh Biggs)

The flooding has forced parts of the park to close, and more flooding was possible on Monday, according to the National Park Service.

"Consider changing your plans if you were going to hike, boat, or paddleboard to a slot canyon or normally dry wash. If you do still decide to recreate, check in at a nearby visitor center or ranger station," the park website reads.

Officials previously said that the repair and replacement project would allow the park to meet its water supply needs for at least the next 50 years.

As the original pipeline was nearing completion in the 1960s, more than a foot of rain fell, which flooded the inner canyon and caused 40% of the project to be destroyed, according to officials.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Algeria’s president seeks death penalty for those who start forest fires
articles.excerpt:
Algeria’s President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has called for the death penalty for anyone who deliberately starts a forest fire after at least 12 people died in wildfires in the country’s northeast.

Tebbo...
articles.body_text:
Algeria’s President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has called for the death penalty for anyone who deliberately starts a forest fire after at least 12 people died in wildfires in the country’s northeast.

Tebboune ordered Algeria’s justice minister on Sunday to submit a proposal by September 15 to amend the penal code to allow capital punishment for those convicted of intentionally setting forest fires, state media reported.

Algeria’s penal code already allows the death penalty for several offences, though the country has not carried one out since 1993.

Deliberately starting forest fires currently carries up to 30 years in prison, or life imprisonment in some cases.

Tebboune also ordered provincial governors to hand over all available information about the fires to security authorities, pointing to the possibility that some of the blazes were started deliberately.

“We saw videos and noticed that a number of fires broke out at the same time, at around 1am, which raises many questions,” he said.

His call came after Algeria observed three days of national mourning over the deaths of the 12 people in the provinces of Jijel, Bejaia, and Tizi Ouzou. At least 54 others were injured.

The president on Monday ordered authorities to compensate affected families and set up committees to assess losses and determine compensation for damaged property.

He instructed officials to restore electricity, gas, water and telecommunications in affected areas by Saturday at the latest, and told housing authorities to arrange repairs to damaged homes.

Tebboune said normal life should resume in the affected areas within a week.

At least 46 fires are still burning across the country, and a total of 193 fires have been recorded in the past 24 hours.

articles.title: Shein shares fall in long-awaited stock market debut
articles.excerpt:
Shein's founder Xu Yangtian, right, and the firm's financial director Poppy Bao at the Hong Kong Stock Exchange

Shares in fast-fashion giant Shein fell in their highly anticipated stock market debut ...
articles.body_text:
Shein's founder Xu Yangtian, right, and the firm's financial director Poppy Bao at the Hong Kong Stock Exchange

Shares in fast-fashion giant Shein fell in their highly anticipated stock market debut on Tuesday as the firm listed in Hong Kong after a long quest to go public.

It comes after failed attempts to list in the US and UK, as concerns were raised over issues including Shein's labour practices and its environmental impact.

Once estimated to be worth nearly $100bn (£74bn), Shein is now valued at around a quarter of that figure, as the firm faces other challenges like heated competition and trade tensions.

Shein became hugely popular, especially among younger people, due to its ability to source the very latest fashions at ultra-low prices through a vast network of factories in China.

At a ceremony to celebrate the listing, chief financial officer Leigh Gui said the company's model of selling large numbers of small orders with rapid payment options now reaches about 160 markets worldwide.

"Let global consumers enjoy the sound of fashion," he said after a gong was struck to mark the start of trading.

On Monday, Shein priced its shares at HK$48.56 each, raising ‌13.6 billion Hong Kong dollars ($1.7bn; £1.3bn) from the listing.

That gave the company a stock market valuation of $26.3bn.

Shein's shares fell by as much as 10% in early trading before the losses eased. At lunchtime, they were around 3.5% lower at just under 47 Hong Kong dollars each.

The disappointing debut suggests the market is not convinced that Shein's growth can make a "comeback", said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at investment bank Saxo.

Shein has more than 273 million active customers who placed a total of more than a billion orders in the year to the end of March 2026, the firm said in a filing ahead of the listing.

But Shein now faces higher costs, regulatory scrutiny and more competition, while investors are increasingly drawn towards technology companies, Chanana said.

For customers, the slump in Shein's shares is a sign that the firm's cheap prices are "becoming harder to sustain", which may lead to higher prices, she added.

The listing marks the largest new share sale in Hong Kong so far this year, which is being seen as a test of investor appetite for the fast fashion industry.

It is a rare "standalone" e-commerce firm that can be assessed on its own merits, fashion industry analyst Louise Deglise-Favre from research firm GlobalData.

Shares in rivals Asos and Boohoo have been battered in recent years as they face regulatory scrutiny and fierce competition.

"Investors have learned to be sceptical," while concerns over sustainability and ethical issues add to the complexity of Shein's share sale, Deglise-Favre said.

The truth behind your $12 dress: Inside the Chinese factories fuelling Shein's success

Shein was founded in China in 2008 and is now headquartered in Singapore.

The firm's long road to the stock market highlights the geopolitical pressures and regulatory scrutiny faced by Chinese companies with global ambitions.

The company once looked set for one of the largest stock market debuts ever by a Chinese firm, with Wall Street in its sights.

Its business had surged during the Covid-19 pandemic as people, stuck at home, turned to online retailers.

Shoppers shared clips of themselves trying on large numbers of its garments, a trend called Shein Hauls, boosting the company's online presence.

An initial public offering (IPO) in the US - by far Shein's largest market - would have offered it a chance to further increase its global profile and tap into Western financing.

But the firm faced resistance from US lawmakers, who objected to the planned listing over concerns of forced labour in Shein's factories. In response to such allegations, the company has said it takes a "zero-tolerance policy for forced labour".

It has also been accused of copying other designers' ideas. Shein has said "it takes all claims of infringement seriously" and that it respects the rights of all designers.

Shein also explored the possibility of making its stock market debut in London but faced similar opposition.

The BBC has contacted Shein for further comment.

In 2025, Shein shifted its attention to Hong Kong, with Chinese authorities approving the move in July this year.

"Shein ran out of venues that could take it," said Ashley Dudarenok, founder of Chinese market research firm ChoZan.

The company attempted to "look less Chinese" by shifting its headquarters to Singapore ahead of its IPO bid, but it never won political backing abroad nor assurances from Beijing, she added.

Shein is backed by a vast network of factories in China

"For Chinese companies increasingly shut out of Western exchanges, Hong Kong is fast becoming the only realistic path to market," Deglise-Favre said.

The move also coincided with Shein's publicity-shy founder Xu Yangtian making a rare public appearance during a major business conference in February.

Xu took to a stage in Guangdong, home to many of China's garment factories, to re-affirm his company's ties to Beijing.

He pledged investments in China's clothing industry, adding that the "nourishment" from the country has been "inseparable" from Shein's success.

Trade tensions and regulatory concerns mean Shein is navigating a very different landscape to when it first started exploring a potential IPO.

In July, it reported a $99m quarterly loss as its sales slowed after the US struck down an import duty exemption on small packages.

The exemption, known as the de minimis rule, had helped Shein and rival Temu grow rapidly as it allowed packages worth less than $800 to enter the US without incurring import duties.

Similarly, the European Union has imposed a €3 (£2.57; $3.50) tax on low-value imports.

The Iran war has also hit demand, raised costs and caused delays to deliveries in some markets, Shein has said.

Shein's fast-fashion model has come under scrutiny over its environmental impact

Its rivals are feeling the pressure too. In August, Temu-owner PDD reported lower-than-expected quarterly revenue.

Shein is also being investigated by US and European regulators over its business practices.

The company also needs to find ways to stand out from its rivals, that are now also using predictive technology to make their websites more appealing to shoppers, said Jason Hsu from Rayliant Global Advisors.

"Shein is not longer a unique player," Hsu said.

Despite these challenges some analysts still see strong potential for Shein.

Investors will be scrutinising whether the company can navigate these issues, such as shifting logistics out of China to avoid the US and EU's import fees, Deglise-Favre said.

The slump in the firm's valuation shows "genuine deterioration", but it is still backed by a "formidable supply chain" and a global reach, she added.

People are still buying the company's goods, but costs have weighed on its business and have shown that its business model does not generate profits in the way it once did, said Dudarenok.

As a listed company, Shein will need to "prove its margins still work in a world of tighter regulation, tariffs and more expensive customer acquisition," she added.

How US shoppers will be hit as 'de minimis' tariff exemption ends

Tech manufacturing has powered Asia - now it's a casualty of Trump's tariffs

articles.title: Madrid residents brace for noise and disruption from new F1 circuit
articles.excerpt:
City council emphasises economic case for Madring amid local outrage over disruption and environmental impact

Opponents of Madrid’s newly constructed Formula One circuit have accused the regional aut...
articles.body_text:
City council emphasises economic case for Madring amid local outrage over disruption and environmental impact

Opponents of Madrid’s newly constructed Formula One circuit have accused the regional authorities of putting profit before people’s wellbeing after tests for the inaugural Spanish Grand Prix at the track later this month yielded noise levels that were almost twice the legal decibel limit.

The regional government of Madrid and the city council are hoping that the 5.4km-long (3.3 miles) Madring circuit – which has been built in the north-east of the Spanish capital at a cost of €83m (£71m) – will attract visitors, boost the local economy and put the city firmly on the motor racing map. The Madring bills itself as “a perfectly connected circuit: just 20 minutes from the city centre”.

But recent track tests using Formula Three cars have worried local people who are taking legal action over the construction of the circuit and the noise it is expected to generate. The Stop F1 Madrid platform, which was formed a year ago, said neighbours had recorded average noise levels of 102.7 decibels during the tests, with peaks of between 107.7 and 109.1 decibels. The maximum noise level permitted in residential areas is 55 decibels.

“It’s not just about the dust and the noise,” said Antonio Ibáñez, a spokesperson. He said there had been complaints from people who argued it was impossible for them to work remotely during the tests, adding: “We’ve also spoken to people who have children with autism and they had to get them out of the area because of [all the distress].”

One of the group’s biggest worries is the huge numbers of people expected to descend on the area for the grand prix itself, putting an enormous strain on public transport and the local area. “An urban Formula One circuit is just a bad idea,” he said. “It’s a nonsense idea.”

Regional and city authorities have sought to reassure residents and are attempting to stress the economic benefits of the track. Borja Carabante, Madrid’s city councillor for urban planning, mobility and the environment, said measures, such as acoustic panels, would be put in place to minimise noise during the grand prix on 11-13 September.

He also said that the Formula Three cars used to test the track “make and emit more noise than Formula One cars, so there’ll be less noise on 13 September than there was during the tests”.

Carabante said the city council would work to ensure traffic disruption was kept to a minimum. But he called on the people of Madrid to celebrate the arrival of Formula One in the city: “We should be congratulating ourselves that Madrid is hosting such an important and significant event that will put us at the epicentre of great sporting events. It’s amazing news for all the people of Madrid and it’s putting Madrid on the map.”

The regional minister for housing, transport, and infrastructure, Jorge Rodrigo, said the event would be of huge economic benefit for Madrid, and well worth one weekend’s disruption. “It’s worth a little bit of sacrifice from all of us … given the profitability of this event for the Madrid region and the city of Madrid, and, above all, given how it’ll position us internationally.”

A spokesperson for the Madring said it was taking “all measures within our reach to minimise the disruption caused by the construction work and the event”, adding: “Protecting the wellbeing of local residents and reducing the environmental impact are a priority for the organisers, and we are therefore working continuously with the relevant authorities and various stakeholders to implement mitigation and improvement measures.”

But environmental groups have questioned the wisdom of building a grand prix circuit in a city where summer temperatures can exceed 40C (104F). According to Stop F1 Madrid , more than 700 trees have been felled or moved to make way for the track, while María Ángeles Nieto, a spokesperson for the Madrid Environmentalist platform, said a seasonal wetland that was home to amphibian species had been destroyed.

“Madrid is a city with significant temperature increases during the summer months – the entire city is a heat island,” said Nieto. “We’ve pointed out that this just exacerbates that heat island effect.”

Nieto said was “no justification whatsoever” for a track that would subject residents to “a living hell” for the duration of the grand prix and other possible events there.

“The people in charge of the city are prioritising the economic interests of Formula One over the wellbeing of the citizens in such an absolutely absurd and unnecessary way,” she said.

articles.title: John Healey invites October budget ideas from Treasury staff of all levels
articles.excerpt:
Chancellor says he wants everyone from apprentices to senior economists to take part in brainstorming exercise

John Healey has asked junior Treasury staff – including IT workers and apprentices – to ...
articles.body_text:
Chancellor says he wants everyone from apprentices to senior economists to take part in brainstorming exercise

John Healey has asked junior Treasury staff – including IT workers and apprentices – to send him ideas for his October budget, saying he will listen to all suggestions regardless of grade or profession.

The chancellor’s unorthodox approach comes as he faces a tricky autumn with expected inflation rises, sluggish growth and potential cuts from other departments to fund extra defence spending.

Healey, who was Andy Burnham’s surprise choice for chancellor, is understood to have written to staff at the Treasury campuses in London, Norwich, Leeds and Darlington asking them to send him ideas.

He said he did not only want to hear from economists but from staff not traditionally involved in policymaking. Those with the most interesting ideas will be invited to pitch to Healey in person.

A Treasury source said the move was designed to challenge “traditional Whitehall hierarchies” and that the chancellor was particularly looking for ideas focused on spreading growth around the country and boosting local industries, as well as measures to cut costs for families and businesses.

Healey has told staff he wants “everyone from apprentices, IT staff and junior officials to senior economists and private secretaries” to contribute to the exercise, and that he hopes October’s budget will include some of the ideas from the brainstorm.

A Treasury spokesperson said: “Just as we want growth in every postcode, we want ideas from every postcode. The chancellor wants to harness the talent in the Treasury and across the country to improve our communities and high streets, and give people and businesses a bit more breathing space.”

Healey told Sky News on Friday that this next phase was a “continuity of a Labour government with a change of leader”, saying he would not sacrifice fiscal discipline. He said a Burnham government “simply can’t deal with the problems we face as a country by maxing out the country’s credit card”.

Healey quit as defence secretary under Keir Starmer over a disagreement about defence spending, including cash for the defence investment plan and the timeline to increase defence spending to 3.5% of GDP. As chancellor, however, he has played down the prospect of setting out that timeline by the October budget.

“Fiscal discipline has been the bedrock of the government that I was part of for the first couple of years, as a Labour government since July 2024,” he told Sky. “We build on that, but it is not easy. It is not easy in a world in which you see global conflict, increasing dangers.”

The Financial Times has reported that Healey will most likely use the budget to fill the gap of about £5bn in the defence investment plan, partially funded by departmental cuts of about £1.2bn a year.

Burnham has said he will stick to Labour’s manifesto, which promises no increases in income tax, national insurance or VAT, though he said in a recent interview that the public needed to be realistic about what needed to be funded and how difficult more spending would be.

articles.title: Child trust fund firms face review over efforts to find who owns £1.5bn worth of pots
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: FCA pressures firms to do more to sort 760,000 accounts as watchdog urges families to use free tracking service

Child trust fund providers are being put under the spotlight to check they a...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: FCA pressures firms to do more to sort 760,000 accounts as watchdog urges families to use free tracking service

Child trust fund providers are being put under the spotlight to check they are treating savers fairly and doing all they can to reunite young people with lost accounts.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said about 760,000 accounts worth an average of £2,000 were yet to be claimed – more than £1.5bn in total – as it launched a review of the market.

The City regulator also urged parents and young adults to use a free checking service to see if they have a forgotten pot of money.

About 6.3 million children born between 1 September 2002 and 2 January 2011 had accounts opened for them under a government scheme designed to encourage saving.

Families received at least £250 and were encouraged to pay in more. While some parents did, others left it to the government to choose a provider.

The scheme closed in 2011, and existing accounts will continue to mature until 2029 as their owners turn 18.

The FCA said it would review whether banks, insurers and fund managers were being active enough in attempts to track down customers.

It will ask all 55 providers to explain the efforts they are making to trace customers who have lost touch with their accounts. It also plans to look at the barriers faced by parents and guardians of vulnerable people who may struggle to access their money.

The review will also look at how firms are checking that charges and fees are fair after the introduction of the consumer duty in 2023, a rule stating that financial firms must deliver good outcomes for their customers.

Chris Knight, the FCA’s director of insurance, said: “Child trust funds can help set young people up for the future. But too many risk losing touch with money that is rightly theirs. Our review will look at how firms are helping customers access their funds, providing fair value, and supporting vulnerable consumers and their families.”

The FCA warned about the cost of claims management companies offering to help people track down missing funds, but charging a fee to do so. It said it had seen cases where customers were charged £400 to locate an account, and others where firms charged a monthly subscription for a one-off tracing service.

Anyone looking for a fund can trace it for free through HMRC.

Knight said: “You don’t need to pay someone else to claim what’s rightfully yours – tracing and accessing your own child trust fund costs nothing, so think twice about handing over a chunk of your savings to a claims firm for a job you can do yourself.”

The regulator said it would ask more detailed questions of some firms, including those with large market shares or where there are potential indicators of consumer harm. It will report back next year, and may take action against providers if necessary.

articles.title: Duane 'Keffe D' Davis found guilty of first-degree murder in 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur
articles.excerpt:
Verdict reached in Tupac Shakur murder trial

A Nevada jury on Monday found Duane "Keffe D" Davis guilty of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon in the 1996 drive-by shooting death of r...
articles.body_text:
Verdict reached in Tupac Shakur murder trial

A Nevada jury on Monday found Duane "Keffe D" Davis guilty of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon in the 1996 drive-by shooting death of rap icon Tupac Shakur.

The verdict came after jurors began deliberating Monday following closing arguments in the closely watched trial, according to The Associated Press.

TUPAC MURDER TRIAL FACES ‘SNITCHES GET STITCHES’ PROBLEM BUT DEFENDANT'S GHOSTWRITER COULD BE KEY

A Nevada jury on Monday reached a verdict in the trial of Duane "Keffe D" Davis, who was charged with first-degree murder in the 1996 drive-by shooting death of rap icon Tupac Shakur. (Raymond Boyd/Getty Images)

The 16-member panel, including four alternates, heard nine days of testimony from 24 prosecution witnesses and three defense witnesses.

A gunman in a white Cadillac opened fire on a BMW carrying Shakur and Marion "Suge" Knight on Sept. 7, 1996, on the Las Vegas Strip.

Knight recovered from minor injuries. Shakur succumbed to his injuries six days later at 25 years old.

This is a breaking news story. Please check back for updates.

Sophia Compton is a Writer at Fox News Digital. Sophia was previously a business reporter covering finance, energy and tourism and has experience as a TV news producer. She graduated with a journalism degree in 2021 from the University of Hawaii at Manoa. Story tips can be sent to sophia.compton@fox.com.

articles.title: Five years after Saied’s power grab, Tunisia’s old grievances resurface
articles.excerpt:
Tunis, Tunisia – More than 15 years after Tunisians rose up to topple longtime President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, familiar grievances are again being heard on the streets from north to south.

A sloga...
articles.body_text:
Tunis, Tunisia – More than 15 years after Tunisians rose up to topple longtime President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, familiar grievances are again being heard on the streets from north to south.

A slogan from the 2011 revolution is being heard again: “employment, freedom and national dignity”.

This time, those demands are being fuelled by water cuts, electricity outages, rising prices, medicine shortages and a struggle to make ends meet, problems increasingly affecting Tunisians across social and economic divides.

But the anger is unfolding in a very different political environment.

The discontent comes as Tunisia marks five years since President Kais Saied suspended parliament, dismissed the government and began ruling by decree, moves he described as necessary to end years of political paralysis and corruption.

Many Tunisians welcomed the move at the time, frustrated with a political system that had failed to address the country’s economic problems after the 2011 revolution.

Five years later, many of those grievances remain while the political space for challenging those in power has narrowed sharply.

The decade that followed Ben Ali’s ouster brought competitive elections and greater space for political parties and civil society, but it also brought frequent government changes, political disputes and little improvement in the lives of many Tunisians.

Unemployment remained high, particularly among young people and in the country’s interior. Public services remained weak while rising prices continued to put pressure on household incomes. By the end of 2020, unemployment stood at 17.4 percent, according to the World Bank.

Tunisia also faced serious security threats, including attacks and political assassinations, adding to economic pressures and hitting sectors such as tourism.

Those frustrations helped Saied build support as an outsider promising to break with the traditional political establishment and what many Tunisians saw as a dysfunctional system.

On July 25, 2021, Saied suspended the Assembly of the Representatives of the People, dismissed Prime Minister Hichem Mechichi and lifted parliamentary immunity. He said he was acting to address a national crisis.

His opponents described the move as a coup.

Saied later dissolved parliament and oversaw the adoption of a new constitution in 2022 that significantly strengthened presidential powers.

Since then, opposition figures, journalists, lawyers and activists have been jailed or prosecuted in cases that rights groups describe as politically motivated. Civil society has faced increasing restrictions while critics have said institutional checks on presidential power have been weakened. Human Rights Watch, for example, has described the “conspiracy case” as part of a broader crackdown on dissent.

The case centres on allegations by Tunisian authorities that opposition politicians, lawyers, activists and other public figures were involved in a conspiracy against state security and sought to destabilise the country and undermine the government. The defendants included figures from different parts of the political spectrum.

In April 2025, a Tunis court sentenced 37 defendants to prison terms ranging from four to 66 years. Human Rights Watch described the case as politically motivated and criticised the trial for failing to provide adequate due-process protections.

On November 27, 2025, a Tunis appeals court upheld convictions against 34 of the 37 defendants, sentencing them to between five and 45 years in prison, and acquitted three.

Human Rights Watch and other rights groups continued to criticise the proceedings and describe the case as part of a wider crackdown on dissent.

The authorities reject those accusations and maintain that the defendants were prosecuted for serious offences against state security.

But the political transformation has yet to produce the economic turnaround Saied promised.

Many of Tunisia’s economic problems predate Saied. Years of underinvestment, financial pressures and ageing infrastructure have left public utilities and other state services struggling to meet demand.

But those failures have become harder to separate from Saied’s record because he came to power promising that a stronger state could overcome the weaknesses of the old political system.

This summer, temperatures approached 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) in parts of Tunisia, pushing electricity demand to record levels. Kairouan reached 49.8C (121.6F) on Thursday, according to the Tunisian Observatory for Weather and Climate. The Tunisian Company of Electricity and Gas introduced rotating power cuts in several regions, and the outages affected water-pumping stations in some areas.

Some people reported going days without running water. Bottled water shortages added to the pressure. Long queues formed outside shops and water trucks delivering supplies to some areas.

For Rebh, a 40-year-old cleaner from Tunis, the demands are not about luxuries but about being able to afford and access the basics of everyday life.

“People are tired. They are choosing to cross the sea and die [trying to reach Europe] instead. I hope we can stand together and find a solution now,” she told Al Jazeera. “We are not asking for the impossible. This is about water and electricity. We want to live as humans. We are feeling dead while we’re still alive.”

For many Tunisians, the shortages are part of a broader squeeze on purchasing power that has made it increasingly difficult to afford basic necessities.

The extreme heat has also put pressure on an already strained health system as doctors warned of increased pressure on emergency departments.

The point, however, is not that Saied created Tunisia’s economic problems. He did not.

The question is whether the more centralised system he built has delivered the more effective government he promised.

For journalist Manel Derbali, the change has been visible not only in the media but in the wider public space.

After the 2011 revolution, she said, Tunisians gained a new ability to speak openly and access information. Despite the protests and political turmoil of the period, journalists felt they were not alone in challenging those in power.

“After years of censorship and police repression, everything opened up. The journalist felt that the street was with you in one way or another,” Derbali said.

She said journalists also had channels to raise concerns about their working conditions and make proposals to officials, including through parliament and ministries, while access to decision-makers remained possible.

“After July 25, all of these spaces became closed,” she said.

Derbali said journalists now struggle to obtain even basic responses from government institutions with official bodies sometimes leaving requests unanswered for months.

“Unfortunately, history is repeating itself, and we have returned to relying on citizens’ videos to investigate and verify information,” she said.

Her account reflects a broader concern among critics of Saied that the institutions and public spaces that emerged after the revolution have been steadily weakened.

The current protests are not limited to Tunisia’s traditional opposition.

The Nafas movement, which has organised recent demonstrations in Tunis, seeks to bring together political parties and independent figures beyond the country’s established opposition to Saied. Its protests have also attracted citizens who had not previously taken part in political demonstrations.

Rabii Qassem, a member of the Nafas collective, said comparisons between the past five years and the decade after the revolution should not be reduced to whether Tunisia was simply better or worse before Saied.

“I’m not saying that Tunisia between 2011 and 2021 was paradise,” he said. “There were very serious crises: unemployment, corruption, economic fragility, political conflicts and a failure to achieve a large part of the revolution’s goals.”

But according to Qassem, that period also brought gains, including greater freedom of expression and protest, a stronger civil society, a more diverse media and elections that allowed for peaceful transfers of power.

“After July 25, the economic and social problems that already existed were not solved,” he said. “They were joined by a decline in political checks and balances, freedoms and the space for civil society.”

For Qassem, many of the demands raised in 2011 remain unresolved.

“Where is employment? Where is the water? Where are the public services? Where is the dignity?” he asked.

He said economic hardship and political repression have been increasingly feeding into each other as people struggling with rising prices and deteriorating services have also found fewer avenues to express their frustration.

That does not mean Tunisia is experiencing another 2011.

Many Tunisians remain wary of the political parties and politicians who dominated the decade after Ben Ali while Saied continues to have supporters who blame that period for years of economic stagnation and political instability.

Nor does every person angry about a water cut, electricity outage or rising price necessarily oppose the president.

But the protests show how economic and political grievances can increasingly overlap.

Before 2021, Tunisians could blame a democratic political system they saw as ineffective for failing to improve their lives.

After 2021, Saied dismantled much of that system and promised that a stronger presidency would deliver better government.

Five years later, many of the same grievances remain.

The difference is that the avenues for challenging them have become narrower.

“Employment, freedom and national dignity” was a demand of the revolution that ended Ben Ali’s rule.

Fifteen years later, Tunisians are again asking for jobs, basic services and greater freedoms – but now from a president who came to power promising to address the failures of the system that followed the revolution.

articles.title: Man shot and killed in Sydney home invasion was ‘targeted attack’, police believe
articles.excerpt:
Alleged offenders at large after man in his early 20s fatally shot in early hours of Tuesday

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily new...
articles.body_text:
Alleged offenders at large after man in his early 20s fatally shot in early hours of Tuesday

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A man in his early 20s has been fatally shot in an alleged home invasion in Sydney’s south-west that police believe was a “targeted attack”. A homicide investigation is under way, with the alleged offenders still at large.

Acting supt Gretchin Atkins said the man, who was yet to be formally identified, was at his Glen Alpine home with his family in the early hours of Tuesday morning when multiple individuals allegedly broke in.

Emergency services were called to the property at about 3.40am, Atkins said, where officers found the man with a gunshot wound. He died at the scene.

Officers were told the unknown offenders fled the scene shortly before police arrived.

“We believe at this point in time it is a targeted attack – that is all the information that we’ve been able to gather at this time,” Atkins said. “Everything is certainly subject to our inquiries.”

A crime scene has been established and an investigation is under way, with the assistance of the New South Wales crime command’s homicide squad.

Atkins said police had confirmed there were “multiple” alleged perpetrators behind the attack but there was “a lot we don’t know”.

“We are appealing to any person who was in the area, who saw, whether cars or people, who can assist us with our our current investigation, our inquiries,” she said.

The victim was only known to police for a traffic offence, Atkins said, and otherwise had no known criminal involvement. She said his family were assisting with inquiries.

Atkins also confirmed police were “aware” of reports of a social media post shared by an alleged Sydney gangland figure on Tuesday, claiming a shooting had been a case of mistaken identity.

“A young man has lost his life today and that’s obviously just tragic,” she said. “There were family who were home and, as I said, they’re assisting us and being very, very helpful.

“It’s an active crime scene and we’re obviously waiting for a lot of that information from our forensics who are on the scene.”

The incident comes three days after a separate home invasion in Guilford where a 28-year-old man was fatally shot, also in the early hours of the morning. NSW police made no suggestion the cases were linked.

It also follows the separate kidnapping murder of 85-year-old Chris Baghsarian earlier this year, who was abducted from his home in Sydney’s north in a case of mistaken identity.

articles.title: Roughly 80 Americans still unaccounted for after Himalayan disaster kills 903, officials say
articles.excerpt:
Isha Foundation coordination leader Jyoti Jankowski discusses efforts to locate the missing people in the deadly Nepal-Tibet floods on 'Fox & Friends Weekend.'

Roughly 80 Americans remain unaccounted...
articles.body_text:
Isha Foundation coordination leader Jyoti Jankowski discusses efforts to locate the missing people in the deadly Nepal-Tibet floods on 'Fox & Friends Weekend.'

Roughly 80 Americans remain unaccounted for following the catastrophic Himalayan flood last Wednesday that killed hundreds of people, the State Department said.

The update marks a decrease from a previous estimate of at least 90 Americans who went missing near the Nepal-China border.

"We can confirm that 13 American citizens have made their way to safety in Nepal," a State Department spokesperson told Fox News.

Meanwhile, Nepal’s death toll has risen to 903, while the number of people still unaccounted for has nearly doubled to roughly 4,200, according to an update from local officials Sunday.

TRAPPED NEPALI WORKERS PULLED FROM HYDROPOWER TUNNEL AFTER CATASTROPHIC FLOODING

A drone view shows mud covering properties following a flash flood at Trishuli in Nuwakot district, Nepal, August 26, 2026. (REUTERS/Stringer)

According to officials, the disaster occurred in north-central Nepal when a distant slope failure involving a glacier triggered a rapidly moving debris flow that traveled roughly 62 miles downstream before striking a populated area. Footage from the disaster showed a massive surge of water and debris suddenly rushing through the valleys, engulfing buildings in its path.

On Sunday, a spokesperson for Nepal’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs provided an update on the toll.

"So far, 903 bodies have been recovered from the areas and about 4200 people are still unaccounted for. Over 10,000 people have been rescued from the regions, including over 323 foreign nationals. As per the available data, about 590 foreign nationals are still missing, from 39 countries," the spokesperson said.

Twenty-two of the missing Americans were part of a pilgrimage affiliated with a Tennessee-based nonprofit group, Isha Foundation coordination leader Jyoti Jankowski told Fox News Saturday. They were inside an immigration building when the flooding struck the area, Jankowski said.

MORE THAN 3,000 MISSING AFTER COLOMBIA EARTHQUAKE AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROVIDES $15.5 MILLION IN RELIEF

A drone view shows a man walking next to damaged buildings and houses covered in mud near the Likhu River following deadly flash floods and mudslides in Devighat, Nuwakot district, Nepal, on Aug. 30, 2026. (REUTERS)

Authorities said Nepal is coordinating with neighboring countries and the international community to provide relief, with supplies already arriving from countries including India and China.

More supplies are expected to arrive from the U.S., United Arab Emirates, Myanmar, Qatar, the U.K., Australia, the Republic of Korea, Japan, New Zealand, Malaysia, Singapore, Bangladesh, Pakistan and other international organizations, officials said.

"Relief and humanitarian assistance are being provided in the affected areas. We are deeply grateful to our friends and partners for their solidarity, goodwill and generous offers of support at this difficult time," the spokesperson said.

DEATH TOLL FROM MUDSLIDES, FLOODING AT NEPAL-CHINA BORDER CLIMBS PAST 670; NEARLY 3,000 MISSING

Employees retrieve banknotes near a bank covered in sludge after flash floods in Trishuli in Nepal's Nuwakot district on Aug. 30, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

The State Department said last Wednesday that it was "monitoring the situation and is deploying a disaster response advisor to the region to support response efforts."

"The Department will also provide $500,000 in assistance through its global award with Catholic Relief Services, supporting emergency shelter, relief items, and water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance to flood-affected communities," the department said.

According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) investigators remain uncertain whether the initial failure was a landslide incorporating part of a glacier or a glacial collapse, in which a portion of a glacier breaks off and rapidly moves downslope with surrounding debris.

The glacier-related event resulted in a magnitude 5.2 earthquake, according to the USGS. A second seismic event was recorded approximately three hours later, generating energy equivalent to a magnitude 4.2 earthquake.

"The glacial debris contained water and ice that rapidly melted, picking up more material and water as it flowed downslope in the existing stream and river channels, creating a fast-moving, far-traveled landslide and flood laden with boulders and other rubble," the agency said.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

articles.title: Trump calls Hollywood a 'total disaster,' pushes federal tax incentive for film after meeting with Jon Voight
articles.excerpt:
