articles.title: James Cleverly resigns from shadow cabinet to run for mayor of London
articles.excerpt:
Shadow minister for housing, communities and local government to resign with immediate effect

James Cleverly has resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for mayor of London.

The Tory heavyweight, wh...
articles.body_text:
Shadow minister for housing, communities and local government to resign with immediate effect

James Cleverly has resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for mayor of London.

The Tory heavyweight, who was once home and foreign secretary and is shadow minister for housing, communities and local government, told the Sunday Times he will resign with immediate effect.

The MP for Braintree, who lost his bid to lead the Conservatives to Kemi Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has lurched to the right. On breaking the news to Badenoch, Cleverly told the Sunday Times: “She took it very well. Kemi has been very gracious.”

He added: “Our route to getting Kemi in No 10 has got to be through success in London,” he said. “It’s a business city, entrepreneurialism, arts, culture. I don’t buy the lazy idea that London is a Labour city. It represents the philosophical heart of the Conservative party.”

Cleverly’s resignation comes in advance of the Conservative party conference in October, where he is expected to make his case to party members.

According to the Sunday Times, sources close to Badenoch said she was “gutted” about the news but added that she “is delighted that someone of his calibre wants to put himself forward to be Conservative nominee for mayor of London”.

Cleverly had kind words for Badenoch. “Frankly, Kemi is doing really well now. She’s getting great cut-through. It took longer than any of us would have liked, but she’s getting it,” he said.

Sadiq Khan is halfway through his third term as mayor. He has not stated whether he will run for a fourth term in the contest to be held in May 2028. Susan Hall was the Tory candidate in 2024 but lost to Khan, who was declared the winner with 43.8% of the vote.

If Khan does step down, the Labour MP for Brent Central and Brent South, Dawn Butler, is expected to throw her hat in the ring, having previously revealed her desire for the job.

Cleverly is the most senior Tory politician to run for mayor of London in recent times. Making his bid, he said Khan was “asleep at the wheel” and accused him of using the role as a stepping stone for a higher-profile position.

“Sadiq has been trying to get out of that job for quite a while. He went in with the intention of doing what Boris [Johnson] did, using it as a high-profile platform to get him his next big job in government. There has been lots of posturing, very little delivery. Lots of picking rows with the president of America, less focus on bringing down street crime. It wouldn’t surprise me if he bows out for 2028. He’s lost the passion for the job.”

Days before Keir Starmer stood down as prime minister, he handed Khan a peerage, potentially opening the door to him joining Andy Burnham’s cabinet in future. However, while Burnham and Khan have worked closely together over the years and have a shared understanding of the challenges of devolution, it is understood Khan has told the former Manchester mayor that he has no wish to be a minister in his government.

articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: Woke Virginia tears down statue of Geneva Convention pioneer
articles.excerpt:
Cully Stimson spoke to Fox News Digital about the need for new Smithsonian leadership, calling its portrayal of American history "bile" that should be "ripped out, root and branch."

Do not adjust you...
articles.body_text:
Cully Stimson spoke to Fox News Digital about the need for new Smithsonian leadership, calling its portrayal of American history "bile" that should be "ripped out, root and branch."

Do not adjust your calendars. You may have seen images this week of Confederate statues coming down in Richmond’s capitol grounds, and thought we had slipped back in time to the tumult of 2020, but no. Rather, the commie Commonwealth of Virginia is still tearing down American history in the year of our Lord 2026.

As bad as the removal of all of these monuments has been, this particular round of damnatio memoriae on Friday, captured in its illiberal net the statue of a man named Dr. Hunter Holmes McGuire, whose work provided a major contribution to the Geneva Convention, the global gold standard of wartime humanitarian rules.

McGuire served as a Confederate surgeon for almost the entirety of the Civil War, saving countless lives. One life he failed to save was that of General Thomas "Stonewall" Jackson, who died under the doctor’s care. A Jackson statue also came down on Friday.

Statues of Stonewall Jackson, William "Extra Billy" Smith and Dr. Hunter Holmes McGuire are loaded onto a truck after being removed from their plinths in Capitol Square, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026 in Richmond, Va. (Mike Kropf/Richmond Times-Dispatch via Getty Images)

GENDER EQUITY, DEI, CLIMATE ACTION: HOW THE SMITHSONIAN'S WOKE PUSH 'INFILTRATED' AMERICA'S MOST BELOVED ZOO

Once again, the good Dr. McGuire could not save Stonewall.

It was under Jackson’s command in 1862 that McGuire established a new humanitarian principle of warfare that we still have with us today, not just in the United States, but across the world.

In May 1862, after the First Battle of Winchester, 6 Union army doctors were captured. It was then that McGuire convinced a reluctant Jackson to release them, and established, with Northern agreement, the Winchester Accord, after which both sides released doctors as non-combatants.

McGuire himself would be released by the North under the accord in 1864, and would go on to be present for the Confederate surrender at Appomattox Courthouse.

The Winchester Accord would be adopted by the Geneva Convention, offering protection to medical personnel in wars that they still enjoy today, and yet, despite all of this, his statue was toppled, just like all the others.

FILE - A statue of Confederate General Thomas "Stonewall" Jackson is removed after years of a legal battle over the contentious monument, in Charlottesville, Virginia, the U.S, July 10, 2021. (REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein/File Photo)

As usual, the destroyers of monuments brook no nuance in their march to destroy American history. If you wore the wrong uniform, your statue has to go and you have to be disgraced.

According to Democratic state Senator Mike Jones, McGuire’s statue had to be removed because, "I remembered seeing white only, colored only pictures in my mother’s scrapbook, and so to have that as a visual and then for these things to remain to remind this area of what took place, I think it’s wrong."

I’m sorry, but the fact that Jones is made uneasy by metal statues because they remind him of racism that occurred 70 years ago is the kind of silly claptrap that should have been left in the madness of 2020, and yet here we are.

A statue of Dr. Hunter Holmes McGuire, Confederate surgeon, stands in Capitol Square, July 20, 2022 in Richmond, Virginia. (Julia Rendleman for The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Allow me to go a bit further and argue that if you took the accomplishments of every person involved with having McGuire’s statue removed, they would not begin to equal his contributions to the humanization of modern military conflict.

It really is incredible. Day and night, night and day, the progressive left goes on and on about alleged war crimes committed by Israel, or the United States, and yet in their ignorance and simple-mindedness they are defaming a man who played a key role in creating the definitions of those very alleged crimes.

TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED

The same people who freak out with hair afire when the Trump administration tries to make the Smithsonian museums just a skosh more patriotic, are perfectly happy tearing down a statue of a man whose work saved thousands, maybe millions of lives.

Democrats will insist that unlike in 2020, when mobs just tore statues down willy-nilly, this decision went through a process run by democratically elected officials, and sure. But we all know that there is never a conservative on the blue ribbon panels they create to destroy Southern heritage.

The very slight silver lining in all of this is that McGuire’s statue, as well as the other two removed on Friday, will be moved to battlefield sites by the Shenandoah Valley Battlefields Foundation.

A spokesperson for that vital organization said, "Preservation is more about the future than the past … At the core of all we do is the belief that our shared history can unite the people of our nation; that there is strength and inspiration for our own times to be found in the struggles of the past."

But those statues belong where they were, in the place of honor the capitol originally provided.

Make no mistake, reports of the demise of Woke 1.0 aren’t just exaggerated, they are nonsense, as Friday’s statue removals prove, and our fight against this anti-historical intolerance must not wane, but rather grow in its strength and dedication.

David Marcus is a columnist living in West Virginia and the author of "Charade: The COVID Lies That Crushed A Nation."

articles.title: Triathlete who survived alligator attack tells harrowing story of his escape: 'I got super lucky'
articles.excerpt:
Jonathan Bruney tells OutKick about his close encounter with 5-foot alligator in Savannah River while training for triathlon.

A triathlete who survived an alligator attack in the Savannah River share...
articles.body_text:
Jonathan Bruney tells OutKick about his close encounter with 5-foot alligator in Savannah River while training for triathlon.

A triathlete who survived an alligator attack in the Savannah River shared his story with OutKick OutDoors.

Jonathan Bruney took a trip to the Georgia/ South Carolina border for what he thought would be a routine day of training for an upcoming Ironman competition.

"This was a work trip for me as a coach to bring my athletes down to the river on a recon course day, is what we call it," Bruney explained.

BOATER SCARED OFF ALLIGATOR, THEN USED ROPE TO STOP BLEEDING AFTER FLORIDA WOMAN LOST ARM

While he was leading the pack, Bruney felt a bump on his elbow that turned the whole day into a fight for survival. (iStock)

"We all went down to Augusta, we got ready to swim, and this was just going to be a nice, easy zone-two, low-heart-rate day. Just going through each portion of the course."

While he was leading the pack, Bruney felt a bump on his elbow that turned the whole day into a fight for survival.

FLORIDA MAN GIVES AN INCREDIBLE INTERVIEW ABOUT HOW HE FOUGHT OFF AN ALLIGATOR WITH A FISHING POLE

"I was breathing and sighting on my left side … and he was on my right. That’s when my elbow felt the brute of the force."

Bruney thought the alligator, which he described to be anywhere between five and six feet, was a log.

"I wasn’t even thinking gator," said Bruney. "I’m thinking, ‘Okay, big log floating in the river.’ But then I looked to my right. I’m like, ‘Okay, this is a lot worse than a log.’"

Almost immediately, Bruney's fight or flight instincts kicked into overdrive.

Bruney explains that he learned about the eyes being sensitive spots from watching "Shark Week."

FLORIDA WILDLIFE OFFICIALS CONFIRM 13-FOOT GATOR KILLED ORLANDO WOMAN WITH 'DEATH ROLL' ON RIVER

"This thing’s big enough to barrel roll and rip the arm off if I don’t get away quickly," he recalls.

His next move may have ultimately saved his life, or at the very least, his arm.

"I did have two moderate punches, but that didn’t do anything… [I] went up the snout and squeezed the eye."

Bruney explains that he learned about the eyes being sensitive spots from watching "Shark Week" (who says you can't learn anything from TV shows).

After making it to shore, Bruney wasn't just worried about his own safety, but for the safety of his fellow athletes, too.

"I hope this gator doesn’t bite one of my athletes," he said.

None of the swimmers had their phones on them, so a good samaritan had to dial 9-1-1.

While that was taking place, a friend of Bruney's was able to stop the bleeding using a cord from his swim buoy.

NEARLY 2,000 OCEAN RESCUES OCCUR AS DANGEROUS SURF SLAMS POPULAR BEACHES THIS SUMMER

Bruney credits the police officers and EMTs, who were first to arrive on the scene, with keeping him calm and treating his wounds. (iStock)

By the time the first responders arrived, Bruney was starting to feel dizzy and his entire arm was running cold.

He credits the police officers and EMTs, who were first to arrive on the scene, with keeping him calm and treating his wounds.

"The police officers, they came on scene pretty quickly. I mean, within a few minutes I heard their sirens," Bruney said. "They actually wrapped my arm up. Pretty good props to them for knowing what to do. And then the ambulance came."

While the doctors cleared him to continue training for his competition, Bruney admits there was a moment of doubt.

But after giving it some thought, he said there was no way he was going to let this deter him.

"Being able to remove my race entry, that’s not on the books. I can’t do that."

When I asked him whether he would ever go back in the water, Bruney didn't hesitate.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

"We’ll be back in there," he said, confidently.

articles.title: Artemis II astronauts receive nation's highest space honor for their successful moonshot
articles.excerpt:
Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen received the Congressional Space Medal of Honor

The Artemis II astronauts who flew around the moon in April received the US’s highest spa...
articles.body_text:
Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen received the Congressional Space Medal of Honor

The Artemis II astronauts who flew around the moon in April received the US’s highest space honor on Friday.

Donald Trump presented the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the three Americans and one Canadian whose lunar flyby for the US space agency Nasa set a new distance record for humanity.

Nasa’s administrator, Jared Isaacman, and other dignitaries took part in the packed ceremony at Houston’s Johnson Space Center, home to mission control. The president used the occasion to announce the creation of a US space academy for the nation’s space force as well as Nasa and the commercial space community.

“Space is the hot thing,” Trump told the crowd, adding that the academy’s location has yet to be determined.

Cmdr Reid Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen, a Canadian, became the first astronauts to travel to the moon in more than half a century, coming within 4,067 miles (6,545km) while test-driving Nasa’s new Orion capsule. They were the first to launch onboard Nasa’s new moon rocket, a 30-story behemoth that had soared only once before from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center.

While they didn’t stop at the moon, the four set the stage for next year’s Artemis III docking rehearsal in orbit around Earth. Artemis IV’s moon landing by two astronauts, near the lunar south pole, could follow as soon as 2028.

Trump said Americans will land back on the moon before his second presidency ends. Mars is next – “very shortly”, he said.

The president called the newest recipients “four intrepid space heroes”. He pointed out that they did not do it alone, thanking all who contributed to the Artemis II mission.

“There are no finer humans we could have sent as our ambassadors to the stars,” Isaacman added.

Wiseman and his crew are in good company, with only 30 astronauts receiving the prestigious honor before them. Many of the recipients were honored posthumously following their spaceflight-related deaths.

Apollo 11 commander Neil Armstrong – whose phrase “that’s one step for man, one giant leap for mankind” gripped the world when he became the first person to walk on the moon on 20 July 1969 – was the first to receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor.

President Jimmy Carter awarded six of these medals in 1978, which also went to Alan Shepard, the first American in space; John Glenn, the first American in orbit; and Apollo 8 commander Frank Borman, whose 1968 mission marked humanity’s first lunar voyage.

The most recent recipients were Doug Hurley and Bob Behnken, the first astronauts to launch aboard a SpaceX rocket. Coming nine years after the space shuttle program’s close, their 2020 test flight to the International Space Station restored the US’s ability to launch crews from home soil. Joe Biden awarded them the medals in 2023, during the third year of his presidency.

Dozens of astronauts participated in the ceremony, including Apollo 17 moonwalker Harrison Schmitt, who is now 91 – and the four men assigned to Nasa’s upcoming Artemis III mission.

Schmitt noted that his mission – Apollo’s last moonshot – was the most productive lunar exploration yet.

“Soon to be surpassed by Artemis,” he said of active astronauts standing behind him.

Nasa plans a sustainable moon base staffed by astronauts and robots near the lunar south pole, where permanently shadowed craters are thought to hold tons of frozen water that could be turned into rocket fuel and drinking water. China is eyeing the same region.

“The second space race has begun,” Nasa’s deputy administrator, Matthew Anderson, said.

As the two-hour ceremony came to a close, the Artemis II astronauts presented Trump with his own blue flight jacket complete with space patches, which they had promised him while visiting him in the Oval Office after their mission.

The president then hustled over to mission control to call the three US astronauts onboard the International Space Station. He informed them of the new US space academy, then briefly handed the phone to two of their spouses for a quick hello.

articles.title: RSS chief’s visit to US denounced as ‘goodwill tour’ for Hindu nationalism
articles.excerpt:
An event in New York City featuring a prominent Hindu nationalist is being promoted as an invitation to send a positive message that “the world is one family”.

But an array of faith groups, advocacy ...
articles.body_text:
An event in New York City featuring a prominent Hindu nationalist is being promoted as an invitation to send a positive message that “the world is one family”.

But an array of faith groups, advocacy organisations and unprivileged-caste organisations say they are not convinced. They fear Saturday’s rally, held at Madison Square Garden, is instead a high-profile effort to whitewash a record of discrimination and violence.

At issue is the Universal Oneness Celebration, hosted by the American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, a nonprofit that purports to advance “greater peace and harmony”.

One of its keynote speakers, however, will be Mohan Bhagwat, the leader of the Hindu paramilitary organisation Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). His organisation has been accused of embracing discriminatory policies and stoking violence against minorities, including India’s Muslim, Christian and Sikh populations.

Protests are expected outside Madison Square Garden to denounce Bhagwat’s appearance.

“This is a movement that has normalised mob violence against Muslims, attacks on Muslim men in relationships with Hindu women and the bulldozing of Muslim homes,” said Safa Ahmed, a Muslim community organiser in North Carolina who has travelled to New York to join the protests.

She told Al Jazeera she is sceptical about the event organisers’ claims about embracing the world as “one family”.

“They may speak about unity, but it’s in stark contrast with the bloody reality faced by minorities in India,” she said.

Advocates say that Hindu nationalist groups are working to expand their influence in the United States, where roughly 2.5 million Hindus live.

To do that, they have utilised a variety of appeals to soften the image of the RSS, such as celebrations of Hindu culture and campaigns to highlight anti-Hindu discrimination.

Sravya Tadepalli, the deputy executive director of Hindus for Human Rights, sees Saturday’s rally as part of that trend. Her group opposes the event.

“This is kind of a goodwill tour to improve the public image of the RSS, which is a fascist paramilitary organisation that has engaged in decades of communal violence against religious minorities in South Asia,” Tadepalli told Al Jazeera.

“The organisations behind this have pitched it as a broad appeal to Hindu history with an emphasis on inclusivity when, in reality, the RSS advocates for the exact opposite.”

Critics have pointed out, however, that Hindu nationalists have also sought to cultivate links with the global far-right, emphasising a shared belief in the purported threats posed by Islam and secular elites.

The RSS is widely considered the ideological parent of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which has ruled India since 2014 and sought to remake the country along Hindu nationalist lines.

In remarks to the 2024 National Conservatism Conference in Washington, DC, BJP Vice President Ram Madhav said that conservatives in the West should view India as an example of how to defeat what he called the “left, liberal, Marxist, radical Islamist cabal”.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who entered politics as an RSS cadre before becoming the head of the BJP, has championed Hindu nationalism throughout his leadership.

Like Bhagwat, he has also taken his message on the road, to speak to overseas supporters in the US.

In September 2019, for instance, the prime minister addressed a crowd of 50,000 at a “Howdy, Modi!” rally in the state of Texas.

The event underscored Modi’s appeal among Indians living abroad and was one of the largest such events in US history. US President Donald Trump, another far-right leader, even joined Modi on stage.

But such appearances were controversial too. Before becoming prime minister in 2014, Modi was banned from entering the US because of his leadership during a 2002 massacre of Muslim residents in the state of Gujarat.

Modi faced accusations of turning a blind eye to the slayings and even offering his support.

Even as he faces protests, though, Modi remains enormously popular in India, consistently ranking as one of the most popular leaders in the world. A survey this month from the magazine India Today found that he is also the top choice for prime minister in India, despite slipping approval ratings.

Still, outreach campaigns to rehabilitate the image of the RSS overseas have had limited success.

For instance, a 2024 survey found that, while Modi enjoyed near-majority support among Indian Americans for his performance as prime minister, 70 percent of respondents acknowledged that his rhetoric exemplified a growing threat to minorities in India.

Bhagwat’s planned appearance at Madison Square Garden has likewise ignited debate over his controversial commentary and leadership.

In a statement on Wednesday, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), an independent initiative within the federal government, called for Bhagwat’s visa to be revoked.

The commission warned that Bhagwat was “complicit in religious freedom violations”, along with other RSS members and Indian officials.

“Religious freedom conditions in India continue to deteriorate as violence and incitement are frequently used to target religious minority communities,” said USCIRF Chair Asif Mahmood. He urged the US to implement targeted sanctions.

When questioned about Bhagwat’s speech at a news conference this week, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani also spoke out against the RSS’s messaging.

“It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision of any country, frankly. And it is one that I find myself in deep opposition to,” Mamdani said, citing his identity as an Indian American.

He added that he does not “support the rally” but said he doubted the city had the jurisdiction to cancel a private event.

Ahmed, the community organiser from North Carolina, said she feels the backlash to Saturday’s event reflects a growing coalition in the Indian diaspora — one that brings together Hindu, Muslim, Sikh and unprivileged-caste voices.

“There is a vocal minority in the diaspora and a new, emerging majority who don’t believe in the politics of Modi and the RSS and who don’t want to see them gain traction here,” said Ahmed.

She predicted that Saturday’s event will ultimately backfire. “I’m very confident that Bhagwat will be met with a resounding rejection that he is not welcome.”

articles.title: Star student rejected by 16 colleges, hired by Google, gets legal win in racial discrimination suit
articles.excerpt:
A Palo Alto, California, family's Title VI lawsuit clears a major legal hurdle as a judge rules sovereign immunity was abrogated for their claims.

A father in Palo Alto, California is declaring a vic...
articles.body_text:
A Palo Alto, California, family's Title VI lawsuit clears a major legal hurdle as a judge rules sovereign immunity was abrogated for their claims.

A father in Palo Alto, California is declaring a victory in court after a federal judge allowed a civil rights lawsuit alleging anti-Asian bias in college admissions to move forward.

Nan Zhong and his son, Stanley Zhong, filed federal lawsuits against several elite institutions — including the University of California system, the University of Washington, the University of Michigan, and Cornell University. The complaints allege the universities engaged in "racially discriminatory admissions practices that disadvantage highly qualified Asian-American applicants."

One of their cases will now proceed in part against the University of Washington after a federal judge granted the university defendants' motion to dismiss in part and denied it in part.

"We got an exciting ruling from the judge," Nan Zhong told Fox News Digital. "Effectively, the judge ruled in our favor by denying the university's motion to dismiss. So this is a major development in the lawsuit. That means the judge found enough factual allegations to support our allegation."

DUKE LAW'S ALLEGED RACE-BASED ADMISSIONS ACCUSED OF DEFYING SUPREME COURT RULING: DOJ

Stanley Zhong graduated from Henry M. Gunn High School in Palo Alto, California with a 4.42GPA and 1590 SAT score. (Nan Zhong)

The ruling centered in part on sovereign immunity. Judge James L. Robart denied the defendants' motion to dismiss Stanley's Title VI claims against the university while dismissing several other claims.

The University of Washington Board of Regents sent Fox News Digital a statement in response to the ruling.

"We're pleased that the court dismissed many of the claims and two of the three plaintiffs. Admission to the Allen School is highly competitive and the vast majority of out-of-state applicants are not admitted because, as Washington’s flagship university, we prioritize Washington residents for admission," a spokesperson said.

"With that ruling, we can now proceed into discovery, request internal documents, internal communication, and most importantly, admissions data," Nan said.

Stanley Zhong, now 21, made headlines after he was rejected by 16 of the 18 colleges he applied to — including top-tier public and private institutions — despite boasting an elite academic record. A 2023 graduate of Gunn High School in Palo Alto, Stanley scored a 1590 out of 1600 on the SAT (99th percentile), held a 4.42 weighted GPA, ranked in the top 9% of his graduating class, and had launched a free e-signing startup featured by Amazon Web Services.

Shortly after the college rejections, Google hired Stanley as a full-time software engineer in a position that his family's court filing says typically requires a Ph.D. or equivalent practical experience. Stanley was first scouted by the tech giant in coding competitions when he was just 13 years old.

CALIFORNIA SOCIOLOGY PROFESSOR CITED 'IRONY' IN REMOVING ACT/SAT, NOT FIXING RACIAL DISPARITIES AS INTENDED

Stanley Zhong received a job offer from Google before graduating high school. (Nan Zhong)

The family spent over a year researching admissions trends before filing the lawsuits, concluding that anti-Asian bias remains a systemic issue despite recent court precedents.

"The story is much bigger than myself, than my son, Stanley, or our family," Zhong told Fox News Digital. "First of all, I have a younger son, so I don't want him to face the same problem that his older brother faced. I think this is something important we should correct so my future grandkids won't have the same problem again."

Zhong added that since taking their battle public, dozens of families across the country have reached out to share similar experiences.

"After the story came out, we received a lot of communication from other Asian-American families telling us about their story, telling about how highly qualified Asian-American students were rejected left and right," Zhong said. "So this is a large-scale issue and I think of it as an issue that's been around for a long time."

CALIFORNIA BOARD OF REGENTS TO REVIEW SAT/ACT TESTING BAN AFTER 1,400 PROFESSORS WARN OF ‘SEVERE’ MATH GAPS

Stanley Zhong's father, Nan, says his son faced racial discrimination after he was rejected by 16 colleges he applied to. (Nan Zhong)

Spokespersons for the University of California system have previously denied the allegations, maintaining that their admissions policies strictly comply with state and federal laws prohibiting race-conscious decisions.

Stanley Zhong was accepted at the University of Maryland and the University of Texas-Austin but decided to take a job offer as a software development engineer at Google in the fall of 2023 instead.

Joshua Q. Nelson is a reporter for Fox News Digital.

Joshua focuses on cultural trends, education, and public policy. He extensively covered reparations developments across the U.S., the Department of Education, and immigration issues.

Joining Fox News Digital in 2019, he previously graduated from Syracuse University's Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs and received the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton Public Policy Certificate.

Story tips can be sent to joshua.nelson@fox.com and Joshua can be followed on Instagram, Twitter and LinkedIn.

articles.title: Ex-Hillary Clinton staffer warns Democrats that courting far-left could cost them Jewish voters
articles.excerpt:
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel told The Atlantic’s "David Frum Show" podcast that Democrats risk driving Jewish voters from the party if their concerns about antisemitism are dismissed.

Michig...
articles.body_text:
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel told The Atlantic’s "David Frum Show" podcast that Democrats risk driving Jewish voters from the party if their concerns about antisemitism are dismissed.

Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel this week issued a blunt warning to Democratic leadership ahead of the upcoming midterms: Stop minimizing Jewish voters’ concerns, or they’ll walk. Former Hillary Clinton staffer Kaivan Shroff agreed, saying the issue is whether Jewish Democrats will feel like they have to "explain or defend a basic part of their identity to remain in good standing with the party."

Appearing on the Atlantic’s "David Frum Show," Nessel accused the Democratic Party of not valuing its Jewish constituents and making them feel less welcome than members of other minority groups.

"I think it’s a fundamental mistake for the Democratic Party to think that you can just push Jewish Democrats out and simply replace them with any other population," Nessel told Frum on Wednesday’s podcast episode.

DEMOCRATIC MICHIGAN AG ACCUSES HER PARTY OF 'ABSOLUTELY NOT' DOING ENOUGH TO COUNTER ANTISEMITISM

Michigan AG Dana Nessel. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Nessel's comments were echoed by Shroff, a media commentator and former digital organizer for Hillary Clinton's 2016 presidential campaign. Shroff told Fox News Digital that Democrats risk losing key Jewish voters as the party grapples with internal divisions over its ideological direction.

"What Nessel is saying should make Democrats nervous because this isn’t really a debate about Netanyahu or even Israeli policy — it’s about whether Jewish Democrats are starting to feel like they have to explain or defend a basic part of their identity to remain in good standing with the party," Shroff told Fox News Digital. "Ironically, Democrats cannot afford to keep shrinking their political tent in the name of expanding it to folks like Hasan Piker — and then act surprised when pieces of the coalition start walking out."

Shroff added that Democratic leaders should stop courting socialist-aligned candidates and start shoring up the establishment supporters who have long defended the party — especially ahead of the midterm elections.

"Of course, Nessel is a prominent Democrat in Michigan — a state where a lot of this debate has now centered around Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and his affiliation with streamer Hasan Piker, who has made controversial comments that many other Democrats have just condemned as antisemitic," Shroff said. "It’s a critical Senate seat for Democrats to win and they need all their voters and more to show up. So turning off loyal Democrats like Nessel is a huge issue and should be causing major alarm."

MICHIGAN'S DEMOCRATIC AG REFUSES TO ATTEND UPCOMING CONVENTION OVER HARASSMENT CONCERNS

According to Nessel, Jewish Democrats have felt ostracized by their own party following the attacks in Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and accused leadership of cherry-picking issues that are relevant to supporters.

"When a Black person says that a phrase that you’re using or the way you’re talking about this issue to me is racist, I’d like you to stop doing it — we respect that," Nessel said on The David Frum podcast.

JEWISH HOUSE DEMOCRAT RECALLS COLLEAGUE SAYING THERE IS NO ANTISEMITISM BECAUSE 'ALL THE JEWS ARE RICH'

Nessel then pointed to what she said was a discrepancy in how members of her party handle concerns raised by Jewish voters.

Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel addresses the Michigan Democratic Party People's Town Hall in Warren, Mich., on March 29, 2025. (REUTERS)

"This has been an outlier to me," Nessel said. "I have people saying, ‘You are not going to tell us what you deem to be antisemitic. We’ll decide what’s antisemitic. That’s not up for you, the Jewish population, to decide.’"

"I find that to be very off-putting and offensive," she continued. "I think that’s totally unacceptable."

BATYA UNGAR-SARGON EXPLAINS WHY SO MANY AMERICAN JEWS BECAME DEMS — AND WHY SOME NOW FEEL POLITICALLY HOMELESS

Following her condemnation of the Democrats’ treatment of Jewish constituents’ concerns regarding antisemitism, Nessel added that if faced with the choice, she would choose her Jewish heritage over her party affiliation.

"If that’s the deal that has to be made, and I’ve been really candid about this, I was Jewish before I was ever Michigan attorney general — I’m going to be Jewish afterwards," Nessel said.

MICHIGAN DEMOCRATIC SENATE CANDIDATE CLAIMS ISRAEL 'JUST AS EVIL' AS HAMAS

Abdul El-Sayed speaks to supporters at his Get Out to Vote rally in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 3, 2026.  (JEFF KOWALSKY/AFP via Getty Images)

"I was Jewish before I was ever a member of the Democratic Party, and if I have to, I’ll be Jewish afterwards too," she continued.

Nessel also took aim at Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, for previous comments he made following an attempted terrorist attack on a synagogue in West Bloomfield earlier this year, in which he remarked, "Hurt people do hurt people."

MICHIGAN SENATE RACE: EL-SAYED’S TIES TO EXTREMIST FUEL ANTISEMITISM CONCERNS AMONG JEWISH VOTERS

"A lot of us perceived that as sort of making excuses for someone that sought to murder over 100 pre-K schoolchildren and that’s the kind of mentality that bothers me a lot," Nessel said.

She added that although El-Sayed has met with Jewish leaders in the community, his unwillingness to retract his previous comments is cause for concern and risks amplifying such views.

Nessel did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment. Fox News Digital also reached out to the El-Sayed campaign for comment.

Piker previously told his viewers, "If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews."

Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who is Jewish, called out Piker this week in response. In a social media post. She wrote, "This shouldn’t be hard: no community should face the threat [of] violence for their political views. Period,"

Slotkin continued, "That goes if you’re pro-Israel, pro-Palestine, pro-choice, pro-life or any other cause you care about. And blaming the victims of violence for bringing it on themselves only further endangers people."

Julia Bonavita is a media and culture writer for Fox News Digital, and a Fox Flight Team drone pilot. You can follow her at @juliabonavita13 on all platforms and send story tips to julia.bonavita@fox.com.

articles.title: 'The Dog Stars' Review: Jacob Elordi fights for survival in Ridley Scott's dull post-apocalyptic western
articles.excerpt:
The trailer for 20th Century Studios' "The Dog Stars" starring Jacob Elordi, Josh Brolin, Margaret Qualley, Guy Pearce, Benedict Wong and Allison Janney. Directed by Ridley Scott.

Ridley Scott has di...
articles.body_text:
The trailer for 20th Century Studios' "The Dog Stars" starring Jacob Elordi, Josh Brolin, Margaret Qualley, Guy Pearce, Benedict Wong and Allison Janney. Directed by Ridley Scott.

Ridley Scott has directed some of Hollywood's most iconic movies, from "Alien" and "Blade Runner" to "Thelma & Louise" and "Gladiator." But over the past decade, his films have mostly ranged from OK to meh.

Unfortunately, his latest falls in the latter category.

"The Dog Stars," adapted from Peter Heller's 2012 novel, follows Hig (Jacob Elordi), a mechanic trying to navigate a post-apocalyptic America that had been ravaged by a deadly flu years earlier. He has taken shelter at an abandoned Colorado airport and is joined by Bangley (Josh Brolin), a brutish former Marine with great aim, and Hig's Belgian shepherd, Jasper.

‘MUTINY’ REVIEW: JASON STATHAM TAKES NO PRISONERS IN MINDLESS BUT AMUSING BRAWLER FLICK ON THE HIGH SEAS

Jacob Elordi as Hig and Jasper in 20th Century Studios' "The Dog Stars."  (Fabio Lovino. © 2026 20th Century Studios. All Rights Reserved.)

The routine is as follows: Hig flies into Denver in his little yellow plane to seek supplies, stops by his old house, triggering flashbacks of his late wife, occasionally makes deliveries to a rural community of Mennonite farmers, and sometimes joins Bangley in killing trespassers who may be infected with the virus before burning their bodies as a precaution.

Hig thinks there is more civilization beyond the mountains, namely in Grand Junction. Bangley thinks it's a fool's errand and that leaving Eric would certainly lead to death. But Hig can't deny his own convictions, so he ultimately decides to seek life elsewhere.

‘THE END OF OAK STREET’ REVIEW: ANNE HATHAWAY, EWAN MCGREGOR FIGHT DINOSAURS IN SURPRISINGLY FUN MOVIE

Josh Brolin as Bangley in 20th Century Studios' "The Dog Stars." (Fabio Lovino. © 2026 20th Century Studios. All Rights Reserved.)

He'll come across some interesting characters on his journey, like the boorish rancher Jack and his daughter Cima (Guy Pearce and Margaret Qualley) and the eccentric Darlene (Allison Janney). There's also what's been dubbed the "Reapers," a group of tatted savages who will kill and destroy anything in their path.

The cast does a fine job. Elordi, the Australian up-and-comer known for his breakout role in HBO's "Euphoria" and appearing more recently in "Wuthering Heights" and Netflix's "Frankenstein" (which earned him his first Oscar nomination), is flexing his leading man muscles. Both Brolin and Pearce earn a few laughs for their rough-around-the-edges performances. And Janney elevates any project she's in, regardless how zany her character is.

'TONY' REVIEW: ANTHONY BOURDAIN'S COMING-OF-AGE STORY UNFOLDS IN CHARMING DRAMEDY

(L-R) Jacob Elordi as Hig and Margaret Qualley as Cima in 20th Century Studios' "The Dog Stars." (Fabio Lovino. © 2026 20th Century Studios. All Rights Reserved.)

However, I never felt strongly invested as a viewer. Except for a few gun battles, "The Dog Stars" was fairly dull. Despite Elordi's best efforts, Hig is a run-of-the-mill dystopian protagonist, so there isn't much to work with (perhaps the source material is to blame).

The guitar-forward score from Harry Gregson-Williams only furthers the film's sleepy western vibe. At least all the mountain scenery was pleasant to look at.

‘SPIDER-MAN: BRAND NEW DAY’ REVIEW: TOM HOLLAND, ZENDAYA RETURN FOR ACTION-PACKED, EMOTIONAL SEQUEL

Jacob Elordi as Hig in 20th Century Studios' "The Dog Stars."  (Photo courtesy of 20th Century Studios. © 2026 20th Century Studios. All Rights Reserved.)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Ridley Scott's "The Dog Stars" is the latest installment in the prolific director's middling stretch of films that will likely leave the mind shortly after viewing. And when that happens, you question why the movie was made to begin with.

"The Dog Stars" is rated R for strong violence and language. Running time: 1 hour, 58 minutes. In theaters now.

Joseph A. Wulfsohn is a media reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to joseph.wulfsohn@fox.com and on Twitter: @JosephWulfsohn.

articles.title: Hilaria Baldwin explains how she stays fit raising 7 kids with ‘bathroom workouts’ and an unexpected diet
articles.excerpt:
The ‘Nation’s Dumbest’ star tells Fox News Digital how she prioritizes fitness while raising seven kids.

Hilaria Baldwin is taking the phrase "squeeze in a workout" to a whole new level.

The 42-year...
articles.body_text:
The ‘Nation’s Dumbest’ star tells Fox News Digital how she prioritizes fitness while raising seven kids.

Hilaria Baldwin is taking the phrase "squeeze in a workout" to a whole new level.

The 42-year-old "Nation's Dumbest" contestant and mother of seven told Fox News Digital her fitness routine doesn’t always happen in a gym — or even in a dedicated workout space. Sometimes, it happens right there in the bathroom.

"I run every day… I found being a mom, if I can get 30 minutes of my cardio, it helps my mind... It gets me like sort of a little bit more regulated with my nervous system, so I really like that," she shared when asked about her go-to workout with a hectic schedule.

HILARIA BALDWIN SHARES MARRIAGE LESSON SHE TELLS FRIENDS AFTER SURVIVING 'UPS AND OUR DOWNS' WITH ALEC BALDWIN

Hilaria Baldwin detailed the unconventional workout routine and diet habits she uses while raising seven children. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images)

"Then I obviously do my yoga, my little bathroom workouts, or just like a stop-and-drop little workout. I love Physique 57. Any kind of barre classes I think are really great."

And Hilaria isn’t just talking about quick bathroom sweat sessions.

Last month, she gave her fans a front-row look at exactly what those workouts can look like, showing off her physique in a bikini while demonstrating glute exercises in a bathroom.

Baldwin's routine included squats and leg raises.  (Hilaria Baldwin Instagram)

HILARIA BALDWIN FLAUNTS FIT FIGURE IN BIKINI AS FANS MARVEL AT MOM OF 7

Despite her fitness-focused lifestyle, Hilaria insisted she isn't living exclusively on lettuce.

"It's not always the same," Hilaria said when asked what a typical day of meals looks like.

"I think people think that I just eat salad all the time, which I’ve definitely done that in the past. But the other day — the baby of the family, we opened up pints of ice cream, two different pints of ice cream at 9 PM. So, sometimes it looks like that."

WATCH: HILARIA BALDWIN SQUEEZES IN ‘BATHROOM WORKOUTS’ AS A MOM OF 7

She added, "Eat good things and then enjoy. Have the slice of pizza once in a while. Have the ice cream. I think it’s just a bit of a balance."

When Fox News Digital asked if her husband, Alec Baldwin, ever joins her workouts, she laughed and said he’s not the most flexible person.

"Can’t touch his toes. I literally married the most inflexible person I have ever met."

Hilaria Baldwin competed on "Dancing with the Stars." (Getty Images)

'PERFECT' WORKOUT FORMULA CAN TAKE JUST 10 MINUTES A DAY, HILARIA BALDWIN SAYS

After more than 15 years together, seven children and plenty of public scrutiny, Hilaria shared the relationship advice she said has helped keep her longtime relationship strong.

"Oh, it’s been more than 15 years. We met February 2011. You both have to want to be there," she told Fox News Digital.

WATCH: HILARIA BALDWIN REVEALS WHAT KEPT MARRIAGE TO ALEC BALDWIN STRONG THROUGH 'UPS AND DOWNS'

"Whenever my friends are coming to me, and they’re like it’s a new relationship, or they’re having a bump in it, I say, ‘if both people don’t really want to be there through your difficult moments, through your best moments, then it’s just not going to probably work out,’" the TV personality explained.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Hilaria Baldwin joined husband Alec at the opening of Planet Hollywood Times Square in New York earlier this month. (Kevin Mazur)

"Both Alec and I, through our ups and our downs and our sideways, we’ve wanted to be there. And I think that that’s what’s kept us strong."

Hilaria's candid comments come as she appears on FOX's celebrity competition series, "Nation's Dumbest."

WATCH: HILARIA BALDWIN PUSHES BACK ON BIGGEST MISCONCEPTION ABOUT HER

The show flips the traditional celebrity competition formula on its head: contestants aren't fighting to prove they're the smartest in the room. They're trying desperately to avoid being crowned the dumbest.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Hilaria Baldwin appears on FOX's "Nation's Dumbest." (Brendan Meadows / Fox)

Hilaria joins an eclectic cast that includes Carmen Electra, Anthony Michael Hall, Ice-T, Elle King, Matt Leinart, Dr. Drew Pinsky, Steve-O, JoJo Siwa, Andrew Yang, Jon Heder and Chase Hudson.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Alec and Hilaria Baldwin share seven children.  (Jason Mendez/WireImage)

At home, Hilaria and Alec have their own seven-member Baldwin brood: daughters Carmen, María and Ilaria, and sons Rafael, Leonardo, Romeo and Eduardo.

Alec is also the father of daughter Ireland Baldwin, whom he shares with ex-wife Kim Basinger. Ireland became a mother herself in 2023 when she welcomed daughter Holland, making Alec a first-time grandfather.

"Nation's Dumbest" airs on Wednesdays at 9:00 PM ET/PT on FOX.

Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Stunned couple unearths 150-pound mystery hidden beneath their backyard for decades
articles.excerpt:
San Francisco residents Greg Gatwood and Judy Gittelsohn revealed to Fox News Digital that they discovered a mysterious 150-pound stone sculpture buried in their backyard.

A couple in San Francisco r...
articles.body_text:
San Francisco residents Greg Gatwood and Judy Gittelsohn revealed to Fox News Digital that they discovered a mysterious 150-pound stone sculpture buried in their backyard.

A couple in San Francisco recently unearthed a 150-pound limestone sculpture buried in their backyard — setting off a search to uncover who created it and how it got there.

Greg Gatwood was doing yard work at the couple's Russian Hill home in May when he came across what he initially thought was a piece of concrete buried in the ground as his partner Judy Gittelsohn stood nearby.

Gatwood told Fox News Digital he tried to pry the object loose with a shovel before grabbing a pickaxe — and then spotted what appeared to be lips and a nose "peering" back at him.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MYSTERIOUS FACE HIDDEN FOR CENTURIES IN BOOK OF REVELATION CITY

"I thought, well, maybe I should just break it into smaller pieces," Gatwood said. "Then I realized it was a statue.

"It was like something you see in a movie, almost cinematic, you know — a big beautiful statue like this."

A San Francisco couple was stunned to uncover a 150-pound limestone sculpture buried in the backyard of their Russian Hill home. Greg Gatwood is shown at right brushing off the sculpture.  (Judy Gittelsohn)

Gittelsohn said she was stunned when Gatwood showed her the enormous, two-foot-wide statue — and was impressed by the quality of its craftsmanship.

"I was just shocked," she said. "What an enormous find."

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MASSIVE ARTIFACT DEPICTING PHARAOH THOUGHT TO HAVE CHALLENGED MOSES IN EXODUS

She added, "I was surprised. I was just gobsmacked."

Three months after their discovery, the couple is still searching for answers.

The couple is searching for answers about the genesis of the mysterious limestone sculpture — and how it ended up buried in their yard. (Judy Gittelsohn)

Gittelsohn, a professional artist, said she researched the sculpture. She believes it dates to the 1930s and may be connected to artists working under the Works Progress Administration (WPA).

The couple's home is near the former San Francisco Art Institute, where prominent sculptor Ralph Stackpole taught for decades — leading Gittelsohn to believe the piece may have a connection to him or one of his students.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

One clue supporting that theory, she said, is that the sculpture was carved from relatively inexpensive limestone rather than costlier materials such as marble or granite.

Gatwood believes the statue may have been used as garden art and that it was eventually buried with time.

The limestone sculpture weighs about 150 pounds and measures roughly 2 feet wide, according to the San Francisco couple who discovered it. (Judy Gittelsohn)

"It's quite possible this statue was displayed in the garden and not so much buried, but just lost," he said.

After the couple received local attention for their find, Gittelsohn said a 93-year-old woman took an Uber to their home with her walker and knocked on their door.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The woman — one of several people who have reached out to the couple since the discovery became public — told them she had previously held a show featuring Ralph Stackpole's work.

Judy Gittelsohn and Greg Gatwood spoke with Fox News Digital about the mysterious discovery they made in their San Francisco backyard. (Fox News Digital)

In September, the couple plans to put the sculpture on public display at the American Messenger Gallery in hopes that someone may recognize the piece or know who created it.

"We think someone will eventually recognize it," Gatwood said.

The story of this enormous sculpture comes about a year after a different couple made a mysterious discovery in their backyard as well.  (Judy Gittelsohn)

The story comes about a year after a New Orleans couple made a similarly mysterious discovery in their backyard.

At the time, Daniella Santoro and Aaron Lorenz unearthed an ancient Roman funerary artifact that had been missing from an Italian museum for decades.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

articles.title: Royal Navy spent three days tracking Russian vessels in UK waters
articles.excerpt:
Three vessels and a helicopter deployed to monitor four ships travelling through the North Sea to the Channel

The Royal Navy spent three days tracking Russian vessels as they passed through UK waters...
articles.body_text:
Three vessels and a helicopter deployed to monitor four ships travelling through the North Sea to the Channel

The Royal Navy spent three days tracking Russian vessels as they passed through UK waters, it has emerged.

The “intense” 72-hour operation took place last week, with radars used to monitor four ships that made their way from the North Sea through to the Channel.

The fleet was surveilled by HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn, with a Merlin helicopter providing support, officials said.

The Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko was observed escorting the cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta, which are under sanctions, towards Dover.

In response, Russia deployed its own military resources, including the Neustrashimy frigate, to guard the shipment. Gen Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord, said there was “no room for complacency” as shadow fleet vessels continued to pose “an unacceptable risk” to UK security.

“Alongside our allies, this approach is forcing Moscow to divert Russian warships away from their core purpose,” he said. “That is because Russia knows we stand ready to act again, should it be required.”

The Royal Navy recently warned of increasing Russian activity in UK waters. In July, it spent 21 days monitoring ships from Moscow, an increase of 25% compared with the previous year. Officials say they have repeatedly observed warships in the Dover strait and the North Sea.

In June, the Royal Marines seized the Russian tanker Smyrtos, the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel, one of more than 500 that have been sanctioned by the UK.

The Kremlin has threatened the UK after Andy Burnham visited Kyiv this week in his first overseas trip as prime minister. During the trip, Burnham said the UK would provide Ukraine with military support, including blueprints for components of long-range Scalp missiles.

Although western officials have tried to play down the prospect of direct conflict between Russia and Nato, the Kremlin has accused the UK and its allies of “playing with fire” in relation to their continued support for Ukraine.

Andrei Fedorov, a former Russian foreign minister, said he could not “100% exclude” the possibility of “semi-military” action against Britain in retaliation, raising the prospect of an attack on British drone factories from “unknown sources”.

Nearly 400 people have been evacuated after a Russian strike on a warehouse near Kyiv killed at least 37 people, Ukrainian authorities have said.

Videos showing the moment of a huge explosion and the plumes of smoke that followed have been shared online.

The strike hit a depot storing weapons for Ukraine's military near a residential area.
