Man – referred to as MM by court – will keep his identity hidden after legal challenge against suppression dismissed

The identity of a high-profile Queensland man drawn into a Cairns extortion case will remain secret, after the state’s supreme court threw out a legal challenge against a suppression order.

The man – referred to as MM by the court – was drawn into an extortion case earlier this year. He is not a party to the case and is not accused of any offence.

In June, magistrate Gelma Meoli ordered his identity be suppressed to avoid identifying the female alleged extortion victim, known as “the complainant”, after an application by the Queensland police commissioner, Brett Pointing.

Media organisations applied for a judicial review of the decision, arguing that the court did not have the power to suppress his identity.

But Justice James Henry dismissed the challenge on Friday.

articles.title: Seven charged with damaging Trump’s Scottish golf course accused of ‘terrorist connection’
articles.excerpt:
Course at Donald Trump’s Turnberry resort was painted with words ‘Gaza is not 4 sale’ and clubhouse was sprayed with graffiti

Seven people charged with vandalising Donald Trump’s Turnberry golf cours...
articles.body_text:
Course at Donald Trump’s Turnberry resort was painted with words ‘Gaza is not 4 sale’ and clubhouse was sprayed with graffiti

Seven people charged with vandalising Donald Trump’s Turnberry golf course in Scotland have been accused of malicious damage “having a terrorist connection”.

The clubhouse at the five-star Trump Turnberry hotel and resort on the west coast of Scotland was graffitied on 8 March last year and the course was dug up and painted with the words “Gaza is not 4 sale”.

Kieran Robson, 35, Uzma Bashir, 56, Ricky Southall, 34, Autumn Taylor Ward, 22, Rebecca Sian Davies, 29, John Moxley, 58, and Dylan Chiaramello, 24, have all been charged in relation to the action and are due to appear in court on 31 August.

The indictment alleges that the defendants “did maliciously damage property there in that you did maliciously dig up turf on the golf course, spray glyphosate [weed killer] or similar substance on the fairways and greens, spray a building and signpost with paint, paint political and offensive slogans on the grass, score a political slogan into the turf, paint political and offensive slogans on a building, walls and pillars, damage a sprinkler system causing flooding, and damage a light”.

It adds that it will be proved “that the aforesaid offence was aggravated by reason of having a terrorist connection”.

A note of a meeting on 13 March last year between the Scottish first minister, John Swinney, and the US president’s son Eric Trump, said it “noted with concern the recent incident at the Trump Turnberry property, condemning the damage caused by vandalism and offered reassurance that the relevant authorities would continue to take the incident seriously”.

Turnberry’s famous Ailsa golf course has staged the Open four times. Tee times for non-residents are listed at up to £1,000 a head at the Ayrshire resort, which Trump added his name to after buying it from a Dubai-based group in 2014 for an undisclosed sum.

articles.title: What could Meta’s US settlement mean around the world – and what now for other claims against firm?
articles.excerpt:
Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands

In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemis...
articles.body_text:
Other governments could seek similar concessions, while separate legal action is pending in places ranging from Kenya to the Netherlands

In October 2021, Abrham Meareg’s father, a professor of chemistry in Ethiopia’s northern town of Bahir Dar, was shot at close range and died outside his family home. This was in the middle of the country’s civil war.

For weeks, Facebook’s algorithm had actively promoted posts calling for the academic to be murdered, according to Meareg and Foxglove, a nonprofit organisation supporting Meareg’s lawsuit against the company in Kenya. These posts included photos of his father and his home address.

Meareg filed the lawsuit in 2022. He said he repeatedly asked Facebook to remove the posts and the company did nothing. Nearly four years later, the case has still not been heard. Foxglove said Meta, Facebook’s parent company, had “fought tooth and nail to avoid responsibility”.

Meareg said: “It’s a matter of numbers to them, a matter of statistics. It has been proven multiple times that our lives do not matter to them.”

On Wednesday, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by 29 US states who argued it had designed addictive products that hooked young people. The social media company agreed to pay $18bn and to change certain features of its platform in the US. California’s attorney general said it was a victory that would make “a world of difference for children and their families”.

But elsewhere in the world, in jurisdictions as far flung as Amsterdam and Nairobi, other claims have yet to be heard. Far bigger questions about the power of a single US technology company to shape politics and democracy everywhere on Earth are still to be answered.

For the US, the settlement is a victory. A jury has done what the US Congress could not – put controls on a powerful tech company. As a part of the settlement, Meta has said it will set time limits on children’s use of its platforms Facebook and Instagram and block night-time usage.

For Meta, the settlement is also a victory. Its share price rose in the hours after the deal was announced. Its CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was not forced to testify. The sum it is to pay, while not meaningless, is far less than the states had sought – $200bn – or the amount Meta itself had suggested in a court filing it might have to pay, which was up to $1.4tn.

For the rest of the world, however, the picture is more mixed. The limits Meta will put on its US platform are, in large part, similar to limits the UK and Australia have already achieved through regulation. There are certain concessions Meta has now made that other governments could also demand: for example, while the UK plans to ban under-16s from social media platforms, it may wish to ask Meta to impose a default daily use limit of two hours for under-18s, which is what the company has agreed to in the US.

None of this meaningfully changes the equation for Meareg or what his case represents, which is that a massive US company, unaccountable to voters, unbound by transparency requirements, owns a worldwide digital commons that shapes reality for billions of people.

Whether courts and governments outside the US have the power to confront this fact is a far thornier question.

The central issue of Meareg’s case is Meta’s algorithm. This is the system that decides what content to show users of Facebook and Instagram. It sees you linger over a video about knitting sweaters, for example, and then decides you’ll like one about how to care for your spider plant.

It sees teenage girls watch diet content and shows them anorexia influencers. It sees young men search for bodybuilding content and shows them Andrew Tate. It is alleged to have amplified content that promoted the ethnic cleansing of the Rohingya in Myanmar. It contributed to the election victory of Donald Trump.

Meareg’s lawsuit rests on the claim that this algorithm promoted the posts that called for the death of his father, and that Facebook’s sparse moderation in east Africa did almost nothing to prevent this.

In the early days of the Meta trial in the US, it seemed plausible that states would push the social media firm to finally make some changes to this algorithm. Those changes had the potential to fundamentally alter how the company does business. Meta’s algorithm is intended to keep users scrolling, stuck on the platform, and then it shows them ads.

But that is not what appears to have happened. The terms of the settlement will slightly change what is shown to minors, in that they will not necessarily have personalised feeds. But it is hard to see this concession changing the equation in war zones or creaking democracies.

Arturo Béjar, an ex-Facebook employee and whistleblower, said the limitations were “the equivalent of saying: ‘Well, you can smoke as many cigarettes as you can in two hours a day.’ It doesn’t make the cigarettes any safer.”

It may be up to groups and individuals elsewhere in the world to try to push for these larger changes. It will be an uphill struggle.

In Kenya, the high court recently ruled that Meareg’s case against Meta could go ahead, after years of legal manoeuvring from the company to try to prevent it. It could now be heard in the next year.

Rosa Curling, Foxglove’s co-executive director, said: “Meta’s lawyers have spent years trying to prevent this important case being heard, thankfully without success. We hope that the news from the US is a sign that Mark Zuckerberg’s time is finally up.”

In the Netherlands, Repro Uncensored, a nonprofit organisation tracking digital censorship, hailed the US settlement as a “major victory”. Repro Uncensored has an ongoing legal case against Meta in the Netherlands for alleged discrimination against queer accounts, and plans further action in other European countries.

Martha Dimitratou, Repro Uncensored’s executive director, said: “The next stage of accountability must address not only addictive design but algorithms, discriminatory moderation and automated decision-making. These systems shape civic participation and democracy, and the companies controlling them must be held accountable globally.”

The European Commission released a charge sheet against Meta this summer saying the company’s features, including its infinite scroll, contributed to “unhealthy habits and compulsive use”.

That charge sheet is part of an investigation into Meta that the commission launched in 2024. It may lead to Europe pushing for larger changes from Meta, including to its personal algorithm.

It is unclear whether any of these groups or parties can succeed. Meta appears to fear US regulators and courts: after all, it caved after just four days of its US trial. It does not appear to be as intimidated by regulators elsewhere.

Earlier this year it managed to dodge a class-action lawsuit brought by a group of Rohingya refugees over its alleged role in contributing to a genocide in Myanmar. It will have the help of the Trump administration in opposing any EU regulation that could curb its reach in Europe.

Meta declined to respond to questions about either Meareg’s or Repro Uncensored’s cases. In an earlier response to whistleblower allegations that it fuelled violence in Ethiopia and Myanmar, it pushed back forcefully, saying it was “just not true” that the company put profits over safety. Regarding Meareg’s case, it has said it employs staff with local knowledge and expertise to “catch violating content” in Ethiopia.

Meareg said he believed that Meta expected him to give up. “They don’t know how I am determined for justice,” he said. “It is the thing you do for the person you love. If you love someone – and I loved my dad from my heart – then he needs justice. He needs a public apology. There has to be accountability.”

articles.title: ‘No precedent’: Lorde and Little Simz to star at world-first festival run on clean power
articles.excerpt:
A zero-emission compact hydrogen power plant will drive the main stage at Clifton Down in Bristol

When Lorde, Little Simz and Wet Leg stride on to stages in Bristol this weekend, they will not only b...
articles.body_text:
A zero-emission compact hydrogen power plant will drive the main stage at Clifton Down in Bristol

When Lorde, Little Simz and Wet Leg stride on to stages in Bristol this weekend, they will not only be entertaining tens of thousands of festivalgoers but taking part in what is being billed as a world-first clean power project.

The two stages at Forwards festival on Clifton Down are being driven almost entirely by green power – a combination of hydrogen and mobile batteries charged with sustainable energy.

Across the globe, artists and major festivals have been taking action to make their events more sustainable. But what makes the clean power pilot (CPP) scheme that is driving this weekend’s festival different is that it is backed with regional public money and political will. Over the summer, the CPP has guaranteed a secure source of green mobile power to festivals, events and television film crews.

About a dozen events, including the Bristol Balloon Fiesta, have been powered with help from the CPP. Television shows that have been filmed in Bristol, such as the drama Mavis Eccleston, have tapped into the CPP. The performances of Lorde and the rest this weekend are seen as the pinnacle.

Ben Price, the head of partnerships at Team Love, which is running the festival on the Downs, said it felt like a gamechanger. The geography and geology of the site means the festival cannot access green energy from the National Grid and the economics of producing such events makes it impractical for them to invest in their own temporary energy supply. “We need the backing of public money to de-risk it,” Price said.

CPP grew out of a homecoming gig in Bristol by the trip-hop collective Massive Attack that was credited with producing the lowest-ever carbon emissions for such an event.

Act 1.5, a creative industry project that brings together artists, technicians and scientists, worked with Massive Attack on the gig and was determined to take the concept further.

The West of England mayoral combined authority bought in, providing financial backing while the Greens-led Bristol city council has given its support, as have clean energy providers and the region’s biggest television studio, Bottle Yard in Bristol.

Mark Donne, the lead producer of Act 1.5, said it was a global first. “There isn’t any comparable programme anywhere, in terms of scale, design or sectors procuring and acting together – no precedent or comparison.”

John O’Sullivan, another senior figure in Act 1.5, said it meant many fewer noisy, diesel-guzzling generators at events and sets. “The only thing you notice is the quiet,” he said.

Act 1.5 added that it was working with other mayoral authorities across England to roll the concept out further and there had been international interest.

This weekend, the main stage is being driven by a compact hydrogen power plant set up by GeoPura. The only byproduct of the setup is pure water – which Lorde and other artists who perform there will be invited to sample at the end of their gigs.

A second stage and other areas are driven by battery units topped with electricity from renewable suppliers. These are backed up by generators powered by hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO).

Robert Del Naja, of Massive Attack, said the group’s 2024 show was never meant to be a one-off. He said: “This project was always about systemic change, so it’s gratifying to see this permanent legacy of decarbonisation for all major festivals and film and TV productions in Bristol.

“Looking at the bigger picture, so much time has been wasted by real bases of power – national governments, transnationals and the tactical misdirection of the corporate media – and now the world finds itself surpassing 1.5 degrees and chronically unprepared for wildfires, drought, violent storms and food insecurity.

“Projects like Act 1.5 can be seen as a catalyst for all sectors and civil society more widely. We don’t have to wait for governments to rehabilitate themselves from fossil fuel cartels, or for the White House to someday relocate its mind. We have the imagination, the intelligence and the will to act now, and act with the required intent.”

Jonathan Pryce, who appears in Mavis Eccleston, also backed the project. He said: “This summer, the severe weather events long predicted by climate scientists have become a vivid reality. Drama, music and art are activities that allow us to understand difficult realities, but they also provide spaces to imagine a better future and find ideas and designs to reach it.”

articles.title: ‘Nature thrives when given a chance’: restored Cheshire wetland now a haven for rare grebe
articles.excerpt:
Woolston Eyes in Warrington, a dumping ground for canal dredgings, has become best place in UK for black-necked grebe

A dumping ground for dredgings from the Manchester Ship Canal has become the best...
articles.body_text:
Woolston Eyes in Warrington, a dumping ground for canal dredgings, has become best place in UK for black-necked grebe

A dumping ground for dredgings from the Manchester Ship Canal has become the best place in Britain for the rare and beautiful black-necked grebe, hosting 64% of Britain’s breeding population.

Since 2021, Woolston Eyes in Cheshire has been restored, extended and turned into a mosaic of freshwater pools, reedbeds, willow scrub and rough grassland, managed by the RSPB and Woolston Eyes Conservation Group.

Wetland areas on a dried-out and overgrown settlement lagoon were revived and nesting islands created, with the aim of attracting black-headed gulls, which black-necked grebes nest beside for protection from predators. The wetlands also provided a new wealth of invertebrate food for the glossy black and chestnut-coloured birds, which sport tufts of gold feathers behind ruby-red eyes.

In 2023, four pairs of black-necked grebes bred on the newly restored area, successfully raising 15 young. By 2025, 35 pairs of black-necked grebes were recorded, 29 of which nested on the newly restored wetland area. The total represents 64% of the average number of breeding pairs recorded annually across the UK.

“It is fantastic to see black-necked grebe numbers increasing at Woolston Eyes thanks to the hard work of staff, volunteers and partners to create prime habitat for this rare and attractive species,” said Gavin Thomas, an RSPB ecologist. “The rapid growth in numbers shows how effective targeted conservation action can be and is a great example of nature thriving when it is given a chance.”

The site of special scientific interest (SSSI) in Warrington is also a stronghold for other rare and unusual species including willow tit, pochard and grasshopper warbler.

While Woolston Eyes relies entirely on rainfall to remain wet, water can be moved between areas so they can be dried out, refreshed and reflooded – a crucial rotation for the black-necked grebe, which will abandon wetlands that become too “mature”.

Thomas added: “Black-necked grebes are just a handful of the millions of breeding, wintering and migratory birds that rely on the UK’s internationally important wetlands. Seeing the number of black-necked grebes continuing to increase at Woolston Eyes makes all the hard work worthwhile.

“It demonstrates that restoring and managing wetlands is vital for species recovery, but we absolutely need to scale this up and deliver far more sites like Woolston throughout the UK.”

articles.title: Fiery views on Lindsay Clancy at work could get you fired — and be perfectly legal, employment lawyer warns
articles.excerpt:
New York lawyer Nicole Brenecki warns that arguing over the Lindsay Clancy case in most workplaces is not protected speech — and could even get you fired.

Sharing fiery views at work about the Massac...
articles.body_text:
New York lawyer Nicole Brenecki warns that arguing over the Lindsay Clancy case in most workplaces is not protected speech — and could even get you fired.

Sharing fiery views at work about the Massachusetts mom accused of killing her three young children could get you canned and still be legal, according to an expert on employment law who is following the case.

Lindsay Clancy, 36, is accused of strangling her children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — and trying to end her own life by dropping from a second-floor window after sending her husband to pick up takeout and something from a pharmacy, according to the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office.

The case has drawn national attention, pro-Clancy protesters to the courthouse and impassioned discussions about who is responsible online after her defense argued she is not guilty by reason of insanity or mental defect.

"That disciplinary measure, it's not on its face illegal if you get fired for starting, you know, fiery speech about Lindsay Clancy and how you support her," said Nicole Brenecki, a New York-based attorney who specializes in employment law.

LINDSAY CLANCY MURDER TRIAL BECOMES SOCIAL MEDIA OBSESSION AS TIKTOKERS, SLEUTHS DEBATE CONTROVERSIAL CASE

Lindsay Clancy is wheeled into Plymouth Superior Court on Friday, Feb. 20, 2026. Clancy became paraplegic when she harmed herself and jumped out of a second-story window at her home after the deaths of her three children. She is charged with murder in the children's deaths. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

Still, Brenecki warned, a fired employee could still raise legal concerns if their Clancy-related statements were used as a pretext to get rid of them for other reasons.

"If a case like this came to the court system, it would not be viewed in the context of the free speech alone," she said. "It would also be viewed in the contexts of employment laws."

Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside of Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 20, 2026. (John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

LINDSAY CLANCY TRIAL: POSTPARTUM IS REAL, BUT CHILD KILLING DEMANDS ACCOUNTABILITY, VETERAN PROSECUTOR SAYS

As a "general rule," however, she said employers would be allowed to prohibit such discussions about the case.

Other considerations would involve whether the speech took place during working hours, disrupted business operations or whether there was discrimination against protected groups involved in the firing.

Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)

"Every single case in our court system is very highly and intensely fact-based," she said. "So we cannot give...any specific explanation as to whether something would be illegal or not. We have to look at the facts."

Still, Brenecki advised against arguing over strong opinions at the water cooler.

Supporters of Lindsay Clancy's pose for a photo outside of Plymouth Superior Court, Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. Clancy is on trial for the murder of her three children in January 2023. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"If you truly want to voice them in a workplace, then be prepared to have to find greener pastures," she said.

There could be other consequences as well. Earlier this month, an attorney named Alex Thomason said in a TikTok video of his own that he has already spoken with men involved in custody disputes with women who have been posting the "solidarity hold a heart thing" for Clancy.

In one instance, he said, he is looking to have a woman's visitation rights stripped away.

"I want to be able to have a forensic psychiatrist interview this woman just to see how wack-a-doodle she is, and we're gonna use her TikTok posts," he said.

LINDSAY CLANCY DESCRIBED A MALE VOICE ORDERING HER TO ‘KILL HER CHILDREN AND KILL HERSELF’: TESTIMONY

Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside of Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 20, 2026. (John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has argued that Clancy was under the effects of postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors allege she acted deliberately and understood what she was doing was wrong.

A Lindsay Clancy supporters dressed in pink outside Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth. Mass., Monday, Aug. 24, 20206. Clancy's murder trial is in its final stages.  (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

Dozens of supporters have rallied outside the courthouse, carrying signs and wearing shirts with phrases like, "Stand in Peace for Lindsay."

LINDSAY CLANCY DIDN'T SHOW 'BREAK WITH REALITY' AS JURY WEIGHS PSYCHOSIS DEFENSE: SUSAN SMITH PROSECUTOR

Jurors began deliberating after both sides delivered their closing arguments Thursday.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Supporters of Lindsay Clancy gather outside of Plymouth Superior Court on Aug. 20, 2026. (John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

PROSECUTOR IN INFAMOUS KILLER MOM CASE SAYS WOMEN ON LINDSAY CLANCY JURY MAY BRING ‘STRANGE TWIST’ TO VERDICT

They will decide whether Clancy is guilty of first-degree murder, second-degree murder or manslaughter in the deaths of her three children — or not criminally responsible by reason of the insanity defense.

WATCH: Jury instructions outline verdict options in Lindsay Clancy trial

Lindsay Clancy listens to the testimony of Dr. Gregory Saathoff during her murder trial in Plymouth Superior Court on Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026 in Plymouth, Massachusetts. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP, Pool)

If convicted of any of the three counts of first-degree murder she faces, Clancy would see a sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.

WATCH: Judge commends attorneys for efforts in 'emotionally taxing' Lindsay Clancy trial

Fox News' Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

articles.title: Suspected human smugglers lead cops on 100-mph chase before bailing and allegedly committing armed carjacking
articles.excerpt: Aerial video shows authorities pursuing suspected human smugglers in Texas before the vehicle was disabled and the occupants fled, with officials saying one suspect later carjacked a civilian at gunpo...
articles.body_text:
Aerial video shows authorities pursuing suspected human smugglers in Texas before the vehicle was disabled and the occupants fled, with officials saying one suspect later carjacked a civilian at gunpoint. (@CBPCommissioner via X)

Two suspected human smugglers led authorities on a 100-mph chase in Texas on Thursday before bailing out of their vehicle, with one allegedly carjacking a civilian at gunpoint, authorities said.

Helicopter video from U.S. Customs and Border Protection's Air and Marine Operations shows the high-speed pursuit unfolding along Interstate 10 in Fabens.

Authorities are seen pursuing the suspected human smugglers before their vehicle was disabled and both occupants fled on foot.

VIDEO SHOWS ILLEGAL ALIENS FOUND CRAMMED INSIDE SEMI-TRUCK SLEEPER CAB IN ALLEGED SMUGGLING BUST

Two suspected human smugglers bailed out of their vehicle after a high-speed pursuit in Texas, authorities said. (CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott via X)

An official can be heard over radio communications saying the vehicle's front right tire may have been damaged by a spike strip.

Moments later, the vehicle slows down and two occupants jump out and run.

"Bail out, bail out, bail out!" someone is heard shouting in the video.

The two men are then seen running across the highway, with one quickly apprehended by a member of the Texas Department of Public Safety.

2 COLOMBIAN NATIONALS ARRESTED IN STOLEN MERCEDES LINKED TO VIOLENT CALIFORNIA CARJACKING

Helicopter video shows authorities pursuing suspected human smugglers during a high-speed chase along Interstate 10 in Fabens, Texas. (CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott via X.)

The other suspect allegedly carjacked a civilian at gunpoint before he was also later taken into custody, authorities said.

Authorities have not released information about how many people were allegedly being smuggled or their nationalities.

"Outstanding coordination by Border Patrol, AMO, HSI and Texas DPS," CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott posted on X alongside video of the pursuit.

"Suspected human smugglers hit 100+ mph and bailed out when their vehicle was disabled," Scott continued. "One then carjacked a civilian at gunpoint. Smugglers risk lives for profit. We will keep taking them down."

The incident took place near a Speedway gas station at around 9:16 a.m., according to KFOX14.

The suspects are expected to face human smuggling and evading arrest or detention charges, the station reported.

One suspect allegedly carjacked a civilian at gunpoint after fleeing a vehicle during a high-speed pursuit in Texas, authorities said. (CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott via X)

Fox News Digital has reached out to U.S. Customs and Border Protection for additional information.

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

Can't Luka Doncic and his Los Angeles Lakers teammates do some team building at a Slovenian nightclub in peace? Can't a former Playboy model also happen to be hanging out there?

The answer to that, apparently, is no. The Lakers trip over the weekend to a Ljubljana restaurant, which reportedly also serves as a nightclub, made news in the Slovenian outlet Nedeljski dnevnik.

Luka Doncic, Bronny James, Austin Reeves and Maxi Kleber look on against the Houston Rockets in the first half of a Western Conference first-round NBA playoff game at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles on Saturday, April 18, 2026. (MediaNews Group via Getty Images)

The exclusive party had strict rules, according to the outlet. There were no pictures or videos allowed inside the nightclub and phones had stickers placed over the cameras.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON’T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Slovenian model Anja Jenko, who appeared on the cover of Playboy back in 2014, was also reported, among others, to have been at the nightclub at the time.

Her attendance became the focus of other headlines, although there were no reports of the model hanging out with any of the players.

Luka Doncic signs an autograph for a fan during the Los Angeles Lakers' visit in Ljubljana, Slovenia, on Aug. 23, 2026. (SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

ADULT ACTRESS MADISON IVY CRASHED A LAKERS PRIVATE DINNER 'THIS MIGHT BE THE GREATEST MOMENT OF MY WHOLE LIFE'

As was already mentioned, this was a team-building event for the Lakers. A business trip, if you will. The Slovenian media even pointed out "the basketball players are said to mostly hang out with each other."

So what are we doing here? Luka is noticeably thinner. He's been dealing with baby momma drama. There's no LeBron James on the Lakers roster, and he can't team build with the guys in his home country?

Luka Doncic of the Los Angeles Lakers reacts from the bench against the Oklahoma City Thunder in Game 4 of the second round of the NBA Western Conference playoffs at Crypto.com Arena on May 11, 2026. (Getty Images)

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

This was supposed to be an exclusive party, stickers on camera for a reason. So a former Playboy model was reported to be in the building. What does this have to do with the Los Angeles Lakers and their superstar?

I can't be the only one who doesn’t see a connection here. When did team building at a nightclub become something more just because a former Playboy model was at the same nightclub at the same time?

Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A California pastor and massage therapist has pleaded not guilty to charges accusing him of molesting two children under the age of 14 over several years, prosecutors said.

David Johnson, 58, of Ojai, faces six felony child molestation charges in Ventura County, according to the Ventura County District Attorney’s Office.

Investigators are also looking for possible additional victims and have publicly asked anyone with information about Johnson or other possible unreported crimes to come forward.

Johnson is accused of molesting two children who were under 14 years old at the time of the alleged abuse.

Prosecutors said the alleged abuse occurred over several years at locations in Ojai and Oxnard.

SAN FRANCISCO ARCHDIOCESE AGREES TO $395M SETTLEMENT WITH 530 CLERGY ABUSE SURVIVORS

David Johnson, 58, of Ojai, Calif., faces six felony child molestation charges involving two children under 14. (Ventura County Sheriff's Office)

Johnson, who worked as both a pastor and massage therapist, had access to the children through a familial relationship, according to prosecutors.

Authorities have not publicly identified the children.

Johnson faces four felony counts of committing a lewd act upon a child and two felony counts of continuous sexual abuse.

Prosecutors have also filed special allegations involving substantial sexual conduct and the victims being under 14 years old, according to the district attorney’s office.

EX-TEXAS MIDDLE SCHOOL TEACHER SENTENCED TO 33 YEARS FOR SEXUALLY ABUSING 13-YEAR-OLD STUDENT

The Ventura County District Attorney’s Office has charged Johnson with six felony child molestation charges. (Ventura County District Attorney's Office/Facebook)

Johnson was arrested Monday on charges of child molestation by the Ventura County Sheriff’s Office, according to sheriff’s inmate records.

The records show Johnson was arrested shortly before 3 p.m. and booked into the Ventura County Main Jail later that evening.

Johnson appeared in Ventura County Superior Court for his arraignment and pleaded not guilty to all six charges.

He remains in custody without bail and is scheduled to return to Ventura County Superior Court on Friday for a bail review hearing.

HIGH SCHOOL TEACHER WHO ALLEGEDLY HAD SEX WITH STUDENT IN CLOSET NOW FACES CHARGES INVOLVING MORE TEENS

Johnson was arrested Monday on charges of child molestation by the Ventura County Sheriff’s Office. (Thousand Oaks Police Department)

Deputy District Attorney Cesar Ponce of the Ventura County District Attorney’s Office Sexual Assault Unit is prosecuting the case.

Investigators have not said publicly how many additional victims they believe there could be.

The district attorney’s office is asking anyone with information about the case or other possible unreported crimes involving Johnson to contact Ventura County Sheriff’s Office Detective Michael Loth at 805-384-4745.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Ventura County District Attorney’s Office for additional information.

articles.body_text:
Foreign affairs minister Penny Wong confirms increase to number of Australians missing

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Foreign affairs minister Penny Wong has confirmed the number of Australians missing in the devastating Nepal floods has increased overnight from 35 to 39.

In a statement, Wong said the government was “rapidly mobilising consular and humanitarian support in response to the catastrophic floods along the Nepal-China border, including through a $5 million assistance package for affected communities.”

double quotation markWe understand at least 39 Australians are among those reported missing. Australian officials are working urgently to confirm their welfare and provide assistance to those affected.

She said the government would send an initial team of three humanitarian response specialists “within the next 48 hours'” to help Australian staff already on the ground.

double quotation markThe extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery.

Voluntary assisted dying laws have been passed in the Northern Territory jurisdiction following debate over a gag clause barring doctors from raising end-of-life options with patients, Australian Associated Press reports.

The rights of the terminally ill bill passed on a conscience vote in the Northern Territory parliament late last night, with the gag intact.

The territory became the first Australian jurisdiction to make voluntary euthanasia legal in 1995, but the laws were overturned in 1997 by the federal government under John Howard.

All six states and the ACT have since passed their own laws allowing it.

The federal veto was only lifted in 2022, restoring the NT’s right to make its own assisted dying laws.

The NT bill requires that only people predicted by doctors to have 12 months or less to live would have access to assisted dying.

In the NT parliament yesterday government backbencher Tanzil Rahman spoke against the gag clause that would bar healthcare professionals from initiating conversations about end-of-life options with patients.

Elderly patients could be bedridden and dying in an aged-care home in a one-clinic town and it would not be compassionate to prevent them talking to a doctor about end-of -life options, he told parliament on Thursday.

“If the facility says no, that’s it,” Rahman said.

“This cannot be a bill for the rights of the terminally ill if we restrict conversations in these premises.”

Opposition leader Selina Uibo also argued against residents of aged care institutions being denied information, saying they must be allowed to make informed choices about end-of-life options.

The small Himalayan town Keshav Kadel migrated from was not the first to be hit by the floods ravaging his native Nepal, Australian Associated Press reports.

Sitting in the Chitwan district, it is further along the Trishuli River than those more directly in the firing line, such as Gorkha and Rasuwa.

The distance afforded residents more time to flee to higher ground, but it has not been spared the dead.

“What’s happening in my town is that bodies are now flowing in the river,” he told AAP.

“They have slid all the way down and people are pulling bodies from the river.”

At least 360 people have died and hundreds more remain unaccounted for, including 39 Australians, since they began on Wednesday.

Kadel was among members of Nepalese community who gathered yesterday at the Australian Nepalese Multicultural Centre at Diggers Rest north-west of Melbourne, which he serves as vice president.

Families gathered for prayers and held a minute’s silence for those lost to the floods, laying candles beside a hand-crafted display of dyed rice reading “pray for Nepal”.

The diaspora was “united in grief, hope and prayer,” secretary of the centre Sudhir Shakya told the event.

“Behind every number is a person - a mother, a father, a son, a daughter, a relative, a friend, and someone deeply loved,” he said.

articles.title: Jerry Jones has no 'succession plan' for Cowboys leadership: 'Just won't be here to toss my two cents in'
articles.excerpt: Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones said that "contending for a Super Bowl is not a reach" as the NFL enters training camp. Danny Parkins, Eric Mangini, and Greg Jennings ask if the Cowboys are actual co...
articles.body_text:
Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones said that "contending for a Super Bowl is not a reach" as the NFL enters training camp. Danny Parkins, Eric Mangini, and Greg Jennings ask if the Cowboys are actual contenders this season, and if this will be Aaron Rodgers’ last dance. Plus, Ohio State QB Julian Sayin joins the show to discuss his Heisman expectations, playing with Jeremiah Smith, and to determine if the Big 10 is better than the SEC.

Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones is 83 years old and continues to lead the way in the front office of his organization.

But Jones’ age also poses questions about when he will step aside and have a successor take his place at the head of the Cowboys’ table. Stephen Jones, his son who has been heavily involved in the Cowboys’ decision-making for years, seems to be the easy guess for who will take Jerry’s spot one day.

However, if you ask him about his eventual handing of the torch, Jones scoffs at it.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones looks on before the game against the Green Bay Packers at AT&T Stadium on Sept. 28, 2025. (Jerome Miron/Imagn Images)

"I don’t have a succession plan, I don’t. One day, I just won’t be here to toss my two cents in," he told The Athletic.

A comment like that seems to indicate that, until his final breath, Jones will be working to get the Cowboys more Super Bowl rings.

The oil and gas businessman purchased the team for $140 million in February 1989, and the team’s success quickly came thereafter.

JERRY JONES 'OPEN' TO CO-OWNING COWBOYS WITH MARK CUBAN: 'ALL THE RESPECT IN THE WORLD FOR HIM'

The Cowboys won the Super Bowl in 1993, 1994 and 1996, restoring the team’s previous glory after Dallas won Super Bowl VI (1972) and Super Bowl XII (1978) prior to Jones’ ownership.

But the Cowboys have not made it back to the Super Bowl since that 1996 win, and the supporters of "America’s Team" are desperate to see it happen. Each season, it feels the Cowboys have the chance to do so, but they’ve either fallen short in the playoffs, or worse, missed the postseason entirely.

However, the Cowboys remain one of the most valued teams in all of American sports since Jones purchased the club. According to Sportico, the team is valued at an estimated $15.5 billion if he were to sell it today.

Jan 27, 2025; Frisco, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys CEO Stephen Jones, head coach Brian Schottenheimer and owner Jerry Jones pose for pictures after a press conference at the Star. (Tim Heitman-Imagn Images)

Still, fans have been worried over the years whether Jones’ involvement in team affairs has cost them the opportunity to win more rings. And Jones hasn’t been afraid to retort when that notion is brought up by fans and reporters alike.

"I’m not pushing Jerry out by any means, but when that day comes, it’s gonna feel a lot different," Cowboys legendary Hall of Fame quarterback Troy Aikman told The Athletic.

Aikman added that he doesn’t feel Stephen has the same ego that his father has, believing that will "serve" him "well."

Jerry has even said Stephen has been a great right-hand man over the years because he’s kept him in check.

Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones looks on prior to an NFL football game between the Philadelphia Eagles and the Cowboys, Sunday, Dec. 29, 2024, in Philadelphia. (AP Photo/Matt Slocum)

"He’s about as good as anybody I’ve ever been around in giving deference when he should," Jerry explained about his son. "Now, don’t confuse that with lack of intensity. He’ll bite back real hard when he has to. Real hard. He just does it with more grace than I do."

The day will eventually come where Jerry won’t be leading the Cowboys, but it doesn’t sound like it will be anytime soon.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Jury deliberating in trial of Lindsay Clancy, US woman accused of killing her children
articles.excerpt:
Watch: What is postpartum psychosis and why is it central in the Lindsay Clancy trial?

Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

The fate of US mother Lind...
articles.body_text:
Watch: What is postpartum psychosis and why is it central in the Lindsay Clancy trial?

Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

The fate of US mother Lindsay Clancy is now in the hands of a Massachusetts jury, who must decide if she is guilty of first-degree murder - the intentional and premeditated killing of another person - in the deaths of her three children.

For five weeks, the trial has gripped the country as Clancy's lawyers have argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis when she killed her children, who ranged in age from eight months to five years. Clancy does not deny killing her two sons and daughter.

The prosecution argued she made a calculated decision to intentionally murder them.

The jury could find Clancy guilty of first-degree murder, guilty of lesser charges, or not guilty.

The jury of nine women and three men completed their first day of deliberations on Thursday. They will return on Friday.

In the state of Massachusetts, a first-degree murder conviction carries a mandatory life in prison sentence without the possibility of parole.

The jury could instead find Clancy guilty of second-degree murder - committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning - or involuntary manslaughter - causing death because of extreme carelessness. Those convictions, too, would lead to some prison time.

If Clancy is found not guilty by reason of insanity, then she will not be set free, but instead sent to a psychiatric hospital, where she possibly could remain for life.

Key moments in trial of Lindsay Clancy, the mother accused of murdering her three children

Attorneys for both sides made closing arguments on Thursday before the jury began deliberating.

Kevin Reddington, Clancy's attorney, repeated the defence's argument that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed the children with exercise bands at their home and then attempted to end her own life by jumping out of a window. Clancy was paralysed by the attempt and has attended the trial in a wheelchair.

"This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children because she was suffering from a disease and defect," Reddington said, adding that he believed prosecutors were "not going to be able to prove otherwise".

The UK's National Health Service (NHS) defines postpartum psychosis as a rare and  serious mental health illness that can affect someone soon after having a baby, and which should be treated as a medical emergency.

One of the more tense moments of the closing arguments came when Reddington directly addressed the prosecutors and asked them to explain why they tried to prove Clancy's suicide attempt was not serious. The judge interrupted and ordered him to address only the jury.

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague did not dispute that Clancy was mentally ill, but told the jury that the defendant could tell the difference between right and wrong at the time of the killings.

"It's not the system or the DSM that caused her to strangle her kids," Sprague told the jury, referencing the US encyclopedia of mental heath diagnoses, which does not give postpartum psychosis its own classification.

Sprague also said Clancy had an "abundance of care", but had hidden thoughts from doctors about harming her kids.

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org.

In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.

articles.title: Former Gitmo prosecutor likens 9/11 trial delay to 'Frankenstein's zombie court'
articles.excerpt:
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the head plotter, will finally go to trial years after the terror attack.

Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the Sept. 11 terror attacks, and three alleged co-c...
articles.body_text:
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the head plotter, will finally go to trial years after the terror attack.

Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the Sept. 11 terror attacks, and three alleged co-conspirators will finally stand trial in 2028, as the case against them has languished amid lengthy delays and a protracted process that one expert has likened to "Frankenstein's zombie court."

A military judge on Wednesday set the long-delayed trial for June 5, 2028, while establishing deadlines for the case. Much to the frustration of the loved ones of those who died during the attacks, Mohammed and his alleged co-conspirators have been held at a military detention center in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, for more than two decades.

The problem, according to Michael Lebowitz, a former Guantánamo military commissions prosecutor, isn't the evidence against the terror suspects — it's the system.

NEW EVIDENCE IN LOCKERBIE PAN AM FLIGHT 103 BOMBING CASE PUSHES FEDERAL JUDGE TO POSTPONE TRIAL

Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks, has been held at Guantánamo Bay since 2003. Mohammed and three of his alleged co-conspirators are expected to stand trial in June 2028, nearly three decades after the terror attacks. (Getty Images)

"It's the system and how it evolved and was created. And it's also an issue of Guantánamo Bay itself, where Gitmo is an adequate, albeit expensive, option for things like detaining suspected war criminals and even migrants," Lebowitz told Fox News Digital.

"The problem is that we used to call it the traveling circus because, in order to even conduct the smallest court hearing, everybody has to go to Washington, D.C., and get on an airplane," he continued. "I'm talking judges. I'm talking prosecutors, defense counsel, witnesses and court people."

TRUMP TURNS TO 'ZOMBIE' COURT AFTER BOASBERG POINTED TO IT IN DEPORTATION FIGHT

The case of Mohammed, as well as Walid bin Attash, Mustafa al-Hawsawi and Ammar al-Baluchi, has been delayed for decades amid lengthy legal wrangling, including failed efforts to resolve the case through plea agreements.

The 2028 date sets a timetable for a case that has remained in pretrial proceedings for years as the military commission has addressed disputes over evidence and other legal issues before a trial on the merits can begin, Fox News Digital previously reported.

NEW 9/11 MUSEUM EXHIBIT AIMS TO CONNECT YOUNGER AMERICANS TO THE ATTACKS THROUGH POWERFUL ARTIFACTS

This Wednesday, Jan. 21, 2009 sketch reviewed by the U.S. military, shows, from top left, Khalid Shaikh Mohammad; Walid bin Attash; Ramzi bin al Shibh; Ali Abdul Aziz Ali, also known as Ammar al Baluchi, and Mustafa al Hawsawi attend a hearing at the U.S. Military Commissions court for war crimes at the U.S. Naval Base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. On Friday, Aug. 30, 2019, a military judge set Jan. 11, 2021 for the start of the long-stalled war crimes trial of the five men being held at the Guantanamo Bay prison on charges of planning and aiding the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. (AP Photo/Janet Hamlin, Pool)

Mohammed, a Pakistani citizen, is accused of masterminding the attacks in which hijackers crashed commercial airliners into the World Trade Center in New York City and the Pentagon. A fourth hijacked plane, United Airlines Flight 93, crashed in Pennsylvania after passengers attempted to overtake the hijackers.

The case has had more than 10 judges, Lebowitz said, meaning lawyers have had to keep relitigating the same "mundane" issues. Lebowitz, an Army veteran, participated in a number of cases in Guantanamo, including the 9/11 case and the bombing of the USS Cole.

TRUMP ADMIN INVOKES 30-YEAR DORMANT TERROR COURT AS IT SEEKS TO DEPORT AFGHAN WOMAN TIED TO ELECTION DAY PLOT

"What I found was that the way the system has kind of been set up and how it evolved and turned into, it's essentially a candy store for defense lawyers, where the judges don't have teeth to control the courtroom like you would in federal court," he said. "It just goes from there where defense lawyers can really grease up the system and grease up the gears and really grind it to a halt."

One issue prosecutors will have to iron out is whether to seek the death penalty, Lebowitz said. Even if Mohammed and the other suspected terrorists are condemned to death, it's highly unlikely to be upheld, he said.

I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES

Two flags flutter on a fence in front of lower Manhattan and One World Trade Center at the Tear Drop 9/11 Memorial at sunset on June 13, 2026, in Bayonne, New Jersey. (Gary Hershorn/Getty Images)

"You're dealing with cases where, essentially, the defense lawyers would put the CIA on trial for their treatment of detainees after 9/11," he noted.

In 2024, Mohammed, bin Attash and al-Hawsawi agreed to admit their roles in the terror attacks in exchange for serving life sentences and avoiding the death penalty. While some 9/11 families supported the idea, others blasted the deal.

Amid the criticism, the Biden administration withdrew the plea deal, resulting in more litigation.

Fox News Digital's Brittany Miller contributed to this report.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

articles.title: Democrats to investigate ‘miraculous’ rise of Trump Jr’s investment firm
articles.excerpt:
Congressman Jamie Raskin asks president’s son to detail firm’s recent success after he joined 1789 Capital as partner

Democrats on a powerful US congressional committee have launched an investigation...
articles.body_text:
Congressman Jamie Raskin asks president’s son to detail firm’s recent success after he joined 1789 Capital as partner

Democrats on a powerful US congressional committee have launched an investigation into a venture capital firm which has thrived since recruiting Donald Trump’s son.

Donald Trump Jr joined 1789 Capital as a partner just days after his father won a second term in office in November 2024. Congressman Jamie Raskin, ranking member of the US House of Representatives judiciary committee, has asked the president’s son to detail the firm’s recent success.

The Guardian previously reported that after Trump Jr joined 1789 Capital, its assets under management ballooned: going from a reported $150m in 2024, to $1bn last August, to $2.7bn at year’s end, to a reported $3.5bn by May, according to SEC filings.

A significant proportion of that capital came from foreign investors, according to CNN reporting and the Guardian’s review of SEC filings. Forty per cent of assets under management were from overseas investors.

In a letter to the US president’s son, and the founders of the firm – Omeed Malik and Christopher Buskirk – judiciary committee Democrats have asked for records that include companies that have received investments from the firm and any communications with any US elected official or federal government officials by 9 September. However, in the minority, Democrats have little subpoena power without Republican support for their cause.

“Two years ago,” Raskin wrote, 1789 Capital was “a struggling venture capital firm that earned consistently disappointing results by serially investing in total market flops” but has since undergone a “miraculous transformation”.

“With Don Jr’s new leadership role, 1789 Capital has developed an uncanny ability to identify companies that are about to receive massive influxes of cash from the Trump administration or to benefit from significant changes in federal policies and regulations,” the top Democrat wrote. “They say there is no such thing as a sure thing in investing, but this is about as close as you can get.”

In a statement to the Guardian, AJ Merton, counsel for 1789 Capital, called the allegations leveled by Democrats “unsubstantiated talking points”.

“Repackaging press clippings on congressional letterhead does not turn news headlines into evidence,” he added. “And that practice is a hallmark of partisan stunts and politically motivated harassment, not oversight.”

Raskin also argued “it is now impossible to believe” that the firm’s “astonishing growth and success are due to anything other than insider political influence and thoroughgoing corruption”.

The ranking member outlined a series of reports of recent investments by 1789 Capital that include millions of dollars in Vulcan Elements, a rare earth company, in August 2025. Before this, the manufacturer had reportedly touted several government contracts they had secured months prior. Raskin then notes that the Pentagon announced a $620m direct loan to Vulcan Elements in November last year. At the same time, the Department of Commerce (DoC) provided the company with a $50m grant under the Chips and Science Act – legislation signed by former president Joe Biden.

“This was an amazing turn of events when the Trump Administration decided to pump over half a billion dollars into an unproven startup company,” Raskin wrote.

He also pointed to a recent July interview with CNBC in which the US president said that his children have “inside information” due to the fact his policies touch nearly every part of the economy.

“I tell my kids, ‘stay away,’” Trump said at the time. “But they also have a life. You know, they were doing business long before I ever thought of running for president.”

In an interview with the New York Times last month, Trump Jr said he only talks to his father, the president, “every few weeks”, and never discusses business with him and – as a private citizen – holds “no policy position and no role within the administration whatsoever”.

Raskin’s letter also cites reporting from the Guardian that Anduril Inudstries, a major military contractor founded by Trump ally and donor Palmer Luckey, has received billions in government contracts over the last year. 1789 Capital, the judiciary Democrats note, has acquired a stake in the company. Anduril says in Trump’s first year in office it doubled its revenue – a growth rate of 100%.

Earlier this month, the Guardian also reported that two appointments to the Defense Policy Board, a key Pentagon advisory body, include two men with ties to 1789 Capital.

Andreessen Horowitz, one of Silicon Valley’s largest venture capital firms, co-invests in three defense contractors alongside Trump Jr’s firm. The other appointee, Blake Masters, also sits on the boards of three ventures tied to 1789 Capital.

Both men now advise the Pentagon on the defense-technology sector those companies operate in.

Footage captures the outbreak of violence inside the ballroom, the heated confrontation in the entryway, and the frantic moments police arrived to restore order as guests fled.

A long-running feud between two families boiled over at an Ohio wedding, triggering a sprawling brawl that left guests injured, drew police from several departments and ended with three men under arrest.

FOX 8 in Cleveland reported that Ali Wahdan, 47, Raed Mahmoud Sulaiman, 46, and Abdallah Wahdan, 48, were arrested following the Aug. 21 fight at the La Centre Banquet Facility in Westlake.

Sulaiman, of Dearborn Heights, Michigan, was charged with assault, inducing panic and tampering with evidence after police accused him of threatening guests with a butter knife and tossing it aside as officers arrived.

BRING THE BEAR SPRAY TO THE WEDDING — YOU NEVER KNOW WHEN YOU NEED TO USE IT ON A FAMILY MEMBER

Wahdan was charged with violating a temporary protection order, while Abdallah Wahdan, of Westlake, was charged with aggravated menacing for allegedly threatening other guests.

Surveillance footage shows a fight outside the La Centre Banquet Facility in Westlake, Ohio, where police said longstanding tensions between two families boiled over during a wedding celebration. (Westlake Police Department)

Fox News Digital obtained 911 calls, body-camera footage and other video showing how the fight unfolded, beginning inside the banquet hall before spilling into the parking lot.

NORTH CHARLESTON OFFICER ATTACKED BY CROWD IN VIRAL VIDEO AFTER GUNFIRE ERUPTS AT BLOCK PARTY

"There’s a fight at our venue," the banquet hall’s general manager told a 911 operator, describing "a bunch of people" fighting inside and outside.

"Someone’s bleeding," he added, telling the operator that one man with a head injury was in a bathroom as the fight continued.

Body-camera footage shows a wedding guest speaking with police outside the La Centre Banquet Facility in Westlake, Ohio, after a brawl broke out during an Aug. 21 wedding celebration. (Westlake Police Department)

STAMPEDE ERUPTS AT SOUTH CAROLINA BIKER FESTIVAL, 19 INJURED IN LATE-NIGHT CHAOS

When asked what was behind the brawl, the manager said it involved relatives.

Another 911 call captured shouting in the background, while a separate caller pleaded for police and said he had been attacked.

FIVE PLEAD GUILTY TO CHARGES IN BRUTAL CINCINNATI BEATDOWN THAT WENT VIRAL LAST SUMMER

"Somebody started beating me," the caller said.

Dashcam footage from the night of Aug. 21 shows an officer arriving at the venue to find a crowded parking lot filled with vehicles and people dressed for the wedding. As the response grew, Westlake police called for additional officers and requested help from neighboring departments.

Dashcam footage shows a crowd gathered outside the La Centre Banquet Facility as police arrive to break up a brawl during an Aug. 21 wedding celebration in Westlake, Ohio. (Westlake Police Department)

WATCH: SOUTH CAROLINA BLOCK PARTY THUGS WITH MACHINE GUN, SPEAR CHARGED IN MOB ATTACK ON OFFICERS, POLICE SAY

Body-camera footage shows officers moving through the crowd and trying to keep groups separated as guests poured out of the venue.

One man approached an officer to make a police report and said his group had been attacked while dancing.

CALIFORNIA FAMILY MEMBERS CLAIM THEY WERE ATTACKED AT LUXURY MAUI RESORT DURING VIOLENT MELEE

"We were dancing and four brothers jumped on us," he told police during the encounter captured on the officer’s body camera.

Cellphone video shows guests inside the La Centre Banquet Facility in Westlake, Ohio, as a brawl broke out during an Aug. 21 wedding celebration. (Westlake Police Department)

Cellphone video from inside the ballroom captured another part of the brawl as screams broke out among guests. A man in a suit, identified by police as Sulaiman, could be seen holding what appeared to be a butter knife as several men rushed toward him and struggled to restrain him.

TEEN BRAWL INSIDE IN-N-OUT SENDS CUSTOMERS RUNNING DURING MONSOON STORM, VIDEO SHOWS

Chairs were knocked over as nearby guests moved away from the confrontation.

Paramedics were called to treat injured guests as officers worked to bring the scene under control.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Police Capt. Jerry Vogel told FOX 8 that officers knew people had already been injured but did not initially know whether anyone had a weapon.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Once the groups were separated, investigators began piecing together what sparked the fight. Police said alcohol was not a factor and instead pointed to longstanding bad blood between the two families.

Investigators said Ali Wahdan was subject to a temporary protection order involving members of a family at the wedding and was required to leave when he encountered them.

"Under the law, if you see this person, even if you’re there accidentally at the same time, you have to leave," Vogel said. "It is your responsibility to leave."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Police said Wahdan instead remained at the venue, allegedly helping set the confrontation in motion.

Despite the brawl, injuries and three arrests, the wedding was not over. Once officers restored order, the celebration resumed without further trouble.

The charges against the three men were filed in Rocky River Municipal Court.

Greg Wehner is a reporter for Fox News Digital covering U.S. news and crime, with a focus on breaking developments, law enforcement, public safety and major stories shaping communities across the country.

articles.title: WATCH: Man accused of aiming flamethrower at officers serving eviction notice in wild bodycam video
articles.excerpt: Bodycam video shows deputies scrambling from an Oklahoma City apartment after a man allegedly ignited an aerosol-fueled flamethrower while they served an eviction order. Credit: Oklahoma County Sherif...
articles.body_text:
Bodycam video shows deputies scrambling from an Oklahoma City apartment after a man allegedly ignited an aerosol-fueled flamethrower while they served an eviction order. Credit: Oklahoma County Sheriff's Office

A routine eviction call turned into a fiery standoff when an Oklahoma man allegedly blasted deputies with a makeshift flamethrower while a wired car-battery device sat inside his apartment, body-camera video shows.

Body-camera video released by the Oklahoma County Sheriff’s Office captures deputies forcing their way into the dark, cluttered Oklahoma City apartment on Aug. 11 after the tenant, identified as Darron Dunn, 61, allegedly barricaded the entrance.

Deputies had arrived to serve an eviction order shortly before noon. Housing Authority staff unlocked the door, but it would not open all the way. Officers said they found cables connected to the door and an electric wheelchair positioned behind it.

NYC LANDLORD PLEADS FOR HELP AS '9-YEAR-SQUATTER' CONTINUES TO DRAIN HIM DRY IN COURT SAGA: 'TWILIGHT ZONE'

Oklahoma County sheriff’s deputies attempt to enter an Oklahoma City apartment while serving an eviction order. (Oklahoma County Sheriff's Office)

Once inside, a deputy spotted Dunn sitting in a bedroom. The incident report notes Dunn immediately sprayed an aerosol can toward the deputy and a Housing Authority security officer, then allegedly lit it on fire.

The bodycam video showed a bright orange flash as the burst of fire filled the doorway.

"Back up!" an officer can be heard yelling as deputies retreated.

LIVE EXPLOSIVE DEVICE FOUND NEAR HOMELAND SECURITY OFFICE IN CLEVELAND, FORCING MASS EVACUATIONS

A burst of flames erupts inside the apartment during the eviction response, according to authorities. (Oklahoma County Sheriff's Office)

Authorities said the deputy felt the "extreme heat" from the flames. The sheriff’s office said the fire traveled about 15 feet in the deputy’s direction.

As deputies backed out, officers spotted a car battery with wires attached near Dunn, and another wired device near the front door. The video captured the growing alarm inside the apartment.

WATCH: EVICTION STANDOFF TURNS TO WAR ZONE AS GUNMAN KILLS DEPUTY IN AMBUSH, GETS RUN OVER BY ARMORED VEHICLE

"He’s got it hooked up to the battery!" one officer shouted.

"Everybody out! Improvised device! Get out!" another could be heard yelling.

NORTH CAROLINA MAN ARMED WITH FLAMETHROWERS, CROSSBOWS, 500 ROUNDS ARRESTED OUTSIDE CHURCH: POLICE

Oklahoma County sheriff’s deputies stand inside the apartment while serving an eviction order on Aug. 11, 2026. (Oklahoma County Sheriff's Office)

According to the incident report, the device consisted of rows of butane lighter-fluid and carburetor-cleaner aerosol cans taped together with bare wires attached.

Deputies evacuated residents from the third floor and nearby levels while the sheriff’s tactical team and bomb squad responded.

Officers later disabled the wires connected to the cans and safely removed Dunn from the apartment in his wheelchair, authorities said.

NYPD OFFICER SHOT, GUNMAN KILLED AFTER ARMED BARRICADED STANDOFF IN BROOKLYN: POLICE

A spokesperson for the Oklahoma County Sheriff’s Office told Fox News Digital that bomb technicians determined the wired aerosol-can device was unlikely to explode as configured. The spokesperson said it could have sparked or heated up if the bare wires touched the car-battery terminal, but technicians did not believe it would detonate.

Dunn was taken to a VA hospital because of medical issues and stress before being placed in a mental hospital, according to the incident report.

Out-of-custody charges were filed against Dunn for assault and battery with a dangerous weapon; possessing, using, manufacturing or threatening to use an incendiary device or explosives; and obstructing an officer.

The sheriff’s office spokesperson said evictions can be "so emotionally charged" and deputies sadly see volatile reactions during such calls. The spokesperson said the confrontation came four years after officers were attacked in another similar eviction-related incident.

In a separate eviction call about a year ago, the spokesperson said, a man allegedly tried to set a deputy on fire before setting himself ablaze and dying.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

"Practical Magic" star Stockard Channing made her red carpet return for the first time in two years after settling into a reclusive life in the United Kingdom.

Channing, 82, basked in the flashing lights while attending the European premiere of "Practical Magic 2" at the Odeon Luxe Leicester Square in London Aug. 26.

Earlier this year, Channing confessed she's "happy being a recluse" as she reflected on her quiet lifestyle after leaving the United States following the death of her longtime partner.

‘GREASE’ STAR STOCKARD CHANNING SAYS SHE’S ‘HAPPY BEING A RECLUSE’ AFTER LEAVING AMERICA

Stockard Channing returned to the red carpet for the first time in years ahead of the "Practical Magic 2" release. (Lia Toby)

The actress, who reprised her role as Aunt Franny in the highly anticipated sequel, sported a chic blue suit with a white button-down and chain-link jewelry to mark her red carpet return.

The following day, Channing turned heads in a monochrome emerald green ensemble for a London photo call. The "Practical Magic" sequel brings stars Nicole Kidman, Sandra Bullock and Dianne Wiest back together 28 years after the original film's release.

Channing began living in London "just before COVID," a move she envisioned after the 2014 death of her partner of 25 years, producer Daniel Gillham.

"I've lived alone since I lost Daniel and I'm happy being a recluse," Channing wrote in an essay for The Sunday Times. "I was married four times before Daniel, and they all represent epochs of me."

"Practical Magic 2" is set for a September debut, 28 years after the original film was released. (Hoda Davaine)

She admitted that Gilham's death "was more devastating than I realized; it had a lag effect."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"The pattern of my life shifted, so I shifted my life from Maine," she wrote of the move, which also vaguely coincided with Trump's second presidential bid.

Her days of stardom are slightly different from now. The "Six Degrees of Separation" actress detailed her morning routine, which begins at 7 a.m. when her dog wakes her up.

By 10 a.m., Channing pursues a "bit of exercise" but admitted that her "favorite exercise days are when I play hooky."

Stockard Channing recently admitted she's "happy being a recluse" after moving to the United Kingdom. (Kate Green)

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I know that exercising is the right thing to do but my brain tells me to go hide behind the bike sheds," she wrote. "Lunch is my first meal of the day and I can follow a recipe, but if my ramen doesn't work out I give it to the dog.

"If I'm leaving the apartment I comb my hair, but I don't have a wardrobe of designer outfits. Well, I do, but they're all from the Eighties and Nineties. Do I care how I look? Most actors do although part of your job is not being self-conscious.

"But I've never considered myself as beautiful. And I'm not a celebrity 'tart.' I'm just me, take it or leave it."

articles.title: Trump executive order bans some foreign equipment in US energy grid
articles.excerpt:
United States President Donald Trump has declared a national emergency over what his administration describes as security risks linked to foreign-made equipment used in the US electricity grid.

Trump...
articles.body_text:
United States President Donald Trump has declared a national emergency over what his administration describes as security risks linked to foreign-made equipment used in the US electricity grid.

Trump signed an executive order on Wednesday that restricts the purchase and installation of certain foreign-produced equipment used in the bulk-power system.

The order cited an “unusual and extraordinary foreign threat” from foreign-made systems, saying they could create vulnerabilities for US national security.

The directive targets certain bulk-power system equipment as well as related software and digital capabilities that the Trump administration said could create cybersecurity or operational risks.

The Department of Energy has 120 days to publish formal rules implementing the policy. In the meantime, experts are watching utility companies, which face the enormous task of compiling an inventory list of equipment flagged by the Trump administration.

“Blocking new purchases is the easy part. Knowing what’s already running is where the real work starts,” John Bruggeman, virtual chief information security officer of the telecommunications company CBTS, told Al Jazeera. “Utilities running foreign-sourced grid equipment … have a live compliance clock starting today.”

The move is the latest effort by the White House to address potential foreign security threats against the grid. Last year, US experts reported finding undisclosed communication devices in some Chinese solar power inverters. In July, the Federal Communications Commission banned all new foreign-made power inverters designed with remote communication capabilities and operating within the electric utility grid.

Still, the order does not prohibit all foreign-made equipment used in the US electricity system. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has been directed to establish conditions for the continued use and operation of affected equipment.

“The executive order establishes the authority to act,” Michael Centrella at the cybersecurity company SecurityScorecard, told Al Jazeera. “The difficult next step will be giving operators scalable, independent visibility into which assets and vendor relationships present the greatest risk without disrupting the reliability of the power system.”

articles.title: Zambia opposition leader questioned over ‘treason’ amid election fallout
articles.excerpt:
Zambia’s main opposition leader Brian Mundubile, who was runner-up in this month’s disputed presidential election, is being questioned by police over alleged treason.

⁠Mundubile and his running mate,...
articles.body_text:
Zambia’s main opposition leader Brian Mundubile, who was runner-up in this month’s disputed presidential election, is being questioned by police over alleged treason.

⁠Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, are in police custody after ⁠being questioned “in connection with an alleged offence of treason”, the Zambia Police ⁠Service said on Thursday.

Zambian state media said Mundubile surrendered to police in Lusaka on August 27, after spending two weeks at an international human rights organisation, where he sought safety after a police raid at his home the day after the country’s August 13 elections.

The two were interviewed by a team of police officers alongside their lawyers. Police did not immediately provide further details of the allegations underpinning the treason investigation. They said that “warn and caution” statements ⁠had been recorded, a ⁠step typically preceding formal charges.

Treason is a serious offence in ⁠Zambia and carries severe penalties upon conviction.

The developments follow an escalation from two weeks ago, during which former cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot and killed during the police crackdown in which 11 people were arrested at Mundubile’s home.

Police said the group were involved in alleged insurrection or militia activity, an accusation Mundubile has denied.

President Hakainde Hichilema won 60 percent of the vote and is due to be sworn in as president for a second term on Tuesday. The election results were disputed by opposition leaders.

Mundubile, who won about 38 percent of the vote, promised to challenge the result in court, but Zambia closed its entire judiciary on Monday, the last day for filing an objection, citing “security reasons”.

Under Article 103 of the Zambian Constitution, an election petition must be filed within seven days of the winner being declared.

Filing the challenge automatically pauses the presidential swearing-in under Article 104.

Shutting the courts before that seven-day deadline expired physically blocked the opposition from filing, preventing the automatic pause on the inauguration.

The Constitutional Court said on Tuesday it had not received any petition challenging the election outcome, clearing the way for Hichilema to be sworn into office.

However, Chief Justice Mumba Malila said he had received a petition from a member of the public on his private email address.

He called the submission “highly irregular” but said he had referred it to the Constitutional Court for consideration.

Legal and rights groups have criticised the timing of the abrupt closure of the courts.

Human Rights Watch (HRW) said it was “a blow to the administration of law, transparency, and due process in Zambia”.

Hichilema entered the race as the clear favourite after steering Zambia, Africa’s second-largest copper producer, through a major economic turnaround and restructuring its debt.

Opposition parties and civil society organisations have raised concerns over increasing repression by Hichilema’s government.

Rights groups and election observer missions have said the post-election dispute has tarnished Zambia’s democratic reputation.

Every change of president since the return to multiparty politics in 1991 has been achieved through elections.
